name: Inter-American Counter-Terrorism Network
description: Secure intelligence-sharing network established by the Organization of American States (OAS) through its Inter-American Committee against Terrorism (CICTE). The Inter-American Counter-Terrorism Network (IACT) aims to facilitate real-time operational information sharing among designated national authorities to prevent and counter terrorism in the region. Participation is voluntary; beneficiary countries connect through a secure online platform with a 24/7 contact directory. As of 2024, 34 OAS member states are listed as beneficiary countries of the IACT Network across the Americas.

name: Counter Terrorism Group
description: Intelligence-sharing group established in response to the September 11, 2001 attacks as an offshoot of the Club de Berne. The Counter Terrorism Group (CTG) focuses on sharing intelligence related to terrorist threats, particularly those stemming from Islamic extremism. It provides threat assessments to EU policymakers and serves as a platform for expert collaboration among member services. While the CTG operates outside the formal EU institutional framework, it maintains communication with EU bodies through the EU Intelligence Analysis Centre (EU INTCEN), a branch of the European External Action Service. The CTG's presidency rotates in alignment with the EU Council presidency. In 2016, the CTG established a permanent cooperation platform in The Hague, Netherlands, to facilitate real-time information exchange and joint operational efforts among member states.

The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) in The Hague verifies compliance and oversees destruction of declared stockpiles.
notes: As of 2024, 193 states have ratified or acceded. Non-parties are Egypt, Israel, North Korea, and South Sudan; Israel has signed but not ratified. Syria acceded in September 2013. Palestine acceded on 17 May 2018. The OPCW implements and verifies the convention.

They are also the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
notes: The acronym NWS is standard in non-proliferation discourse. This record covers only the five NPT-recognized nuclear-weapon states, not other nuclear-armed states outside that treaty framework (India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea). notes: Originally 34 state parties; the United States withdrew in November 2020 and the Russian Federation withdrew in December 2021, leaving 32 parties. Member states adopted a declaration on denuclearization of the South Atlantic at Brasília in 1994.
notes: Established by UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/41/11 (27 October 1986). Comprises 24 member states in South America and West Africa. Holds periodic ministerial meetings on a rotating presidency basis. The South Atlantic is not itself a treaty-based nuclear-weapon-free zone, though member states are parties to the African Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Treaty and the Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean.

description: International agreement between Iran and the P5+1 (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, plus Germany) together with the European Union to limit Iran's nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief and enhanced IAEA monitoring. Finalized in Vienna on 14 July 2015 and implemented from 16 January 2016. The United States withdrew in May 2018; Iran announced termination of the agreement on 18 October 2025.
notes: Not a signed treaty under U.S. law; the JCPOA reflects political commitments between Iran, the P5+1, and the EU. Negotiations built on the 2013 Joint Plan of Action interim agreement. Iran agreed to limits on enrichment, centrifuges, and stockpiles, and to IAEA verification at Natanz, Fordow, and Arak; in return UN, EU, and U.S. nuclear-related sanctions were lifted. U.S. withdrawal in 2018 reimposed sanctions and largely nullified the economic provisions. Iran officially terminated the agreement on 18 October 2025, ten years after Adoption Day.

description: Autonomous intergovernmental organisation that provides policy advice, data, and analysis on the global energy system to 32 OECD member countries. Established in 1974 under the International Energy Programme within the OECD framework, the IEA focuses on energy security, market stability, clean energy transitions, and energy efficiency. Member countries maintain mandatory emergency oil stocks equivalent to 90 days of net imports and participate in coordinated emergency releases during supply disruptions.
notes: Membership is limited to OECD member states meeting oil stock, data reporting, and emergency response requirements. An Association country category (since 2015) enables deeper engagement with major emerging economies; 14 countries hold association status. Six countries are in accession as of 2024 (Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Israel, and Romania). The Executive Director is Fatih Birol (since 2015). Headquarters moved from the Château de la Muette to 9 rue de la Fédération in 1996. The IEA hosts secretariats for the Clean Energy Ministerial and Energy Efficiency Hub.

description: International intergovernmental organization of leading natural gas-exporting countries, providing a platform for exchanging experience and information and fostering dialogue between gas producers and consumers. Established at the inaugural Ministerial Meeting in Tehran in May 2001 and constituted as a formal organization in Moscow in December 2008, the GECF Secretariat is headquartered in Doha, Qatar. Member countries collectively hold about 70% of the world's proven natural gas reserves and account for a major share of global gas production and LNG exports.

description: Non-profit, non-governmental organization dedicated to promoting geothermal energy worldwide.
