notes: Original members in 2005 were Burundi, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, and Sudan; Tanzania joined in 2010, Libya in 2011, Djibouti and Uganda in 2012, and South Sudan and Somalia joined later. Eritrea may join. Governance includes a Council of Ministers, an Executive Committee, a Management Committee of utilities, and the General Secretariat. The Independent Regulatory Board (IRB) coordinates cross-border electricity trade; Uganda's cabinet approved hosting the IRB headquarters in Kampala in 2023. Four synchronized grid clusters operate in the region as of 2019.

name: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
recognition_status: Intergovernmental organization established at the Baghdad Conference on 14 September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela; OPEC Statute entered into force in January 1961; headquarters relocated from Geneva to Vienna in September 1965

secretariat.head: Secretary General
secretariat.organization: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries

description: Intergovernmental organization of major oil-exporting countries coordinating petroleum policies to secure fair and stable prices, an efficient economic supply of petroleum to consuming nations, and a fair return on capital. Founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by five founding members, OPEC is headquartered in Vienna and holds the OPEC Conference as its supreme decision-making body. Member countries collectively account for a large share of global proven oil reserves and crude oil production.

other_names.name: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
Organisation des pays exportateurs de pétrole
Organización de Países Exportadores de Petróleo

notes: The United Arab Emirates withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ effective 1 May 2026 after nearly 60 years of membership. Former members also include Angola, Ecuador, Indonesia, and Qatar. OPEC+ is a separate larger framework formed in late 2016 that coordinates production policy between OPEC members and selected non-OPEC producers such as Russia and Kazakhstan. Canada, Egypt, Norway, and Oman have attended OPEC meetings as observers.

name: Nuclear Suppliers Group
recognition_status: Politically binding multilateral export control arrangement of 48 participating governments; established in 1974 following India's nuclear test; first plenary meetings held in London in November 1975 (informally the "London Club"); implements NSG Guidelines published as IAEA INFCIRC/254 for nuclear transfers and Part 2 for nuclear-related dual-use items; decisions taken by consensus; complements the parallel Zangger Committee under NPT Article III.2

secretariat.organization: NSG Point of Contact (Permanent Mission of Japan to the International Organizations in Vienna)

description: Multilateral export control regime through which 48 nuclear supplier countries coordinate national export policies on nuclear material, equipment, technology, and nuclear-related dual-use goods to prevent proliferation of nuclear weapons. Established after India's 1974 nuclear test and first convened in London in November 1975; commonly known as the "London Club". Participating governments implement two sets of NSG Guidelines (IAEA INFCIRC/254) covering nuclear and dual-use items; the arrangement is politically binding but not a treaty.

official_documents.name: NSG Guidelines for Nuclear Transfers (IAEA INFCIRC/254, Part 1)
NSG Guidelines for Nuclear-Related Dual-Use Transfers (IAEA INFCIRC/254, Part 2)
The Nuclear Suppliers Group — Its Guidelines, Origins, Structure, and Role (IAEA INFCIRC/539)

notes: No permanent secretariat; administrative support and the NSG point of contact are provided by the Permanent Mission of Japan to the International Organizations in Vienna. The rotating NSG Chair is held by a participating government for one-year terms. Guidelines were first published in 1978 as IAEA INFCIRC/254; Part 2 dual-use controls were added in 1992.

name: African Petroleum Producers' Organization
recognition_status: Founded in Lagos, Nigeria on 27 January 1987 as the African Petroleum Producers Association (APPA); reorganized and renamed the African Petroleum Producers Organization (APPO) in 2017
description: Intergovernmental forum of African oil-producing countries promoting cooperation, knowledge sharing, and harmonization of petroleum policies. Founded in Lagos in 1987 as the African Petroleum Producers Association and renamed APPO in 2017, the secretariat is headquartered in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo. Works to advance hydrocarbon research, energy security, and sustainable development across the continent.

other_names.name: Organización Africana de Productores de Petróleo
Association des producteurs de pétrole africains
Organização dos Produtores Africanos de Petróleo

notes: Venezuela has observer status since 2021. Organizational reforms include the Africa Energy Investment Corporation (AEIC) and the Africa Energy Bank initiative. Eight founding members joined at the 1987 Lagos meeting; membership has since expanded to 18 African producer states.

name: Clean Energy Ministerial
recognition_status: High-level global multilateral forum of energy ministers established in 2010; institutional framework adopted in 2016 at CEM7 (San Francisco) as CEM 2.0, aligning work with the Paris Agreement and UN Sustainable Development Goals; independent multilateral secretariat hosted by the International Energy Agency in Paris since 2016

secretariat.head: Head of Secretariat
secretariat.organization: Clean Energy Ministerial Secretariat (hosted by the International Energy Agency)

description: High-level global forum that promotes policies and programs to accelerate the deployment of clean energy technologies. The Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM) facilitates collaboration among member countries to share best practices and encourage the transition to a global clean energy economy. Established in 2010, CEM comprises 29 countries and the European Commission, collectively representing 90% of installed clean power generation capacity and 80% of global clean energy investments. The CEM Secretariat is hosted by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris, France.
notes: Governance includes a rotating Steering Committee of member governments, annual ministerial meetings hosted by rotating member countries, and voluntary technical initiatives and campaigns. The secretariat was initially housed in the U.S. Department of Energy (2010–2016) before moving to the IEA in Paris. Since 2016, Mission Innovation ministerial meetings have been co-located with CEM meetings.

name: Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean
recognition_status: Treaty-based regional organization under the Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean (Treaty of Tlatelolco), signed 14 February 1967 in Mexico City; first nuclear-weapon-free zone treaty covering a densely populated region; entered into force through progressive ratification beginning 22 April 1968; Cuba was the last regional state to accede (ratified 2002); OPANAL has United Nations General Assembly observer status
description: Intergovernmental organization established under the Treaty of Tlatelolco to ensure the prohibition of nuclear weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean. Signed on 14 February 1967 in Mexico City, the treaty created the world's first nuclear-weapon-free zone covering a densely populated region. OPANAL verifies treaty compliance, convenes biennial General Conferences of its 33 member states, and maintains the Council and Secretariat in Mexico City. Member states commit not to develop, manufacture, store, or acquire nuclear weapons and not to permit testing or stationing of nuclear weapons on their territory.

other_names.name: وكالة حظر الأسلحة النووية في أمريكا اللاتينية ومنطقة البحر الكاريبي
Organismo para la Proscripción de las Armas Nucleares en la América Latina y el Caribe
Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean
Organismo para la Proscripción de las Armas Nucleares en la América Latina y el Caribe
Organismo para a Proscrição das Armas Nucleares na América Latina e no Caribe
拉丁美洲和加勒比禁止核武器组织

official_documents.name: Treaty for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean (Treaty of Tlatelolco)

notes: Governed by a General Conference (ordinary sessions every two years), a Council, and a Secretariat headed by the Secretary General, all elected by the General Conference. First Secretary General was Leopoldo Benites of Ecuador. Flávio Roberto Bonzanini of Brazil was re-elected Secretary General in September 2021. Cuba was the last country in the region to accede, ratifying in 2002. Official working language is Spanish. The OPANAL website (opanal.org) was under renovation as of 2026.

name: Southern African Power Pool
recognition_status: Regional power pool established in August 1995 through an Inter-Governmental Memorandum of Understanding signed at the SADC summit in Kempton Park, South Africa; governed by four agreements covering intergovernmental, inter-utility, operating-member, and operating-guideline frameworks; first power pool established in Africa

secretariat.location: SAPP Co-ordination Centre, 24 Golden Stairs Road, Emerald Hill, Harare, Zimbabwe

description: Regional power pool coordinating cross-border electricity trade and grid interconnection among Southern African member states under the Southern African Development Community (SADC). Established in 1995 through an Inter-Governmental Memorandum of Understanding, SAPP was the first power pool in Africa and develops regional generation and transmission infrastructure, synchronizes national grids, and operates competitive electricity markets including day-ahead and intra-day trading. The Coordination Centre is based in Harare, Zimbabwe.
notes: Created at the August 1995 SADC summit in Kempton Park, South Africa; the Revised Inter-Governmental Memorandum of Understanding was signed on 23 February 2006. SAPP is governed by four agreements covering intergovernmental, inter-utility, operating-member, and operating-guideline frameworks. Nine countries are interconnected in the synchronized grid; Malawi is scheduled to connect by end of 2025, with Tanzania and Angola planned for connection by 2028. Operating members include national utilities such as Eskom, ZESCO, and BPC; non-operating members include Malawi (ESCOM), Angola (RNT), and Tanzania (TANESCO). Governance includes an Executive Committee of utility CEOs, a Management Committee, four sub-committees (Environmental, Markets, Operating, Planning), and the Coordination Centre Board. SAPP established the Short-Term Energy Market in April 2001 and the day-ahead market in December 2009, later adding forward physical and intra-day markets.

name: International Energy Forum
recognition_status: Established in Paris in July 1991 as an informal producer-consumer ministerial dialogue; permanent Secretariat opened in Riyadh in 2002; IEF Charter signed at an Extraordinary Ministerial Meeting in Riyadh on 22 February 2011, formalizing the global energy dialogue framework
description: Neutral inter-governmental forum for energy dialogue among producing, consuming, and transit countries. Established in Paris in July 1991 as an informal ministerial dialogue; member states signed the IEF Charter in Riyadh in February 2011. The permanent Secretariat is based in the Diplomatic Quarter of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Coordinates the Joint Organisations Data Initiative (JODI) with partner organizations including IEA and OPEC through a long-standing trilateral work program.
notes: Biennial Ministerial Meetings are among the world's largest gatherings of energy ministers. Member countries collectively account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supply and demand. The IEF coordinates JODI (Joint Organisations Data Initiative) with APEC, EUROSTAT, GECF, IEA, OLADE, OPEC, and UNSD. The `includes` list may not reflect the current full Charter membership roster published by the IEF.

name: Energy Regulators Regional Association
recognition_status: Inter-institutional non-profit association inaugurated on 11 December 2000 in Bucharest by 15 founding energy regulators; legally registered in Hungary in April 2001; secretariat headquartered at Logodi utca 44/B, Budapest
description: Inter-institutional non-profit association bringing together independent energy regulatory bodies from Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Americas to strengthen energy regulation through cooperation, education, research, and information exchange. Founded in Bucharest on 11 December 2000 by 15 regulators and registered in Hungary in April 2001, ERRA is headquartered in Budapest. As of 2026, the association lists about 50 member regulatory organisations across 46 countries on five continents.
notes: Predecessor cooperative platform began in 1998 with 12 regulatory bodies; institutionalised with USAID support from 1999 to 2008 and early technical assistance from NARUC. Founding members were Albania, Armenia, Bulgaria, Estonia, Georgia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russia, and Ukraine. Membership is open to energy regulatory organisations (full and associate categories). ERRA runs training programmes, annual conferences, regulatory committees on grids, markets, and customers in the energy transition, and publishes research papers and regulatory stories.

provenance.note: membership_count counts member energy regulatory authorities; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: Energy Community
recognition_status: Established by the Treaty establishing the Energy Community, signed in Athens on 25 October 2005 and in force since 1 July 2006; extends the EU internal energy market and relevant energy, environment, and competition acquis to Contracting Parties in Southeast and Eastern Europe
description: International organization extending the EU internal energy market to Southeast and Eastern Europe. Contracting Parties commit to implementing relevant EU energy acquis, developing compatible regulatory frameworks, and liberalizing energy markets. The Secretariat in Vienna monitors compliance, supports transposition of legislation, and coordinates institutional bodies including the Ministerial Council, Permanent High Level Group, and Energy Community Regulatory Board.

other_names.name: Energy Community of South East Europe

notes: The European Union is a treaty Party alongside nine Contracting Parties. Armenia, Norway, and Türkiye hold observer status; 19 EU member states participate in institutional meetings without being treaty Parties. Georgia joined as a Contracting Party on 1 July 2017; Moldova and Ukraine acceded in 2010 and 2011 respectively. Bulgaria, Croatia, and Romania transitioned from Contracting Party to Participant status upon EU accession. The Ministerial Council extended the treaty duration to 2026 in October 2013. Regional project offices operate in Kyiv, Chișinău, and Tbilisi.

name: FutureCoal
recognition_status: International non-profit industry association originally established as the International Coal Development Institute in 1985; renamed the World Coal Institute in 1988, the World Coal Association in 2010, and rebranded as FutureCoal in November 2023

secretariat.location: Suite 2.06, Bridge House, 181 Queen Victoria Street, London EC4V 4EG, United Kingdom

description: International non-profit organization representing the global coal value chain. FutureCoal, formerly known as the World Coal Association (WCA), was originally established as the International Coal Development Institute in 1985, renamed to the World Coal Institute in 1988, and to the World Coal Association in 2010, before rebranding as FutureCoal in November 2023. The organization represents major players across the entire coal value chain, advocating for an inclusive international policy framework that supports the rights of all coal-producing and consuming nations. FutureCoal's membership comprises corporate members, associate members, and strategic partners from various countries, including companies engaged in coal production, sale, or use, as well as manufacturers of equipment for the industry, industry associations, and research bodies.
notes: CEO Michelle Manook appointed in 2019. Participates in United Nations and International Energy Agency forums, including the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the IEA Coal Industry Advisory Board, and is part of the Carbon Sequestration Leadership Forum. Membership is corporate and industry-based rather than sovereign; includes lists countries where corporate members and national industry partners are based, per the FutureCoal launch announcement (November 2023). National chapters include a Southern Africa Chapter and an India Chapter (launched 2026).

provenance.note: membership_count counts member companies; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity
recognition_status: Association of European electricity transmission system operators established on 19 December 2008 and operational from 1 July 2009 under mandates in the EU Third Energy Package, including Regulation (EC) No 714/2009 on cross-border electricity exchanges; registered as an AISBL under Belgian law
description: Association of 40 European electricity transmission system operators (TSOs) from 36 countries, coordinating the secure operation of Europe's interconnected power grids — the world's largest synchronized electricity system. Established under EU law through the Third Energy Package, ENTSO-E delivers legally mandated tasks including ten-year network development planning, adequacy assessments, market and transparency platforms, and technical coordination across synchronous areas. The Secretariat is based in Brussels, Belgium.

other_names.name: الشبكة الأوروبية لمشغلي أنظمة نقل الكهرباء
European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity
Red Europea de Gestores de Redes de Transporte de Electricidad
Réseau européen des gestionnaires de réseau de transport d'électricité

notes: The largest interconnected electrical grid in the world. Comprises multiple synchronous areas including Continental Europe Synchronous Area (CESA), Nordic Synchronous Area, and the Irish system, plus isolated systems in Cyprus and Iceland. Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) synchronized with CESA in February 2025. Ukrenergo (Ukraine) became the 40th member TSO on 1 January 2024. Great Britain-based TSOs left on 12 February 2021 following Brexit; only SONI (Northern Ireland) remains from the United Kingdom. Malta has no electricity TSO and is not a member. Türkiye (TEİAŞ) and Moldova (Moldelectrica) hold observer status.

name: World Association of Nuclear Operators
recognition_status: Non-profit membership organisation of commercial nuclear power plant operators, established 15 May 1989 in Moscow after the Chernobyl accident; registered in England and Wales as a company limited by guarantee (No. 2383396); not a regulatory body and does not advocate for the nuclear industry

secretariat.location: Level 11, 5 Churchill Place, Canary Wharf, London E14 5HU, United Kingdom
secretariat.head: Chief Executive Officer

description: Nonprofit international organisation of commercial nuclear power plant operators founded on 15 May 1989 after Chernobyl to maximize the safety and reliability of nuclear power plants worldwide. WANO enables mutual support, exchange of operating experience, and peer review among members; it is not a regulator and does not advocate for the industry. Members operate 400+ nuclear units, with offices in London and Shanghai and regional centres in Atlanta, Moscow, Paris, and Tokyo.

other_names.name: 世界原子力発電事業者協会

notes: Membership comprises operator and owner organisations (120+ members), not sovereign states; includes lists countries with operating commercial nuclear power plants whose operators participate in WANO. US operators are largely represented through the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO). Emerging programmes with units under construction (e.g. Bangladesh, Egypt, Turkey) may hold Category 5 membership but are not listed here. Current CEO is Naoki Chigusa.

provenance.source: Wikipedia (nuclear power by country / IAEA PRIS operating reactors)
derived from includes (countries with operating commercial NPPs)

name: Energy Efficiency Hub
recognition_status: Voluntary government-to-government collaboration proposed at the 2017 G20 Leaders' Summit in Hamburg; established in 2019; IEA Governing Board approved hosting the Secretariat as a Special Activity in 2019; Secretariat operations began in Paris in 2021 with an official launch in December 2021

secretariat.head: Head of Secretariat
secretariat.organization: Energy Efficiency Hub Secretariat (hosted by the International Energy Agency)

description: Voluntary government-to-government platform for global collaboration on energy efficiency, established in 2019 to strengthen deployment of energy efficiency policies through information exchange and best practices. The Hub's 17 member governments collectively account for about two-thirds of global final energy use. Members coordinate through a Steering Committee and thematic Task Groups on digitalisation, appliances and equipment, buildings, energy management, and practical energy-saving solutions. The Secretariat is hosted by the International Energy Agency in Paris, France.
notes: Proposed at the 2017 G20 Hamburg Summit; founding members established a Steering Committee in 2018; IEA Governing Board approved hosting in 2019; Secretariat recruited and launched in December 2021. Membership is open to national governments that are IEA Members, IEA Association countries, or Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM) Members. India joined in January 2025. Governance includes a Steering Committee (one representative per member), a Chair appointed by the Committee (European Commission as of 2024), and three Vice Chairs (Canada, China, and the United States). Task Groups include the Digitalisation Working Group (DWG), Super-efficient Equipment and Appliance Deployment (SEAD), Energy Efficiency in Buildings, TOP TENs, and the Energy Management Action Network (EMAK).

name: Regulatory Energy Transition Accelerator
recognition_status: Launched on 3 November 2021 at COP26 in Glasgow as part of the Green Grids Initiative (GGI-OSOWOG) by Ofgem, the International Energy Agency (IEA), IRENA, the World Bank, RMI, the Regulatory Assistance Project (RAP), and Energy Innovation; the IEA invited to provide coordinating administrative functions
description: Global initiative launched at COP26 in November 2021 to enhance the capacity of energy regulators to accelerate clean energy transitions. RETA works directly with energy regulators worldwide to facilitate knowledge sharing, peer-to-peer learning, and thought leadership on regulatory issues, and serves as a central resource for knowledge products and regulatory tools. Founded by Ofgem, the International Energy Agency (IEA), IRENA, the World Bank, RMI, the Regulatory Assistance Project (RAP), and Energy Innovation as part of the Green Grids Initiative; the IEA provides coordinating administrative functions. More than 60 regulatory authorities from over 40 countries participate.
notes: Focus areas include flexible renewable-based systems, regulatory frameworks for the energy transition, network planning for wide-scale electrification, regional interconnection, and fair and inclusive energy transitions. Activities are delivered through dissemination workshops, bilateral and multilateral exchanges, bespoke technical assistance, and knowledge products. Delivery partners include RAP, RMI, and Energy Innovation. Participating regulatory networks include AFUR, CAMPUT, ERERA, ERRA, ICER, MEDREG, NARUC, OOCUR, and RAERESA. CEER participates indirectly via ICER membership.

name: Central African Power Pool
recognition_status: Specialized agency of the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS/CEEAC), established in 2003 through intergovernmental and inter-utility memoranda of understanding; made an autonomous specialized ECCAS agency by the 12th ECCAS Conference of Heads of State and Government in January 2005

secretariat.location: 14th floor, Namemba Tower, Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo
secretariat.organization: Permanent Secretariat of the Central African Power Pool (PEAC)

description: Specialized agency of the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS) responsible for implementing regional energy policy, developing cross-border electricity interconnections, and organizing power exchanges among Central African member states. One of five African regional power pools, CAPP coordinates national utilities through intergovernmental and inter-utility agreements to build integrated transmission infrastructure and a liberalized regional electricity market.
notes: Governance includes a Council of Ministers for Energy, an Executive Committee of energy ministry directors, a Management Committee of national power utilities, and the Permanent Secretariat in Brazzaville. Public ECCAS and PEAC documentation generally references ten member states; Rwanda also participates according to its national power utility (REG). Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are also members of the Eastern Africa Power Pool (EAPP).

name: World Energy Council
recognition_status: UN-accredited global energy body and UK registered charity; formed in 1923 with a permanent organisation established on 11 July 1924 at the first World Power Conference in London; operates as a UK company incorporated under the laws of England and Wales with a coordinating Global Secretariat in London
description: Global forum for impartial energy leadership and engagement promoting the sustainable supply and use of energy for the greatest benefit of all. Founded in 1923 and formally established in 1924, the UN-accredited World Energy Council convenes governments, industry, academia, and civil society through autonomous national Member Committees across six regional networks. The Council publishes flagship tools including the World Energy Trilemma Framework, World Energy Issues Monitor, and World Energy Scenarios, and hosts the triennial World Energy Congress.
notes: Originated from Daniel Nicol Dunlop's initiative to convene energy experts; the first World Power Conference met in London in 1924 with 1,700 experts from 40 countries. Governance includes an annual Executive Assembly of Member Committees, an Officers Council chaired by Michael Howard (2022–present), and Standing Committees on Strategic Communities, Insights, Communications and Strategy, Finance, and Nominations. Angela Wilkinson has served as Secretary General since 2019. Activities are coordinated through the Global Secretariat in London; WEC Services Limited is a wholly owned UK trading subsidiary. The official member directory lists 67 national Member Committees; the Council reports a presence in nearly 100 countries and over 3,000 member organisations.

name: Biofuture Platform
recognition_status: Government-led, multi-stakeholder initiative launched at COP22 in Marrakech, Morocco, in November 2016 under Brazilian leadership; integrated into the Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM) as the CEM Biofuture Platform Initiative at CEM11 in 2020
description: Government-led, multi-stakeholder initiative established in November 2016 during COP22 in Marrakech to accelerate the development and deployment of sustainable bio-based alternatives to fossil fuels, chemicals, and materials. In 2020, the Biofuture Platform became part of the Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM) as the CEM Biofuture Platform Initiative. The initiative is chaired by Italy (via the Politecnico di Torino), with the International Energy Agency (IEA) serving as Facilitator since February 2019. The platform focuses on fostering consensus on biomass sustainability, promoting policy best practices, enabling supportive financing mechanisms, and promoting cooperation on policy, regulations, and technologies.
notes: Brazil served as interim facilitator from launch until the IEA assumed the facilitator role in February 2019. Official partners include the IEA Bioenergy Technology Collaboration Programme (TCP), IRENA, and GBEP. The initiative operates a Biofuture Industry Council and a 2025–2027 Action Plan focused on sustainable fuels, feedstock carbon-intensity standards, and bio-based chemicals and materials.

name: North American Electric Reliability Corporation
recognition_status: Not-for-profit international regulatory authority designated as the U.S. Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on 20 July 2006 under the Energy Policy Act of 2005; registered as a 501(c)(6) organization; successor to the North American Electric Reliability Council formed in 1968
description: Not-for-profit international regulatory authority ensuring reliability and security of the North American bulk power system. NERC develops and enforces mandatory Reliability Standards, monitors the grid, assesses resource adequacy, and coordinates six regional reliability entities across the Eastern, Western, Texas, and Quebec interconnections covering the contiguous United States, Canada, and northern Baja California, Mexico.

other_names.name: 北米電力信頼度協議会

notes: The North American power grid consists of four major interconnections that operate synchronously within their regions but are linked asynchronously through HVDC ties: Eastern Interconnection (east of Rocky Mountains), Western Interconnection (Pacific to Rocky Mountains), Texas Interconnection (independent within Texas), and Quebec Interconnection (Quebec province). NERC oversees six regional reliability entities coordinating standards across these interconnections.

name: African Energy Commission
recognition_status: Specialized agency of the African Union under the Department for Infrastructure and Energy; created by OAU Decision AHG/Dec.167 (XXXVII) at the 37th Summit in Lusaka, 11 July 2001; launched through the Algiers Declaration AU/EXP/EN/Decl.(III) at the meeting of AU Ministers in charge of Energy, 15–17 February 2008; membership governed by the AFREC Convention
description: Specialized agency of the African Union (AU) responsible for coordinating and harmonizing energy policies across the continent. The African Energy Commission (AFREC) was established in 2001 by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and officially launched in 2008. AFREC's objectives include developing energy policies, creating and updating African energy statistics, mobilizing technical and financial support for member states, and implementing capacity-building programs. As of 2024, 46 African Union member states have signed the AFREC Convention, with 35 of them having ratified and deposited it. AFREC actively engages with a broad network of experts and partners across the 55 AU member states to ensure that energy initiatives align with Africa's development goals.
notes: Operates the Africa Energy Information System (AEIS) and publishes the African Energy Statistics Database annually since 2012. Programmes include oil and gas, biomass, energy efficiency, energy transition, and capacity building. Membership reflects states that have ratified and deposited the AFREC Convention, not the full AU roster.

name: International Hydropower Association
recognition_status: Non-profit membership organisation established in 1995 to advance sustainable hydropower; serves as the global voice for the hydropower sector, building and sharing knowledge on its role in renewable energy systems, freshwater management, and climate change solutions

secretariat.location: One Canada Square, London E14 5AA, United Kingdom
secretariat.head: Chief Executive Officer

description: International non-profit membership organisation representing organisations committed to the responsible and sustainable development and operation of hydropower. The International Hydropower Association (IHA) serves as the global voice for sustainable hydropower, building and sharing knowledge on its role in renewable energy systems, responsible freshwater management, and climate change solutions. IHA has over 100 corporate and affiliate members operating in more than 120 countries, including hydropower owners, operators, developers, designers, suppliers, and consultants. Approximately one-third (450 GW) of global installed hydropower capacity is directly managed and operated by IHA members.
notes: Membership comprises corporate and affiliate organisations rather than sovereign governments; member organisations operate in over 120 countries. CEO Eddie Rich leads the Central Office, which manages IHA's work programmes; the Board governs the association on behalf of members. Hosts the World Hydropower Congress and publishes the Hydropower Status report series.

provenance.note: membership_count counts member companies and organizations; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: International Solar Alliance
recognition_status: Treaty-based intergovernmental organization launched jointly by India and France at COP21 in Paris on 30 November 2015; Framework Agreement opened for signature in Marrakesh in November 2016 and entered into force after ratification by 15 countries; headquartered at the National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE) in Gurugram, India; India serves as President and France as Co-President; open to all United Nations member states, with countries outside the tropics eligible to join but without voting rights

secretariat.head: Director General
secretariat.organization: International Solar Alliance Secretariat (hosted at the National Institute of Solar Energy)

description: Treaty-based intergovernmental organization dedicated to promoting solar energy adoption to combat climate change and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. The alliance aims to mobilize $1 trillion in solar investments by 2030, provide energy access to 1 billion people, and install 1,000 gigawatts of solar energy capacity.
notes: The alliance primarily focuses on countries located between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn (sunshine countries), but is open to all United Nations member states. Countries outside the tropics can join but do not have voting rights. As of 2026, 112 countries have signed and ratified the Framework Agreement and 15 additional countries are signatories. The United States joined in 2021 but announced withdrawal on 7 January 2026. Also known as the International Agency for Solar Policy and Application (IASPA).

name: Baltic Sea Region Energy Co-operation
recognition_status: Ministerial cooperation process under the Council of the Baltic Sea States (CBSS), established by energy ministers of the Baltic Sea region and the European Commission; steered by the Group of Senior Energy Officials (GSEO)
description: Regional energy cooperation forum under the Council of the Baltic Sea States, bringing together energy ministers and senior officials from eleven Baltic Sea countries with the European Commission. Promotes dialogue on energy policy, energy efficiency, renewable energy, and integrated regional energy markets. Format revised in 2015; meetings are now convened ad hoc at the Group of Senior Energy Officials level.
notes: Founded at the 1998 Stavanger ministerial conference; formal establishment confirmed at the 1999 Helsinki ministerial meeting. Before the 2015 format revision, BASREC operated as a three-year ministerial process with rotating annual presidencies (1 July–30 June), an Executive Committee, and project funding. Under the revised format there are no regular ministerial meetings or new project budgets; any member may propose a GSEO-level meeting on a topic of common interest.

name: West African Power Pool
recognition_status: Specialized institution of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), created by Decision A/DEC.5/12/99 at the 22nd ECOWAS Authority summit on 5 December 1999; Articles of Agreement adopted by Decisions A/DEC.18/01/06 and A/DEC.20/01/06 at the 29th summit in Niamey on 18 January 2006, granting the General Secretariat status as an ECOWAS specialized institution; headquarters agreement with Benin signed 5 July 2006

secretariat.location: PK6, Zone des Ambassades, Akpakpa, 06 BP 2907, Cotonou, Republic of Benin
secretariat.head: Secretary General
secretariat.organization: General Secretariat of the West African Power Pool

description: Specialized institution of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) that integrates national power systems into a unified regional electricity market. WAPP coordinates public and private generation, transmission, and distribution utilities across fourteen mainland West African member states to develop cross-border interconnections, harmonize grid planning and operation, and facilitate competitive regional electricity trade. The General Secretariat is based in Cotonou, Benin.

other_names.name: Pool énergétique de l'Afrique de l'Ouest

notes: Covers fourteen of fifteen ECOWAS member states; Cape Verde is excluded because its island geography prevents connection to the mainland transmission grid. Governance comprises the General Assembly of member utilities, a fifteen-member Executive Board, five Organizational Committees (engineering and operations, strategic planning and environment, finance, human resources and governance, and distribution and commercial), and the General Secretariat. Regional infrastructure planning follows the ECOWAS Master Plan for Regional Power Generation and Transmission Infrastructure (2019–2033). Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger remain members despite their withdrawal from ECOWAS in 2024.

name: ECOWAS Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency
recognition_status: Specialized agency of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), established by Council of Ministers Regulation C/REG.23/11/08 at the 61st session in Ouagadougou on 23 November 2008; operates as an autonomous body within the ECOWAS legal, administrative, and financial framework; secretariat inaugurated in Praia on 6 July 2010 following a headquarters agreement with Cabo Verde; governed by ECOWAS Regulation PC/REX.5/06/2020 on organization and functioning (adopted 5 November 2020)

secretariat.location: Achada Santo António, 2nd Floor, Electra Building, Praia C.P. 288, Cabo Verde
secretariat.head: Executive Director
secretariat.organization: ECOWAS Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency (ECREEE)

description: Specialized agency of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) that promotes renewable energy and energy efficiency markets across West Africa. ECREEE coordinates regional policy, builds capacity through National Focal Institutions, mobilizes investment, and operates programmes spanning solar, bioenergy, energy efficiency, and clean cooking to improve access to modern and affordable energy services.

other_names.name: ECOWAS Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency
Centro de la CEDEAO para las Energías Renovables y la Eficiencia Energética
Centre de la CEDEAO pour les énergies renouvelables et l'efficacité énergétique
Centro da CEDEAO para Energias Renováveis e Eficiência Energética
Центр ЭКОВАС по возобновляемым источникам энергии и энергоэффективности
西共体再生能源与能源效率中心

notes: Operates ECOWREX, the ECOWAS Observatory for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency. Initial establishment supported by UNIDO, Austria, and Spain, with later support from USAID, the EU, GIZ, and Brazil. Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger remain listed as members despite their 2024 ECOWAS withdrawal.

name: Nuclear Energy Agency
recognition_status: Intergovernmental agency established by OECD Council Decision C(57)255 entering into force on 1 February 1958 as the European Nuclear Energy Agency; renamed the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency in 1972; governed by the Steering Committee for Nuclear Energy reporting to the OECD Council
description: Intergovernmental agency within the OECD that facilitates cooperation among countries with advanced nuclear technology infrastructures. Established on 1 February 1958 as the European Nuclear Energy Agency (ENEA), it was renamed the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency in 1972 as membership expanded beyond Europe. The NEA assists member countries in developing the scientific, technological, and legal bases for the safe, environmentally sound, and economical use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, covering nuclear safety, technology, science, environment, and law.
notes: Originally established as the European Nuclear Energy Agency (ENEA) in 1958. Renamed the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency in 1972 following Japan's accession. Russia joined in 2013 but membership was suspended following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The Director-General is William D. Magwood, IV (since September 2014). Seven specialised standing technical committees operate under the Steering Committee for Nuclear Energy.

name: Global Renewables Alliance
recognition_status: Industry alliance formed through a memorandum of understanding signed at COP27 (November 2022) by six global renewable energy industry associations; co-leads advocacy for the COP28 UAE Consensus target to triple global renewable energy capacity to at least 11,000 GW by 2030; signed a partnership MoU with IRENA in June 2023
description: Global alliance of six leading renewable energy industry associations representing wind, solar, hydropower, geothermal, long-duration energy storage, and green hydrogen. Formed at COP27 in November 2022 through a memorandum of understanding, the alliance provides a unified private-sector voice advocating for the COP28 UAE Consensus target to triple global renewable energy capacity to at least 11,000 GW by 2030. GRA works with governments, industry, investors, NGOs, and multilateral organisations including IRENA, and hosts initiatives such as the Global Renewables Summit and the Electrify Now campaign.
notes: Founding members signed an MoU at COP27 in Sharm El-Sheikh in November 2022. GRA signed a partnership MoU with IRENA in June 2023. The alliance co-hosts the Global Renewables Summit (first held in New York in September 2024 during UN General Assembly High-Level Week) and maintains a Global Renewables Hub presence at COP meetings. Over 20 multinational companies participate as coalition partners alongside strategic partners including IRENA and Ember. Ben Backwell (CEO of GWEC) chairs the alliance from January 2025; Bruce Douglas serves as Chief Executive Officer. The Electrify Now campaign, co-led by GRA and the European Commission, launched on 23 June 2026 at London Climate Week to accelerate electrification to 35% of final energy consumption by 2035.

name: International Partnership for Energy Efficiency Cooperation
recognition_status: Voluntary ministerial forum established when G8 members plus China, South Korea, Brazil, and Mexico signed the Terms of Reference in Rome on 24 May 2009; the International Energy Agency hosted the Secretariat from establishment; membership grew to 17 G20 economies; mandate extended through 31 December 2019, after which functions transferred to the Energy Efficiency Hub

secretariat.head: Head of Secretariat
secretariat.organization: IPEEC Secretariat (hosted by the International Energy Agency)

description: High-level voluntary international forum of developed and developing economies that promoted global cooperation on energy efficiency. IPEEC facilitated policy exchange, joint projects, and coordination of sectoral task groups among its 17 G20 member economies, which together represented over 80% of global energy use and greenhouse gas emissions. From 2014 it coordinated implementation of the G20 Energy Efficiency Action Plan and, from 2016, the G20 Energy Efficiency Leading Programme. The IPEEC Secretariat was hosted by the International Energy Agency in Paris. Its mandate ended on 31 December 2019; activities and staff transferred to the Energy Efficiency Hub.

other_names.name: International Partnership for Energy Efficiency Cooperation
國際能源效率合作夥伴關係
Международное партнерство по сотрудничеству в области энергоэффективности
Partenariat international pour la coopération en matière d'efficacité énergétique
Asociación Internacional para la Cooperación en Eficiencia Energética

notes: Founded at the May 2009 G8 Energy Ministers meeting in Rome following the 2008 Aomori Declaration; founding members were Brazil, Canada, China, the European Commission, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with Argentina, Australia, and South Africa joining later. Governance included an Executive Committee and a Policy Committee, each meeting twice yearly. Sectoral work was organized through task groups including SEAD, BEET, EMWG/EMAK, TTG, HELE, NDTG, EEFTG, IPEEI, and TOP TENs. The EU Council extended the Terms of Reference through 31 December 2019 to complete the G20 energy efficiency work programme and enable administrative transfer of task groups, funds, and Secretariat staff to the Energy Efficiency Hub.

name: Nordic Electricity Market
recognition_status: Cooperation body of Nordic transmission system operators (TSOs) in Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden, founded in 1963 to harmonize the Nordic electricity market and power system; wound up on 1 July 2009 when operational tasks transferred to ENTSO-E
description: Former cooperation body of Nordic transmission system operators (TSOs) in Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden. Founded in 1963 to create preconditions for an effective and harmonized Nordic electricity market, maintain security of supply in the Nordic power system, and serve as a forum between TSOs, authorities, and market participants. Wound up on 1 July 2009; operational tasks transferred to ENTSO-E.

other_names.name: Organisation for the Nordic Transmission System Operators

notes: NORDEL was dissolved on 1 July 2009 and integrated into ENTSO-E alongside UCTE and ETSO. The Nordic synchronous grid continues to operate, connecting Norway, Sweden, Finland, and eastern Denmark (Zealand). Western Denmark (Jutland and Funen) is synchronized with Continental Europe. Iceland operates independently and is not synchronized with the Nordic grid.

name: Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization
recognition_status: Intergovernmental public organization established by the Lima Convention signed on 2 November 1973 and ratified by 27 Latin American and Caribbean states; governed by the Convention and ministerial meetings; officially renamed the Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization (OLACDE) in November 2025 after all member states ratified a 2007 amendment to Article 1

secretariat.location: Av. Mariscal Antonio José de Sucre N58-63 y Fernández Salvador, Edif. Olacde – San Carlos, Quito, Ecuador
secretariat.head: Executive Secretary
secretariat.organization: Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization

description: Intergovernmental public organization for cooperation, coordination, and technical advisory services in the energy sector across Latin America and the Caribbean. Established on 2 November 1973 by the Lima Convention and ratified by 27 member states, OLACDE (formerly OLADE) promotes regional energy integration, conservation, rational use, commercialization, and protection of energy resources. Headquartered in Quito, Ecuador, it serves as the region's principal technical-political energy body, publishing economic-energy statistics (SieLAC), training programmes (capevLAC), and policy coordination on oil, gas, renewables, methane emissions, and clean hydrogen.

other_names.name: Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization
Organización Latinoamericana y Caribeña de Energía

notes: Officially renamed from the Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) to the Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization (OLACDE) in November 2025 after all 27 member states ratified an amendment to Article 1 of the 1973 Lima Convention; the process began in 2007 and concluded with Haiti's ratification in October 2025. The record id remains OLADE for dataset continuity. Operates programmes including SieLAC (energy statistics), capevLAC (training), OEMLAC (methane emissions monitoring), and CertHiLAC (clean hydrogen certification). Partner in the Joint Organisations Data Initiative (JODI) alongside APEC, Eurostat, GECF, IEA, IEF, OPEC, and UNSD.

name: World Nuclear Association
recognition_status: Non-profit industry association founded in 2001 as the successor to the Uranium Institute (established 1975); serves as the global voice for the nuclear industry, promoting peaceful uses of nuclear energy and representing members across the full nuclear fuel cycle at international forums including the IAEA, OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, UN sustainable development and climate policy bodies, and ICRP deliberations on radiological protection

secretariat.location: York House, 23 Kingsway, London WC2B 6UJ, United Kingdom
secretariat.head: Director-General

description: International non-profit membership organisation representing the global nuclear industry. The World Nuclear Association (WNA) facilitates industry cooperation across the nuclear value chain, represents the sector in key international forums, and provides authoritative public information on nuclear power. WNA members include reactor vendors, utilities, uranium mining and fuel-cycle companies, engineering and construction firms, waste management organisations, research institutions, and service providers. As of 2026, WNA comprises about 3,000 member organisations from 180 member states, with member utilities responsible for roughly 70% of global nuclear generation.
notes: Membership comprises institutional organisations across the nuclear value chain rather than sovereign governments; member organisations are located in 44 countries. Members appoint the Director General and elect a 20-member Board of Management; current Director General is Sama Bilbao y León. Publishes World Nuclear News, hosts the annual World Nuclear Symposium in London, and coordinates the World Nuclear University with the IAEA, OECD-NEA, and WANO. Successor to the Uranium Institute (1975–2001).

name: World Wind Energy Association
recognition_status: International non-profit association founded on 1 July 2001 in Copenhagen, Denmark, at a meeting preparing the first World Wind Energy Conference; headquarters relocated to Bonn, Germany in 2003 near the UN Campus; membership spans national wind energy associations, scientific institutions, companies, and individuals in approximately 100 countries
description: International non-profit organization dedicated to promoting wind energy worldwide. The World Wind Energy Association (WWEA) provides a platform for communication among wind energy stakeholders, advises national governments and international organizations, and enhances international technology transfer. WWEA has over 600 members across approximately 100 countries, including national and regional wind energy associations, scientific institutions, companies, and individuals. Membership categories include ordinary members (wind energy associations), scientific members (scientific and research institutes), corporate members (companies and public bodies), and individual members.
notes: Founded in Copenhagen on 1 July 2001; Dr. Preben Maegaard served as founding president and Stefan Gsänger as secretary general. Headquarters moved to Bonn in 2003 at Charles-de-Gaulle-Str. 5, 53113, near the UN Campus. Governance includes a board with a president, vice presidents, and a secretary general leading the secretariat.

name: Integrated Power System / Unified Power System
recognition_status: Wide-area synchronous transmission grid inherited from the Soviet Union's unified energy system; the Russian Unified Power System (UPS) and interconnected national grids of the Integrated Power System (IPS) operate in parallel synchronous mode; coordinated by AO SO UPS (System Operator of the Unified Power System) under Russian law, with bilateral parallel-operation agreements among participating national grids including the BRELL arrangement (2001–2025) for Belarus, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania

secretariat.organization: AO SO UPS (System Operator of the Unified Power System)

description: Wide-area synchronous transmission grid connecting the Russian Unified Power System (UPS) with national power networks of Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. One of the world's largest synchronized electricity systems with approximately 300 GW installed capacity, spanning eight time zones and serving roughly 280 million customers. Evolved from the Soviet unified energy system; the Russian portion is operated by AO SO UPS.

other_names.name: Integrated Power System / Unified Power System

notes: The Unified Power System of Russia formed around 1956 when the Center and Middle Volga power systems were interconnected; the Central Asian IPS was established in 1960. After the dissolution of the USSR, the grid continued to operate synchronously across participating states. Ukraine and Moldova disconnected on 24 February 2022 during the Russian invasion of Ukraine and subsequently synchronized with the European grid. The Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) permanently disconnected on 8 February 2025 under the BRELL agreement to join the Continental Europe Synchronous Area; Kaliningrad now operates as a power island. Armenia operates asynchronously via HVDC links to Georgia and Iran. Turkmenistan disconnected in 2009 and is linked to the Iranian national grid. The system produces around 1,200 TWh annually.

name: International Renewable Energy Agency
recognition_status: Treaty-based intergovernmental organization established at the Founding Conference in Bonn on 26 January 2009; statute entered into force on 8 July 2010 after ratification by 25 member states; official United Nations observer; first international organization focused exclusively on renewable energy

secretariat.location: Masdar City, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
secretariat.head: Director-General

description: Intergovernmental organization mandated to facilitate cooperation, advance knowledge, and promote the adoption and sustainable use of renewable energy worldwide. Established in 2009 and operational since July 2010, IRENA is the first international organization focused exclusively on renewable energy, serving both industrialized and developing countries. It provides policy advice, capacity building, technology transfer, and authoritative data on renewable energy deployment, and holds official United Nations observer status.

other_names.name: Agencia Internacional de las Energías Renovables
Agence internationale pour les énergies renouvelables
Agência Internacional para as Energias Renováveis
Международное агентство по возобновляемым источникам энергии

notes: Founding Conference held in Bonn on 26 January 2009 with 75 signatory states; headquarters selected at the Preparatory Commission meeting in Sharm el-Sheikh in June 2009. The Innovation and Technology Centre is in Bonn, Germany, and a liaison office for United Nations and international institutions is in Vienna, Austria. The Assembly is the supreme governing body; a 21-member Council oversees budget and programme matters. Francesco La Camera (Italy) has served as Director-General since April 2019. The UN General Assembly declared 26 January as International Day of Clean Energy in 2023, marking IRENA's founding anniversary.

name: Mission Innovation
recognition_status: Global government initiative launched at COP21 in Paris on 30 November 2015 by 20 founding governments committed to doubling clean energy research and development investment over five years; Mission Innovation 2.0 relaunched on 2 June 2021 with action-oriented Missions and an Innovation Platform; member governments approved hosting the Secretariat at the International Energy Agency headquarters in Paris

secretariat.head: Head of MI Secretariat
secretariat.organization: Mission Innovation Secretariat (hosted by the International Energy Agency)

description: Global government initiative to catalyse action and investment in research, development, and demonstration to make clean energy affordable, attractive, and accessible. Launched at COP21 in November 2015, Mission Innovation (MI) comprises 22 countries and the European Commission, representing a large share of global clean energy R&D investment. MI 2.0, launched in June 2021, coordinates public-private Missions and an Innovation Platform to accelerate progress toward Paris Agreement goals and net-zero pathways. The Secretariat is hosted by the International Energy Agency in Paris, France.
notes: Founding launch at COP21 on 30 November 2015 alongside the Breakthrough Energy initiative. MI 2.0 (June 2021) introduced public-private Missions and an Innovation Platform with Insights, Collaborate, and Accelerate modules. Ministerial meetings are held annually and often co-located with the Clean Energy Ministerial. Mexico holds observer status. Partner organisations include UNIDO (joined August 2025 at MI-10 in Korea), the EIB Group (joined at MI-8 in Dubai), and the World Economic Forum. The Secretariat previously operated with UK government support before member governments approved IEA hosting in Paris in early 2026.

name: Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries
recognition_status: Regional intergovernmental organization established by agreement signed in Beirut, Lebanon on 9 January 1968 by Kuwait, Libya, and Saudi Arabia; domiciled in Kuwait; membership expanded to eleven countries by 1982; Tunisia's rights and obligations suspended since 1986 pending possible reactivation; at the 113th Ministerial Council Meeting in December 2024, members approved rebranding as the Arab Energy Organization (AEO) to broaden scope to conventional and renewable energy

secretariat.head: Secretary General
secretariat.organization: Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries

description: Regional intergovernmental organization coordinating energy policy among Arab oil-producing states. Founded in Beirut in 1968 by Kuwait, Libya, and Saudi Arabia, OAPEC promotes cooperation in petroleum development, safeguards members' interests in the oil industry, and sponsors joint ventures and the Arab Center for Energy Studies. Six of its ten active members are also OPEC members. At the December 2024 Ministerial Council Meeting, members approved rebranding as the Arab Energy Organization (AEO) to expand focus beyond petroleum to all energy sectors including renewables.

other_names.name: Organisation der arabischen Erdöl exportierenden Staaten
Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries
Organización de Países Árabes Exportadores de Petróleo
Organisation des pays arabes exportateurs de pétrole
Organização dos Países Árabes Exportadores de Petróleo
阿拉伯石油输出国组织

acronyms.value: 阿拉伯石油出口国组织

notes: Tunisia joined in 1982 but its rights and obligations were suspended in 1986 after requesting withdrawal; membership remains open for reactivation. Egypt was expelled in 1979 after signing the Camp David Accords and readmitted in 1989. OAPEC organs include the Council of Ministers, Executive Bureau, General Secretariat, and Judicial Tribunal (established 1980). The Arab Energy Conference merged with the Arab Petroleum Congress in 1982.

name: Southern African Customs Union
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established by the Southern African Customs Union Agreement (signed 11 December 1969, effective 1 March 1970); world's oldest surviving customs union; maintains free interchange of goods, a common external tariff and common excise duties; customs revenue pooled and shared among members with South Africa as custodian; administered by the SACU Secretariat in Windhoek
description: Customs union among Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia and South Africa — the world's oldest surviving customs union. Established in 1910 in its present configuration and relaunched under the 1969 SACU Agreement (effective 1 March 1970). Maintains free interchange of goods, a common external tariff and common excise duties; customs revenue is pooled and shared among members.
notes: Closely associated with but distinct from the Common Monetary Area (CMA), which includes Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa and Eswatini but excludes Botswana. BLNS members (Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia, Eswatini) receive shares of pooled customs and excise revenue; South Africa is custodian of the revenue pool. Namibia joined in 1990 following independence; institutional reforms were pursued after South Africa's 1994 democratization. Executive Secretariat based in Windhoek.

name: Union of South American Nations
recognition_status: Intergovernmental regional organization established by the UNASUR Constitutive Treaty (signed 23 May 2008, in force 11 March 2011); evolved from the South American Community of Nations (Cusco Declaration, 8 December 2004); pursued trade and economic integration including customs union goals that were never fully implemented; headquartered in Quito, Ecuador; largely inactive since 2018 after widespread suspensions and withdrawals; Argentina, Brazil and Colombia rejoined in 2023; Secretary General post vacant since January 2017

secretariat.organization: General Secretariat of the Union of South American Nations
secretariat.head: Secretary General (vacant since January 2017)

description: South American intergovernmental union established by the UNASUR Constitutive Treaty (23 May 2008, in force 11 March 2011). Pursued trade and economic integration including customs union goals that were never fully implemented. Largely inactive since 2018, though Argentina, Brazil, and Colombia rejoined in 2023.
notes: Evolved from the South American Community of Nations proclaimed by the Cusco Declaration (8 December 2004). The Constitutive Treaty was signed in Brasília on 23 May 2008 and entered into force on 11 March 2011 when Uruguay became the ninth ratifying state. Peru suspended its participation in 2018. Chile, Ecuador, Paraguay, and Uruguay have withdrawn. Argentina rejoined on 6 April 2023, Brazil on 5 May 2023, and Colombia on 5 December 2023. The Secretary General post has been vacant since Ernesto Samper's term ended in January 2017. A South American Parliament is planned for Cochabamba, Bolivia. The political profile of the same organization is recorded as UNASUR.

name: West African Economic and Monetary Union
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs and monetary union established by the Treaty of 10 January 1994 at Dakar; succeeded the West African Monetary Union (WAMU/UMOA, founded 1962); eight-state customs union sharing the West African CFA franc (XOF) with a common external tariff; administered by the Commission of UEMOA in Ouagadougou

secretariat.organization: Commission of the West African Economic and Monetary Union
secretariat.head: President of the Commission

description: Treaty-based intergovernmental organization binding eight West African states that share the West African CFA franc (XOF). Established in 1994 to promote monetary and financial stability, economic integration, and a common external tariff; succeeded the West African Monetary Union (WAMU/UMOA), founded in 1962.
notes: Territorially overlaps with ECOWAS, with which UEMOA coordinates trade liberalisation and macroeconomic convergence. Common institutions include the Council of Heads of State and Council of Ministers; Commission, Court of Justice, and Court of Accounts in Ouagadougou; the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) in Dakar; the Banking Commission (CB-UMOA) and Financial Markets Authority (AMF-UMOA) in Abidjan; and the West African Development Bank (BOAD) in Lomé. Guinea-Bissau joined on 2 May 1997 as the eighth and only non-francophone member. France revised the monetary cooperation agreement in December 2019, ending the operations account mechanism in January 2020 while maintaining euro convertibility guarantees.

other_names.name: West African Economic and Monetary Union
Unión Económica y Monetaria del África Occidental
União Econômica e Monetária do Oeste Africano

name: European Union Customs Union
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established as the Community Customs Union (completed 1 July 1968) under the EEC/EU treaties; comprises all EU member states, Monaco, and the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia with a common external tariff and no internal customs duties; administered by the European Commission on behalf of the Union in international trade negotiations; Andorra, San Marino and Türkiye participate through separate bilateral customs union agreements

secretariat.organization: Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union, European Commission
secretariat.head: Director-General

description: Customs union comprising all European Union member states, applying a common external tariff and eliminating internal customs duties; established in 1968 as the Community Customs Union and administered by the European Commission on behalf of the Union in international trade negotiations.
notes: Monaco and the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia are integral parts of the EU customs territory. Andorra, San Marino and Türkiye participate through separate bilateral customs union agreements, with partial exclusions for agricultural goods in the Andorra and Türkiye arrangements. Some EU member state territories—including Büsingen am Hochrhein, Heligoland, Livigno, Ceuta and Melilla—do not participate. The United Kingdom and Gibraltar are outside the customs union; Northern Ireland has special post-Brexit trade arrangements under the Windsor Framework.

other_names.name: Unión Aduanera de la Unión Europea

name: Andean Community of Nations
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established by the Cartagena Agreement (26 May 1969) and institutional reforms under the Trujillo Protocol (1996); operates a free trade zone and common external tariff (NANDINA) among Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru; administered by the General Secretariat in Lima

secretariat.organization: General Secretariat of the Andean Community
secretariat.head: Secretary General

description: South American integration organization and customs union established by the Cartagena Agreement (1969). Operates a free trade zone and common external tariff among Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru; formerly known as the Andean Pact (Pacto Andino) until institutional reforms in 1996–1997.
notes: Venezuela joined in 1973 and withdrew in 2006. Chile was a founding member but withdrew in 1976; it has been an associate member since 2006. Mercosur members Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay are associate members since 2005. The common external tariff was approved in 1994; the Trujillo Protocol (1996) renamed the bloc the Andean Community of Nations. Peru temporarily suspended liberalization obligations in 1992 and rejoined the free trade zone in 1997. The EU trade agreement with Colombia, Peru and Ecuador entered into full force in 2024. Also known as Comunidad Andina de Naciones or Andean Community.

name: Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs and monetary union established by the Treaty of N'Djamena (16 March 1994); superseded the Customs and Economic Union of Central Africa (UDEAC); six-state customs union sharing the Central African CFA franc (XAF) with a common external tariff; administered by the Commission of CEMAC in Bangui

secretariat.organization: Commission of the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa
secretariat.head: President of the Commission

description: Treaty-based intergovernmental organization binding six Central African states that share the Central African CFA franc (XAF). Established by the 1994 Treaty of N'Djamena and operational since 1999, when it superseded the Customs and Economic Union of Central Africa (UDEAC, founded 1964); promotes economic integration through a customs union with a common external tariff and a monetary union.
notes: Strong overlap in membership and mandates with ECCAS. Common institutions include the Commission in Bangui, Court of Justice in N'Djamena, Parliament in Malabo, Bank of Central African States (BEAC) in Yaoundé, Central African Banking Commission (COBAC) and Central African Financial Market Supervisory Commission (COSUMAF) in Libreville, and Development Bank of the Central African States (BDEAC) in Brazzaville. Equatorial Guinea joined in 1983. Full tariff elimination within the bloc has been delayed; capital movement is free.

other_names.name: Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa
Comunidad Económica y Monetaria de África Central
Communauté économique et monétaire de l'Afrique centrale
Comunidade Económica e Monetária da África Central
中部非洲经济与货币共同体

name: Schengen Area
recognition_status: Treaty-based open-border area established by the Schengen Agreement (1985) and Schengen Convention (1990); operational since 26 March 1995; integrated into EU law by the Amsterdam Treaty (1999); 29 participating states comprising 25 EU member states plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland through EFTA association agreements; common rules on external border controls, visa policy and police cooperation administered within the EU Area of Freedom, Security and Justice

secretariat.organization: Directorate-General for Migration and Home Affairs, European Commission
secretariat.head: Director-General

description: Area of 29 European states that have abolished passport and many other types of border control at their mutual borders; governed by the Schengen Agreement and Convention, integrated into EU law since 1999, and extended to Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland through EFTA association agreements.
notes: Ireland and Cyprus are EU member states outside the Schengen Area (Ireland maintains the Common Travel Area with the United Kingdom; Cyprus is committed to join). Bulgaria and Romania completed land-border integration on 1 January 2025 after air and sea controls were lifted on 31 March 2024. Monaco, Andorra, San Marino, and Vatican City maintain open or semi-open borders with Schengen states but are not formal members.

name: Customs Union of the Eurasian Economic Union
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established on 1 January 2010 as the Customs Union of Belarus, Kazakhstan and Russia with implementation of the common external tariff; successor to the Eurasian Economic Community customs framework (terminated 1 January 2015) and now regulated under Part Two of the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union, the EAEU Customs Code and decisions of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council and Eurasian Economic Commission; five-state union (Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia) with no internal customs duties and a common external tariff; negotiates international trade agreements in goods as a single entity under Article 35 of the EAEU Treaty

secretariat.head: Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission

description: Customs union comprising all member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, applying a common external tariff and eliminating internal customs duties. Established on 1 January 2010 as the Customs Union of Belarus, Kazakhstan and Russia and now governed under Part Two of the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union and the EAEU Customs Code, administered by the Eurasian Economic Commission.
notes: Rooted in 1995 bilateral and trilateral customs agreements between Russia, Belarus and Kazakhstan; the launch date was set in 2007 and the common external tariff took effect on 1 January 2010. Internal customs borders were removed after July 2011. Armenia joined on 2 January 2015 and Kyrgyzstan on 6 August 2015 with the EAEU accession. Superseded the EurAsEC customs union framework; older agreements remain in force where not contrary to the EAEU Treaty. Also known historically as the Customs Union of Belarus, Kazakhstan and Russia (Таможенный союз, TSOUZ).

other_names.name: Customs Union of the Eurasian Economic Union

name: Central American Common Market
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established by the General Treaty on Central American Economic Integration (Managua, 13 December 1960); readjusted under the Guatemala Protocol (1993) within the SICA economic subsystem; administered by the Secretariat for Central American Economic Integration (SIECA); five-state customs union (Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua) with elimination of internal tariffs and a common external tariff

secretariat.organization: Secretariat for Central American Economic Integration
secretariat.head: Secretary-General

description: Regional customs union and common market established by the General Treaty on Central American Economic Integration (Managua, 13 December 1960). Seeks to eliminate internal tariffs, adopt a common external tariff and coordinate economic policy among Central American states. Administered by the Secretariat for Central American Economic Integration (SIECA).
notes: Founded by Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua at Managua in 1960; Costa Rica acceded in 1963. The treaty entered into force on staggered dates (Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua in June 1961; Honduras in April 1962; Costa Rica in September 1963). Integration stalled after the 1969 Honduras–El Salvador war and ODECA was suspended in 1973. Revived under the Guatemala Protocol (1993), which readjusted the 1960 treaty within the Central American Integration System (SICA). Panama participates in the broader Central American economic integration process through SICA but is not part of the five-state customs union. Deep integration between El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras is advancing toward a single customs territory. The Unified Central American Declaration (DUCA) customs form entered into force on 7 May 2019. Also known as Mercado Común Centroamericano (MCCA).

name: East African Community
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established by the Protocol on the Establishment of the East African Community Customs Union (signed March 2004, effective 1 January 2005); first regional integration milestone under Article 75 of the EAC Treaty; operates a Common External Tariff and duty-free trade among partner states; administered by the East African Community Secretariat in Arusha
description: Customs union of the East African Community, established by the Protocol on the Establishment of the East African Community Customs Union (signed March 2004, effective 1 January 2005). Applies a Common External Tariff on third-country imports, duty-free trade among partner states, and common customs procedures.
notes: Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda were the founding customs-union partners; Rwanda and Burundi joined with their EAC accession in 2009. South Sudan (2016), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (2022) and Somalia (2024) are EAC members but do not yet participate to the same extent on customs integration. Implementation remains incomplete — member states retain excise duties and sensitive-tariff exceptions beyond the four-tier CET (0%, 10%, 25%, 35%) adopted since July 2022, and Rules of Origin have not been updated since 2015. The customs union is one pillar of broader EAC integration alongside the 2010 Common Market Protocol.

name: Southern Common Market
recognition_status: Treaty-based customs union established by the Treaty of Asunción (26 March 1991) and Protocol of Ouro Preto (16 December 1994); free trade among founding members from 1994 and common external tariff effective 1 January 1995; administered by the Secretariat of Mercosur in Montevideo; five active full members (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay) with Venezuela formally a member but suspended since December 2016
description: South American trade bloc and customs union established by the Treaty of Asunción (1991) and Protocol of Ouro Preto (1994). Free trade among founding members began in 1994; the customs union with a common external tariff took effect on 1 January 1995. Bolivia became a full member in July 2024.
notes: Venezuela remains a formal member but has been suspended since 1 December 2016 and does not participate in bloc decisions. Associate countries (Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Panama, Peru, and Suriname) have trade agreements with Mercosur but are not part of the customs union. Also known as Mercosur (Spanish) and Mercosul (Portuguese).

name: World Trade Organization
description: Intergovernmental organization that regulates and facilitates international trade. Established in 1995, succeeding the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). Provides framework for negotiating trade agreements and resolving disputes among member countries.
notes: The WTO was established on January 1, 1995, succeeding the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) which was created in 1948. As of 2024, the WTO has 166 members, representing over 98% of global trade and GDP. The most recent additions are Comoros (joined August 21, 2024) and Timor-Leste (joined August 30, 2024). The WTO provides a framework for negotiating trade agreements and resolving disputes among its members.
