name: Pacific Alliance
recognition_status: Regional integration initiative established by the Lima Declaration on 28 April 2011; Framework Agreement signed on 6 June 2012; four member states (Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru); Singapore is the first associated state after its free trade agreement entered into force on 3 May 2025; Costa Rica admitted as a membership candidate in December 2024; Panama is an official membership candidate; 64 observer states as of January 2025
description: Latin American regional integration initiative and trade bloc comprising Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru, established by the Lima Declaration on 28 April 2011 and consolidated through the Framework Agreement signed on 6 June 2012. Aims at deep integration toward free movement of goods, services, capital and people, with strategic orientation toward the Asia-Pacific region. Singapore became the first associated state when the Pacific Alliance–Singapore free trade agreement entered into force on 3 May 2025. Costa Rica and Panama are official candidates for full membership. As of January 2025 the bloc recognized 64 observer states.
notes: Full member count is four. membership_count reflects founding members plus associated state (Singapore) and membership candidates (Costa Rica, Panama). Observer roster sourced from member-state foreign ministry listings; the Pacific Alliance published an updated list of 64 observer states in January 2025.

name: Tripartite Free Trade Area
recognition_status: Free trade agreement among the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), East African Community (EAC), and Southern African Development Community (SADC); agreed at the First Tripartite Summit in Kampala in October 2008 and officially launched at the Third Tripartite Summit in Sharm El Sheikh on 10 June 2015; entered into force on 25 July 2024 after 14 member states deposited instruments of ratification
description: African free trade agreement uniting the 29 tripartite member and partner states of COMESA, the EAC, and SADC. Signed on 10 June 2015 and in force from 25 July 2024 after 14 ratifications, it aims to integrate markets, infrastructure, and industrial development across eastern and southern Africa as a stepping stone toward the African Continental Free Trade Area.
notes: The Tripartite Free Trade Area (TFTA) Agreement was finalized and opened for signature in 2015. The agreement officially entered into force on July 25, 2024, after reaching the required threshold of 14 ratifications among its member states. The TFTA comprises 29 member states, collectively representing 53% of the African Union's membership, more than 60% of the continent's GDP (approximately $1.88 trillion), and a combined population of 800 million. The TFTA focuses on three main pillars: market integration, infrastructure development, and industrial development. It serves as a critical step toward the broader objectives of the African Union, particularly in accelerating economic integration across the continent.

name: BASIC countries
recognition_status: Informal bloc of Brazil, South Africa, India, and China formed by agreement on 28 November 2009 ahead of the Copenhagen climate summit; coordinates a common negotiating position in UNFCCC proceedings
description: Informal coordination bloc of Brazil, South Africa, India, and China (the acronym reflects the four member states) formed by agreement on 28 November 2009 ahead of the 2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference in Copenhagen. The four large newly industrialized countries coordinate a common negotiating position in UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) proceedings, including on emission-reduction commitments, climate finance for developing nations, and equitable development space for the Global South. The grouping brokered the Copenhagen Accord with the United States in December 2009 and holds regular ministerial meetings to align positions before UN climate summits. All four members also participate in BRICS.
notes: Distinct from BRICS: BASIC comprises the four BRICS members excluding Russia and focuses specifically on climate-change negotiations rather than broader geopolitical cooperation. Sometimes referred to as the G4 bloc in climate contexts. Not to be confused with the WTO G4 (Brazil, India, China, and South Africa on agricultural trade) or the UN Security Council G4.

name: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
description: Multilateral agreement regulating international trade from 1948 to 1995. Established as a provisional framework to promote international trade by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers. Succeeded by the World Trade Organization (WTO) on January 1, 1995.

other_names.name: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
Acuerdo General sobre Aranceles Aduaneros y Comercio

notes: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) was signed on October 30, 1947, by 23 original signatories and came into effect on January 1, 1948. It was established as a provisional framework to promote international trade by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers. Over nearly five decades, GATT played a pivotal role in liberalizing global trade, with its membership expanding to 128 contracting parties by the end of 1994. The GATT was succeeded by the World Trade Organization (WTO) on January 1, 1995, following the conclusion of the Uruguay Round negotiations. The original GATT text continues to exist under the WTO framework as "GATT 1994," subject to modifications from the original "GATT 1947."

name: African Solidarity Fund
recognition_status: Multilateral financial guarantee institution established under the Agreement creating the African Solidarity Fund (Paris, 21 December 1976); recognized as a specialized agency of the African Union (February 2025)
description: Multilateral financial guarantee institution headquartered in Niamey, Niger. Established in December 1976 and operational since September 1979, the African Solidarity Fund supports economic and social development across its African member states by guaranteeing bank loans and bond issues, providing refinancing and interest-rate subsidies, and mobilizing local and external savings to finance productive investment projects in industry, agriculture, infrastructure, and services.

name: European Investment Bank
recognition_status: International financial institution established under the Treaty establishing the European Economic Community (Treaty of Rome), which entered into force on 1 January 1958
description: The European Union's investment bank and the world's largest multilateral lender by volume. Established in 1958 under the Treaty of Rome and owned by EU member states, the EIB provides long-term loans, equity investments, and guarantees to public and private projects aligned with EU policy objectives in climate, infrastructure, SMEs, cohesion, and development. Headquartered in Luxembourg, it focuses about 90% of lending inside the EU while also supporting EU development and cooperation policies in partner countries worldwide.
notes: EU member states are the sole shareholders, with capital subscriptions broadly proportional to GDP. Part of the EIB Group together with the European Investment Fund (EIF). Issued the world's first green bonds in 2007. Also an institutional shareholder of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Headquarters moved from Brussels to Luxembourg in 1968.

name: Inter-American Development Bank
recognition_status: Multilateral development bank established under the Agreement Establishing the Inter-American Development Bank (1959), adopted through the Organization of American States
description: Multilateral development finance institution and the leading source of development financing for Latin America and the Caribbean. Established in 1959 under the Agreement Establishing the Inter-American Development Bank, the IDB provides sovereign loans, technical assistance, and policy support to borrowing member governments and works with the private sector through IDB Invest and IDB Lab. Headquartered in Washington, D.C., it has 48 member countries—26 borrowing and 22 non-borrowing—with Latin American and Caribbean members holding a majority of voting power.
notes: Regional multilateral development bank with 48 members (26 borrowing, 22 non-borrowing). Formally established 8 April 1959 when OAS members signed the Articles of Agreement; Annex A lists 21 original signatories. Latin American and Caribbean borrowing members hold 50.02% of voting power. Host country is the United States. Private-sector operations are carried out through IDB Invest; innovation and venture activities through IDB Lab.

name: International Investment Bank
recognition_status: Multilateral development finance institution established under the Agreement Establishing the International Investment Bank (10 July 1970), registered with the United Nations as treaty no. 11417
description: Multilateral development bank established in 1970 under Comecon auspices to finance joint investment projects among Eastern Bloc and associated states. Operations were suspended after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and later revived by Russia. Headquarters were in Moscow until relocation to Budapest in 2019–2020, then returned to Moscow in 2023. Four member states remain as of 2023 (Cuba, Mongolia, Russia, and Vietnam); Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, Romania, and Slovakia withdrew following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
notes: Originally a Comecon-era institution with Warsaw Pact and associated members. Poland withdrew in 2000; most European members exited in 2022–2023 after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Headquarters moved from Moscow to Budapest in 2019 and returned to Moscow in October 2023. The bank was subject to U.S. sanctions in April 2023.

name: Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency
recognition_status: Multilateral development finance institution established under the Convention establishing the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (entered into force 12 April 1988)
description: Political risk insurance and credit enhancement arm of the World Bank Group, established on 12 April 1988 to promote foreign direct investment in developing countries. MIGA provides guarantees against non-commercial risks—including currency transfer restrictions, expropriation, war and civil disturbance, breach of contract, and non-honoring of sovereign financial obligations—for cross-border investments in eligible developing member economies. As the hub of the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform, it mobilizes private capital by giving investors confidence to commit in frontier markets. IBRD membership is a prerequisite for MIGA membership.

notes: One of five World Bank Group institutions alongside IBRD, IDA, IFC, and ICSID. Convention entered into force on 12 April 1988 with 29 founding members. IBRD membership is a prerequisite for MIGA membership. As of 2024, six World Bank member states (Brunei, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, San Marino, Tonga, and Tuvalu) are not MIGA members.

name: Islamic Development Bank
recognition_status: Multilateral development bank established under the Agreement Establishing the Islamic Development Bank, signed in Jeddah on 12 August 1974 following the December 1973 conference of Finance Ministers of OIC member states; formally opened on 20 October 1975
description: Multilateral development bank established in 1974 to foster economic development and social progress in member countries and Muslim communities worldwide in accordance with Shari'ah principles. The IsDB Group comprises five entities — the Islamic Development Bank, IsDB Institute, Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector (ICD), Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC), and International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (ITFC). With 57 shareholding member states across four continents, it provides project financing, trade finance, equity investments, and technical assistance. Membership requires OIC membership; Saudi Arabia is the largest shareholder. The bank holds AAA credit ratings and is an observer at the United Nations General Assembly.
notes: South-South multilateral development finance institution with 57 OIC member-state shareholders across four continents. Opened with 22 founding members in 1975; membership has grown to 57. IsDB Group comprises five entities (IsDB, IsDB Institute, ICD, ICIEC, ITFC). Holds AAA credit ratings from S&P, Moody's, and Fitch; Saudi Arabia is the largest shareholder (~22.5% paid-up capital). Observer at the United Nations General Assembly.

name: Nordic Environment Finance Corporation
recognition_status: International financial institution established in 1990 by the five Nordic governments (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden)
description: Nordic-owned international financial institution established in 1990 by Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden to finance environmental and climate projects. Known as the Nordic Green Bank, Nefco lends from paid-in capital and manages trust funds to support Nordic green SME scale-up and public-sector environmental investments, with a primary focus on Eastern Europe, the Baltic Sea region, and Ukraine. Headquartered in Helsinki, Finland.
notes: Also known as the Nordic Green Bank. One of three Nordic international financial institutions alongside the Nordic Investment Bank (NIB) and Nordic Development Fund (NDF). Manages donor trust funds including the Nordic Project Fund (Nopef) and implements EU and multilateral programmes such as E5P and NDEP. Suspended remaining projects in Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and ceased new funding in Belarus after the 2020 election dispute.

name: Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa

Owned by 21 League of Arab States shareholder countries, BADEA provides concessional project finance, technical assistance grants, trade finance, and private-sector support exclusively to non-shareholder countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, with a focus on infrastructure, agriculture, SME development, and Arab–African trade.
notes: Arab-owned MDB operating exclusively in Sub-Saharan Africa (44 non-shareholder beneficiary countries as of 2025). Shareholders are League of Arab States members. Member of the Arab Coordination Group. Pursues lending through rolling five-year plans aligned with SDGs and AU Agenda 2063.

recognition_status: Common central bank of the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), established under the 22 November 1972 Brazzaville cooperation conventions; exclusive issuer of the Central African CFA franc (XAF)
description: Central bank of the six-member Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC), serving Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, and Gabon. Established in 1972 to succeed the Banque Centrale des États de l'Afrique Équatoriale et du Cameroun (BCEAEC) and operational since April 1973, BEAC holds the exclusive right to issue the Central African CFA franc (XAF) and conducts monetary policy, banking supervision, and financial stability functions for the union.
notes: Succeeded the BCEAEC (Institut d'Émission, 1955–1959; headquartered in Paris through the early 1970s). Member states chose Yaoundé as headquarters in February 1973; full transfer from Paris completed in early 1977. Equatorial Guinea joined on 1 January 1985. Central African Banking Commission (COBAC) established within BEAC in 1990 and operational from 1993. One of the CEMAC common institutions alongside BDEAC (development bank, Brazzaville), COBAC, and COSUMAF (Libreville).

description: Multilateral treaty-based development finance institution, formerly known as the PTA Bank, established in 1985 as the financial arm of COMESA to finance trade, regional economic integration, and sustainable development across eastern and southern Africa. Rebranded as the Trade and Development Bank (TDB) in 2017, it provides trade finance, project and infrastructure finance, asset management, and advisory services. Shareholders comprise 26 African member states plus non-regional and institutional investors; the bank operates principle offices in Bujumbura and Port Louis, Mauritius, and regional offices in Nairobi, Harare, Addis Ababa, and Kinshasa.

name: International Development Association
recognition_status: Multilateral development finance institution established under the Articles of Agreement of the International Development Association (entered into force 24 September 1960)
description: Concessional lending arm of the World Bank Group, established in 1960 to provide interest-free loans and grants to the world's poorest countries that lack access to commercial capital or IBRD lending. Together with IBRD it forms the World Bank, sharing executive leadership and staff in Washington, D.C. IDA financing supports poverty reduction, human development, infrastructure, and climate resilience in eligible low-income and lower-middle-income economies.

includes.name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

notes: Concessional arm of the World Bank Group. Articles of Agreement entered into force on 24 September 1960 with 15 founding signatories. IBRD membership is a prerequisite for IDA membership. Shares governance with IBRD as the World Bank; replenished by donor contributions every three years.

name: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
recognition_status: Multilateral development bank established under the Articles of Agreement of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (entered into force 27 December 1945)

IBRD provides loans, guarantees, and advisory services to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries for projects in infrastructure, education, health, agriculture, and environmental management. Together with IDA it forms the World Bank; membership in IBRD is a prerequisite for joining other World Bank Group institutions. Owned by 189 member governments, it is AAA-rated and raises capital on international bond markets.

Governed by an Assembly of Governors (all member central bank governors), a Bureau, five African Union sub-regional committees (North, West, Central, East, and Southern Africa), and an Executive Secretariat hosted by BCEAO in Dakar, Senegal. Supports capacity building through research, seminars, symposiums, and technical training, and works toward deeper monetary and financial integration including the long-term goal of an African Central Bank and single currency.

notes: Concept proposed at the May 1963 OAU summit in Addis Ababa; first meeting of African central bank governors held in Addis Ababa in February 1965; Articles of the Association adopted in 1968. The Assembly of Governors is the governing body; five AU sub-regional committees coordinate North, West, Central, East, and Southern Africa. Secretariat relocated to BCEAO premises in Dakar following the 25th Assembly decision (August 2001, Johannesburg). Membership comprises 41 central banks representing 53 African countries (BEAC and BCEAO are regional central banks covering multiple member states).

name: Bank for International Settlements

description: International financial institution established in 1930 to support central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation, and to act as a bank for central banks. notes: Central-bank-owned institution serving as a forum for international monetary and financial cooperation and as a bank for central banks. Hosts the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and supports related standard-setting bodies. UMOA treaty signed 12 May 1962; headquarters relocated from Paris to Dakar in 1978 and inaugurated 26 May 1979. Mali left in 1962 (rejoined 1984); Mauritania withdrew 1973; Guinea-Bissau joined 1997. description: Multilateral development bank established by Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development in emerging markets and developing countries. Headquartered in Shanghai, NDB finances clean energy, transport, water and sanitation, digital infrastructure, environmental protection, and social infrastructure projects, with AA+ long-term issuer ratings from S&P and Fitch.

Headquartered in Almaty, the EDB finances transport infrastructure, digital systems, green energy, agriculture, manufacturing, and water and energy projects with a focus on integration effects across Eurasia.
notes: Also known internationally by the English acronym EDB. Uzbekistan joined as the seventh member in 2025. The Bank maintains a branch in Saint Petersburg and representative offices in Astana, Bishkek, Dushanbe, Yerevan, Minsk, and Moscow.

Unlike IBRD and IDA, which lend to governments, IFC provides loans, equity, guarantees, and advisory services to private enterprises and financial institutions without requiring sovereign guarantees. Owned by 186 member governments and consistently AAA-rated, it mobilizes capital for projects in infrastructure, manufacturing, agribusiness, financial markets, and climate finance across emerging markets.

name: Central American Bank for Economic Integration

description: Leading multilateral development bank for Central America and the financial arm of regional integration and development. Founded in 1960 by Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica, CABEI (BCIE in Spanish) invests in projects that reduce poverty and inequality, strengthen regional integration, and support the competitive insertion of its 15 member countries in the global economy, with emphasis on environmental and social sustainability. Headquartered in Tegucigalpa, Honduras, with regional offices in Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama.
notes: Founding shareholders are Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica; Panama and the Dominican Republic joined as regional non-founding members; Mexico, Argentina, Colombia, Spain, Cuba, Taiwan, and South Korea are extra-regional shareholders. Belize participates as a beneficiary country eligible for loans and guarantees but is not a shareholder.

name: OPEC Fund for International Development
recognition_status: Multilateral development finance institution established under the Agreement Establishing the OPEC Fund signed on 28 January 1976; became a permanent international development agency in May 1980; holds UN General Assembly observer status since 1981
description: Multilateral development finance institution established in 1976 by OPEC member states to reinforce financial cooperation with other developing countries. Owned by 12 shareholder countries, the OPEC Fund provides concessional loans, grants, trade finance, and technical assistance exclusively to non-member low- and middle-income countries across 125+ partner economies, focusing on infrastructure, energy, food security, MSME employment, water and sanitation, healthcare, and education.
notes: OPEC Fund membership is distinct from OPEC; the two organizations are separate entities. Does not lend to member countries except emergency grants. Rebranded as OFID in 1981 and reverted to the OPEC Fund name in 2007; ceased using the OFID abbreviation in 2020. Holds AA+/Stable credit ratings from Fitch and S&P. Committed over US$32 billion to development projects since inception.

description: Regional not-for-profit institution serving central banks and monetary authorities across the Asia-Pacific. Established in 1982 as a legal entity following governor conferences dating to 1967, The SEACEN Centre provides learning programmes, collaborative research, and networking platforms in macroeconomic and monetary policy management, financial stability and supervision, payment and settlement systems, and leadership and governance. Membership comprises 19 full members plus associate and observer central banks invited to learning programmes and the annual Governors' Conference.
notes: Concept proposed at the 1967 SEACEN Governors Conference in the Philippines; governors agreed in 1972 to establish a single research and training centre in Kuala Lumpur; work commenced in 1973. Incorporated as a legal entity in 1982 with eight member central banks, growing to 19 full members. Relocated to the Sasana Kijang complex (Bank Negara Malaysia) in 2011. Also collaborates with 26 regional and international strategic partners and invites 15 additional central banks to learning programmes.

description: Multilateral development bank with an exclusively social mandate, promoting social cohesion across Europe. Established in 1956 as the Resettlement Fund for National Refugees and Over-Population in Europe, renamed the Council of Europe Social Development Fund in 1994 and the Council of Europe Development Bank in 1999. Provides loans, co-financing, and grants to member states for social infrastructure, housing, education, health, disaster recovery, refugee and migrant integration, and job creation. Headquartered at 55 Avenue Kléber in Paris; financially autonomous with AAA/Aaa credit ratings.
notes: Oldest European multilateral development bank. All 43 members except the Holy See and Kosovo are Council of Europe member states; Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Monaco, and the United Kingdom are CoE members eligible for CEB membership but not currently shareholders. Ukraine joined in June 2023.

Bilateral members comprise G20 donor countries; multilateral members include the World Bank Group, African Development Bank Group, European Commission, European Investment Bank, and Development Bank of Southern Africa. Secretariat is hosted by the African Development Bank in Abidjan.

Owned by 77 countries plus the European Union and European Investment Bank as institutional shareholders, the EBRD invests primarily in the private sector alongside commercial partners, providing loans, equity investments, and guarantees to support competitiveness, governance, inclusion, and green-economy transition in its countries of operations.

name: European Stability Mechanism
recognition_status: Intergovernmental financial institution established under the Treaty Establishing the European Stability Mechanism, which entered into force on 27 September 2012
description: Permanent intergovernmental financial institution and lender of last resort for euro area member states. Established in 2012 under a dedicated treaty to replace temporary crisis facilities (EFSF and EFSM), the ESM provides conditional financial assistance—including sovereign loans, bank recapitalisation, and precautionary credit lines—to safeguard financial stability in the euro area. Headquartered in Luxembourg, it has an authorised lending capacity of €500 billion, with shareholders limited to euro area states.
notes: Replaced temporary EFSF and EFSM crisis facilities. Operations commenced on 8 October 2012. Later euro adopters joined as ESM shareholders when they entered the euro area (Latvia 2014, Lithuania 2015, Croatia 2023, Bulgaria 2026). Article 136 TFEU amendment authorizing euro area stability mechanisms entered into force on 1 May 2013. Also administers legacy EFSF bond programmes.

name: Arab Monetary Fund
recognition_status: Regional Arab monetary cooperation institution established under the Agreement Establishing the Arab Monetary Fund (1976); affiliated with the Arab League

description: Regional Arab monetary cooperation institution founded in 1976 and operational since 1977. Headquartered in Abu Dhabi, the AMF provides short- and medium-term balance-of-payments financing to Arab League member states, promotes Arab monetary and financial market integration, and issues the Arab Accounting Dinar as its unit of account. It operates the Buna regional payment and settlement platform and supports central banking cooperation through the Council of Arab Central Banks and Monetary Authorities Governors.
notes: All 22 Arab League member states are AMF members. Operational since 1977. Operates the Buna (formerly ARPS) regional payment system, which went live in 2023. Issues the Arab Accounting Dinar (AAD) as its unit of account.

name: Norsad Capital
recognition_status: Nordic-SADC development finance institution established in 1990 as the Norsad Fund and Agency, a multilateral entity in Lusaka, Zambia; restructured as Norsad Finance Limited in Botswana in 2011 and rebranded Norsad Capital in 2022; regulated by Botswana NBFIRA and accredited under BITC
description: Nordic-SADC development finance institution providing medium- to long-term debt and mezzanine capital to financially, socially, and environmentally sustainable mid-market growth companies in sub-Saharan Africa. Established in 1990 as a multilateral fund and agency in Lusaka on collaboration between Nordic governments and SADC member states; incorporated as Norsad Finance Limited in Botswana in 2011 and rebranded Norsad Capital in 2022. Owned by Nordic development finance institutions (Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden) and SADC national development finance institutions. Impact investor and private credit provider; member of UNPRI and GIIN. Headquartered in Gaborone, Botswana.
notes: Formerly Norsad Finance Limited. Originated as the Norsad Fund and Agency (1990) before transitioning to a Botswana-registered development finance company in 2011. Relocated headquarters from Lusaka, Zambia to Gaborone, Botswana in 2012. As of 2022, shareholders comprised 15 Nordic and SADC development finance institutions per audited financial statements.

name: World Bank
recognition_status: Collective name for the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and the International Development Association (IDA), two Bretton Woods institutions established at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference (July 1944); IBRD Articles of Agreement entered into force 27 December 1945
description: Global multilateral development institution comprising IBRD and IDA, the two Bretton Woods lending arms collectively known as the World Bank. Headquartered in Washington, D.C., it provides loans, grants, guarantees, and technical assistance to governments for poverty reduction, infrastructure, education, health, and environmental projects. Part of the broader World Bank Group, which also includes IFC, MIGA, and ICSID; shares executive leadership and staff with its constituent institutions.

description: Autonomous international arbitration institution and one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group. Established under the ICSID Convention, which entered into force on 14 October 1966, ICSID provides facilities for the conciliation and arbitration of international investment disputes between contracting member states and foreign nationals. Member states participate through the Administrative Council and may nominate arbitrators and conciliators to ICSID panels; the Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General, manages proceedings and institutional support. ICSID is designated as the forum for investor–state dispute settlement in most bilateral investment treaties and in numerous national investment laws and contracts.

description: Multilateral development financial institution established in 1963 to promote economic cooperation, trade integration, and sustainable development among member states. description: International financial institution owned by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, and Sweden. Headquartered in Helsinki, Finland, with a regional hub in Riga, Latvia.
notes: One of three Nordic international financial institutions alongside the Nordic Environment Finance Corporation (NEFCO) and Nordic Development Fund (NDF). Operations began in August 1976. description: Multilateral development bank established in 1966 to foster economic growth and cooperation in Asia and the Pacific. description: Supranational central bank serving the eight member states and territories of the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union within the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States. Established under the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank Agreement signed at Port of Spain on 5 July 1983 as successor to the Eastern Caribbean Currency Authority, ECCB issues the Eastern Caribbean dollar (XCD), conducts monetary policy, and supervises the banking system across its member jurisdictions. notes: Succeeded the Eastern Caribbean Currency Authority (1965–1983), which had replaced the British Caribbean Currency Board. Its 28 members comprise 19 regional borrowing members, four regional non-borrowing members (Brazil, Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela), and five non-regional non-borrowing members (Canada, China, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom). Headquartered in Wildey, St. Michael, Barbados, with a country office in Haiti.

description: Regional economic cooperation framework launched by the United States on 23 May 2022 with thirteen Indo-Pacific partner governments at a summit in Tokyo. Fiji joined as the fourteenth member on 27 May 2022. The framework covers four pillars — trade, supply chains, clean economy, and fair economy — and represents roughly 40% of global GDP. Partners concluded treaty-level agreements on supply chain resilience (November 2023), clean economy, fair economy, and the umbrella Agreement on IPEF (June 2024); trade-pillar negotiations remain ongoing. India participates in the supply-chain, clean-economy, and fair-economy pillars but opted out of trade-pillar negotiations in September 2022. notes: Distinct from CPTPP/TPP and RCEP: IPEF is not a traditional tariff-reduction FTA and does not grant U.S. market access. Eight international organisations participate as observers (African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, European Investment Bank, Inter-American Development Bank, IMF, UNDP, World Bank, WHO). recognition_status: Regional sea convention under the UNEP Regional Seas Programme and the only treaty-based instrument covering all six Black Sea riparian states
description: Regional convention for the protection of the Black Sea against pollution, signed in Bucharest on 21 April 1992 by all six coastal states. Establishes the Commission on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution (Black Sea Commission) and provides the legal framework to prevent, reduce, and control pollution and to ensure sustainable use of the Black Sea marine environment. Entered into force on 15 January 1994.

other_names.name: Convention on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution
Конвенция за опазване на Черно море от замърсяване
Convenția privind protecția Mării Negre împotriva poluării
Конвенция о защите Чёрного моря от загрязнения
Конвенція про захист Чорного моря від забруднення

notes: All six Black Sea coastal states signed the convention in Bucharest on 21 April 1992. Three protocols on land-based sources, dumping, and emergency oil-spill response were adopted alongside the convention and entered into force with it; a biodiversity and landscape conservation protocol was adopted in Sofia in 2002. The Black Sea Commission Permanent Secretariat has been hosted in Istanbul, Türkiye, since December 2000.

name: Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council
recognition_status: Five permanent seats on the UN Security Council established by Article 23(1) of the UN Charter, each with veto power over substantive resolutions
description: The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States — designated under Article 23 of the UN Charter. Each holds veto power over substantive Security Council resolutions. The seats were established when the Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945; the People's Republic of China has represented China since 25 October 1971, and the Russian Federation succeeded the Soviet Union's seat on 24 December 1991.

other_names.name: عضو دائم في مجلس الأمن التابع للأمم المتحدة
permanent members of the United Nations Security Council
Miembros permanentes del Consejo de Seguridad de las Naciones Unidas
membre permanent du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies
membro permanente do Conselho de Segurança das Nações Unidas
聯合國安全理事會常任理事國

notes: Article 23(1) of the UN Charter designates China, France, the Soviet Union (now the Russian Federation), the United Kingdom, and the United States as permanent Security Council members. The People's Republic of China assumed China's seat on 25 October 1971; the Russian Federation succeeded the Soviet Union on 24 December 1991.

name: Rotterdam Convention
recognition_status: United Nations multilateral environmental treaty establishing the prior informed consent (PIC) procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides in international trade; registered as Treaty Series vol. 2244, p. 337; administered jointly by UNEP and FAO under the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat

secretariat.organization: Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat (United Nations Environment Programme) jointly with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

description: Global treaty that promotes shared responsibility and cooperative efforts in the international trade of certain hazardous chemicals and pesticides. It establishes a prior informed consent (PIC) procedure so that parties can make informed decisions about the import of chemicals listed in Annex III. Adopted in Rotterdam on 10 September 1998 and entered into force on 24 February 2004. As of 2026, 168 parties have ratified or acceded; Angola, Seychelles, Saint Lucia, and the United States signed but have not ratified.

other_names.name: Rotterdamer Übereinkommen über das Verfahren der vorherigen Zustimmung nach Inkenntnissetzung für bestimmte gefährliche Chemikalien sowie Pestizide im internationalen Handel
Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade

notes: Parties comprise UN member states, the Cook Islands, the European Union, and the State of Palestine. Angola, Seychelles, Saint Lucia, and the United States are signatories that have not ratified as of May 2026. The secretariat is jointly administered by UNEP (Geneva) and FAO (Rome) under the BRS Conventions framework with the Basel and Stockholm conventions.

name: Treaty of Pelindaba

includes.name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

description: International treaty that establishes Africa as a nuclear-weapon-free zone. Also known as the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty (ANWFZ), it prohibits the research, development, manufacture, stockpiling, acquisition, testing, possession, control, or stationing of nuclear weapons within the territories of its parties. It also bans attacks against nuclear installations in the zone and requires IAEA full-scope safeguards for peaceful nuclear activities. Opened for signature in Cairo on 11 April 1996 and entered into force on 15 July 2009. Implementation is overseen by the African Commission on Nuclear Energy (AFCONE), headquartered in Pretoria.
notes: Membership lists States Parties that have deposited instruments of ratification or accession with the African Union depositary (44 parties as of 2025–2026 per AFCONE). The roster includes the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Western Sahara, EH), which UNODA's public party list omits. Signatories that have not yet ratified include the Central African Republic, Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Liberia, São Tomé and Príncipe, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Sudan, and Uganda; South Sudan has neither signed nor ratified.

name: Treaty of Rarotonga
recognition_status: Regional nuclear-weapon-free zone treaty concluded under Pacific Islands Forum auspices; the PIF Secretary General serves as depositary
description: International treaty that establishes a nuclear-weapon-free zone in the South Pacific. Also known as the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty (SPNFZ), it prohibits the manufacture, possession, stationing, and testing of nuclear weapons within the zone and commits parties to prevent environmental pollution by radioactive waste. Opened for signature at Rarotonga on 6 August 1985 and entered into force on 11 December 1986. The Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat in Suva acts as focal point and depositary; three protocols are open to the NPT nuclear-weapon states.

other_names.name: South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty

notes: Thirteen States Parties as listed by UNODA (Australia, Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, Nauru, New Zealand, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu). Join dates are deposit of ratification per the UN Treaty Collection. The Marshall Islands signed the treaty on 3 March 2025 but had not ratified as of mid-2026 and is not counted among parties. Federated States of Micronesia and Palau remain outside the original geographic scope and have not become parties. Protocols 1–3 are open to nuclear-weapon states; France, the United Kingdom, China, and Russia have ratified (protocols vary); the United States signed in 1996 but has not ratified.

name: COVAX
description: Global mechanism for equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines, led by Gavi, CEPI, and WHO.

name: Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians
recognition_status: Multilateral framework convention and the only treaty-based regime covering the entire Carpathian mountain region; alongside the Alpine Convention, one of two sub-regional mountain treaties worldwide
description: Framework convention adopted in Kyiv in May 2003 by the seven Carpathian states to pursue a comprehensive policy for the protection and sustainable development of the Carpathian Mountains. Provides a platform for cooperation on biodiversity, forestry, tourism, transport, and climate adaptation across the transboundary mountain ecosystem. Entered into force on 4 January 2006; the UNEP Vienna Programme Office has hosted the Secretariat since May 2004.

other_names.name: Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians
Рамкова конвенція про охорону та сталий розвиток Карпат

notes: Adopted at the Fifth Ministerial Conference "Environment for Europe" in Kyiv, Ukraine, in May 2003 and signed by all seven Carpathian states. UNEP Regional Office for Europe facilitated negotiations from 2001 onward. Supplementary protocols address biodiversity, sustainable forestry, tourism, transport, and agriculture; Serbia ratified as successor to the 2003 signatory Serbia and Montenegro.

name: OSPAR Commission
recognition_status: Regional sea convention for the North-East Atlantic, successor to the 1972 Oslo Convention and 1974 Paris Convention; administered by the OSPAR Commission with a secretariat in London

headquarters.note: Secretariat at The Aspect, 12 Finsbury Square, London EC2A 1AS

description: Intergovernmental organization established by the Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the North-East Atlantic (the OSPAR Convention). Opened for signature in Paris on 22 September 1992 and entered into force on 25 March 1998, replacing the 1972 Oslo Convention on dumping and the 1974 Paris Convention on land-based sources of marine pollution. OSPAR works to prevent and eliminate pollution and to protect the maritime area against the adverse effects of human activities, including biodiversity and ecosystems under Annex V.

other_names.name: Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the North-East Atlantic
Convention pour la protection du milieu marin de l'Atlantique du Nord-Est

notes: The name OSPAR combines Oslo and Paris, reflecting the predecessor 1972 Oslo and 1974 Paris Conventions. France is the depositary. Finland is a Contracting Party because some of its rivers drain to the Barents Sea; Luxembourg and Switzerland participate as upstream states in the Rhine catchment. Working languages are English and French. The Commission comprises 15 governments and the European Union (16 Contracting Parties).

name: Barcelona Convention
recognition_status: Regional sea convention under the UNEP Regional Seas Programme covering the Mediterranean Sea and its coastal region
description: Regional convention for the protection of the marine environment and the coastal region of the Mediterranean, established under the UNEP Regional Seas Programme. Adopted in Barcelona on 16 February 1976 and entered into force on 12 February 1978; amended in 1995 and renamed the Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment and the Coastal Region of the Mediterranean, with amendments entering into force on 9 July 2004. The convention aims to prevent, reduce, and control pollution and to ensure the sustainable use of the Mediterranean marine environment.

other_names.name: Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment and the Coastal Region of the Mediterranean
Convention for the Protection of the Mediterranean Sea Against Pollution

notes: Spain serves as depository. The Barcelona Convention and its seven protocols form the legal framework of the Mediterranean Action Plan (MAP), administered by the UNEP/MAP Coordinating Unit in Athens. Fourteen coastal states and the European Communities signed the original 1976 convention; the current roster comprises 21 Mediterranean countries and the European Union. Bosnia and Herzegovina has not ratified the 1995 amendments. Contracting Parties meet biennially at the Conference of the Parties.

name: Basel Convention
recognition_status: United Nations multilateral environmental treaty on the control of transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and their disposal; registered as Treaty Series vol. 1673, p. 57; administered by the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat

secretariat.organization: Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat (United Nations Environment Programme)

description: Global treaty to reduce transboundary movements of hazardous wastes, ensure their environmentally sound management as close as possible to the source of generation, and minimize hazardous waste generation. Adopted in Basel on 22 March 1989 and entered into force on 5 May 1992. As of 2026, 191 parties have ratified or acceded; Haiti and the United States signed but have not ratified.

other_names.name: Baseler Übereinkommen über die Kontrolle der grenzüberschreitenden Verbringung gefährlicher Abfälle und ihrer Entsorgung
Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal

notes: Parties comprise 188 UN member states, the Cook Islands, the European Union, and the State of Palestine. Fiji, Haiti, South Sudan, Timor-Leste, and the United States are not parties as of 2026; Haiti and the United States remain signatories that have not ratified. The secretariat is jointly administered with the Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions under the BRS Conventions Secretariat in Geneva.

name: Treaty of Bangkok
recognition_status: Regional nuclear-weapon-free zone treaty concluded under ASEAN auspices; Thailand serves as depositary
description: International treaty that establishes Southeast Asia as a nuclear-weapon-free zone. Also known as the Treaty on the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone (SEANWFZ), it obligates signatory states not to develop, manufacture, acquire, possess, or control nuclear weapons, and not to allow the stationing or testing of nuclear weapons within their territories, continental shelves, or exclusive economic zones. Signed in Bangkok on 15 December 1995 by ten Southeast Asian states and entered into force on 27 March 1997. Timor-Leste acceded in October 2025.

other_names.name: Treaty on the Southeast Asia Nuclear Weapon-Free Zone

notes: All ten Southeast Asian states listed in Article 15 signed the treaty in Bangkok on 15 December 1995. The treaty entered into force on 27 March 1997 after the seventh instrument of ratification was deposited. A protocol open to the five NPT nuclear-weapon states (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States) commits them not to use or threaten to use nuclear weapons against treaty parties; as of 2025 none have signed the protocol. Timor-Leste acceded on 25 October 2025 following its ASEAN membership.
