name: Antarctic Treaty System
description: Multilateral treaty system governing Antarctica south of 60°S latitude. Opened for signature on 1 December 1959 and entered into force on 23 June 1961. Demilitarizes the continent, guarantees freedom of scientific investigation, and freezes territorial claims; related agreements cover environmental protection, marine living resources, and other Antarctic governance.

name: Open Government Partnership
description: International organization.

other_names.name: 开放政府伙伴关系联盟

name: Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area
recognition_status: ASEAN subregional growth area established by the four participating member governments to accelerate socioeconomic development in remote and less developed areas
description: Intergovernmental subregional cooperation initiative established in March 1994 by Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines to accelerate balanced and inclusive growth in geographically remote and less developed areas of the four countries. Covers Brunei in full; Indonesian provinces of Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku, and Papua; Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak and the Federal Territory of Labuan; and Mindanao and Palawan in the Philippines. Operates as an ASEAN subregional grouping with sectoral clusters on transport, trade and investment facilitation, energy, ICT, agriculture and fisheries, tourism, and environment. The BIMP-EAGA Facilitation Centre in Kota Kinabalu serves as the subregional secretariat.

other_names.name: Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area

notes: Launched at the inaugural ministerial meeting in Davao City, Philippines, on 24 March 1994. Membership covers subnational areas rather than entire national territories. The Asian Development Bank serves as Regional Development Advisor. Vision 2025 guides current strategic priorities on connectivity, food security, tourism, natural resource management, and people-to-people links.

name: Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
recognition_status: United Nations multilateral environmental treaty to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants; registered as United Nations Treaty Series vol. 2256, p. 119, No. 40214; administered by the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat

secretariat.organization: Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions Secretariat (United Nations Environment Programme)

description: Global treaty to protect human health and the environment from persistent organic pollutants (POPs) by eliminating or restricting the production, use, trade, and release of listed chemicals, and by promoting the environmentally sound management of POPs wastes and stockpiles. Adopted in Stockholm on 22 May 2001 and entered into force on 17 May 2004. As of 2026, 186 parties have ratified or acceded; Brunei Darussalam, Haiti, Israel, Malaysia, and the United States signed but have not ratified.

other_names.name: اتفاقية استكهولم بشأن الملوثات العضوية الثابتة
Stockholmer Übereinkommen über persistente organische Schadstoffe
Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
Convenio de Estocolmo sobre contaminantes orgánicos persistentes
Convention de Stockholm sur les polluants organiques persistants
Стокгольмская конвенция о стойких органических загрязнителях
关于持久性有机污染物的斯德哥尔摩公约

notes: Parties comprise 182 UN member states, the Cook Islands, Niue, the European Union, and the State of Palestine. Andorra, Bhutan, Brunei Darussalam, Haiti, Israel, Malaysia, San Marino, South Sudan, Timor-Leste, Turkmenistan, and the United States are not parties as of 2026; Brunei Darussalam, Haiti, Israel, Malaysia, and the United States remain signatories that have not ratified. The secretariat is jointly administered with the Basel and Rotterdam conventions under the BRS Conventions Secretariat in Geneva.

name: The Convention on the Prohibition of the Use, Stockpiling, Production and Transfer of Anti-Personnel Mines and on Their Destruction

official_documents.name: Convention on the Prohibition of Anti-Personnel Mines (UN Office for Disarmament Affairs)

description: Multilateral disarmament treaty comprehensively banning the use, stockpiling, production, and transfer of anti-personnel mines and requiring destruction of stockpiles. Adopted in Oslo on 18 September 1997, opened for signature in Ottawa on 3 December 1997, and entered into force on 1 March 1999 after 40 ratifications. Deposited with the United Nations Secretary-General; implemented through annual Meetings of States Parties.

other_names.name: Convention sur l'interdiction des mines antipersonnel
Convención sobre la prohibición de minas antipersonales

notes: As of July 2026, 162 states are parties per the UN treaty database. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania withdrew effective 27 December 2025; Finland effective 10 January 2026; Poland effective 20 February 2026. Lebanon acceded on 1 May 2026 (entry into force 1 November 2026). Recent accessions also include Marshall Islands (2025) and Tonga (2025). Ukraine remains listed as a party at the UN but announced withdrawal in June 2025.

name: Digital Economy Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Standalone digital trade agreement establishing common rules on data flows, e-commerce, digital identity, and emerging technologies; open to accession by economies meeting its standards
description: World's first standalone digital trade agreement, signed virtually on 12 June 2020 by Chile, New Zealand, and Singapore and designed as an open plurilateral framework for digital economy cooperation. Covers modules on business and trade facilitation, treatment of digital products and data, trust in the digital environment (including personal information protection and consumer safeguards), and emerging trends such as artificial intelligence and financial technology. Entered into force for Singapore and New Zealand on 7 January 2021 and for Chile on 23 November 2021. The Republic of Korea acceded as the first new Party on 3 May 2024. A Protocol reinforcing key rules entered into force on 19 March 2024.
notes: Original signatories Chile, New Zealand, and Singapore concluded negotiations in January 2020 and signed electronically on 12 June 2020. Costa Rica was formally invited to accede in January 2025 and Peru in January 2026. Accession Working Groups are underway for Canada, China, and the United Arab Emirates; El Salvador, Thailand, Ukraine, and Uruguay have also lodged formal accession requests.

name: Budapest Convention on Cybercrime
description: Council of Europe treaty and global reference framework for international cooperation on cybercrime.

name: GCC Patent Office
description: Regional patent office of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf (GCC), established under the GCC Patent Regulation approved at the Supreme Council's 13th session in September 1992. A single GCC patent application, once granted, provides protection across all six member states. Based at the GCC Secretariat General in Riyadh. Since 5 January 2021, the office no longer accepts general filing of new applications pending amendment of the Patent Regulation, but continues to process pending applications and grants patents upon request from a member state.
notes: The GCC Patent Office began accepting applications on 3 October 1998; the first patent was granted in 2002. The patent system was amended in November 1999 to align with TRIPS. The GCC is not a party to the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) or the Paris Convention, though member states have individually adopted the regulation into national law. The GCCPO is distinct from national patent offices such as the Saudi Patent Office despite sharing Riyadh as its location.

other_names.name: مكتب براءات الاختراع لمجلس التعاون لدول الخليج العربية
Oficina de Patentes del Consejo de Cooperación de los Estados Árabes del Golfo
Office des brevets du Conseil de coopération des États arabes du Golfe
海湾阿拉伯国家合作委员会专利局

name: European Patent Organisation
description: Intergovernmental organization established by the European Patent Convention (signed 5 October 1973, in force 7 October 1977) to grant European patents valid across its contracting states. A single European patent application filed at the European Patent Office in Munich can designate all member states; the office also handles PCT international applications entering the European regional phase. Non-member states may participate through extension agreements (Bosnia and Herzegovina) or validation agreements (Morocco, Tunisia, Cambodia, Georgia, Laos).
notes: The Organisation comprises the European Patent Office (executive body) and the Administrative Council. Seven states were founding members when the EPC entered into force on 7 October 1977. Bosnia and Herzegovina is the sole remaining extension state. Moldova was a validation state from 2015 until acceding as a full member on 1 June 2026; the validation regime continues for applications filed before that date. Validation agreements with Costa Rica (signed December 2024) and Angola (signed June 2026) are not yet in force. Distinct from the EU unitary patent system administered by the EPO under EU law but separate from EPO membership.

name: Organisation Africaine de la Propriété Intellectuelle
description: Regional intellectual property office providing centralized system for protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights across French-speaking African countries.

other_names.name: Organisation Africaine de la Propriété Intellectuelle
Organización Africana de la Propiedad Intelectual
Organisation Africaine de la Propriété Intellectuelle

name: Eurasian Patent Organization
description: Intergovernmental organization established by the Eurasian Patent Convention (signed 9 September 1994) to administer a unified Eurasian patent system. A single Eurasian application can grant patent protection across all eight contracting states. The Eurasian Patent Office in Moscow serves as the executive body; Russian is the official working language.
notes: Moldova was a contracting state from 1996 until denouncing the convention effective 26 April 2012. Georgia and Ukraine signed the convention in 1994 but never ratified it. Turkmenistan joined by accession rather than as an original signatory. Distinct from the European Patent Organisation (EPO) and from the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), though five EAEU members overlap with current EAPO membership.

name: African Regional Intellectual Property Organization
description: Intergovernmental organization established by the Lusaka Agreement (1976) for cooperation among African states in patent, trademark, and other intellectual property matters. ARIPO administers regional protocols including the Harare Protocol (patents, industrial designs, and utility models), Banjul Protocol (marks), and Arusha Protocol (plant varieties). Headquartered in Harare, Zimbabwe; membership is open to UNECA and African Union member states.
notes: Cabo Verde became the 22nd member on 14 July 2022. Seychelles joined effective 1 January 2022. Mauritius was an original Lusaka Agreement signatory but acceded on 25 September 2020 and became a Harare Protocol contracting state effective 27 August 2025. Somalia has not yet acceded to the Harare Protocol. Distinct from OAPI, which serves French-speaking African countries. The organization was renamed from African Regional Industrial Property Organization in 2005.

other_names.name: Organización Regional Africana de Propiedad Intelectual
非洲区域知识产权组织

name: Caribbean Organisation of Tax Administrators
description: Regional intergovernmental organisation of national tax administrations from CARICOM member states and associate members, established in 1971 to promote regional tax cooperation and harmonisation. Operates under the auspices of the CARICOM Secretariat and provides a forum for capacity building, sharing best practices, and technical cooperation among Caribbean tax authorities.
notes: COTA was established in 1971 when its Constitution was ratified at a meeting of Caribbean tax administration heads in Saint Lucia; the Constitution was approved by CARICOM finance ministers in October 1972. Governance comprises a biennial General Assembly and an Executive Council (President plus five members). The Secretariat is administered through the CARICOM Secretariat in Georgetown, Guyana. COTA is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

name: Study Group on Asia-Pacific Tax Administration and Research
description: Annual forum for tax administrators in the Asia-Pacific region, established in 1970 to enhance cooperation, improve tax administration, and discuss issues related to tax administration. Promotes collaboration and communication among member tax administrations and facilitates alignment of regional tax systems to support trade and investment.
notes: SGATAR was established in 1970 under the auspices of the Ministerial Conference for the Economic Development of Southeast Asia (SEAMCED). The organization comprises 19 member tax jurisdictions and has no permanent headquarters; annual meetings rotate among members. Australia currently chairs SGATAR. Cambodia, Lao PDR, and Vietnam were founding members who later left and re-joined (Cambodia in 2014, Vietnam in 1997, Lao PDR in 2021). Fiji joined during the 54th Annual Meeting in September 2025 (hosted by Australia). Singapore will host the 55th Annual Meeting on 8–10 September 2026. Annual meetings typically attract more than 200 delegates. SGATAR is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

other_names.name: Study Group on Asia-Pacific Tax Administration and Research
亚太税务管理与研究组织
アジア太平洋税務管理研究グループ

name: Commonwealth Association of Tax Administrators
description: Associated organisation of the Commonwealth established in 1978 by Commonwealth Finance Ministers with headquarters in London. Promotes improvement of tax administration across 47 member countries, with emphasis on developing countries, through annual technical conferences, training programmes, publications, and knowledge sharing among Commonwealth tax administrators.
notes: CATA was established in 1978 by a decision of the Commonwealth Finance Ministers and operates as an Associated Organisation of the Commonwealth. Governance comprises an annual General Meeting of senior tax officials and a Management Committee (Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and 12 members elected by the General Meeting). Besides its yearly technical conference, CATA offers up to six training programmes each year for middle-level and senior tax managers. CATA is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO) and chairs the NTO Council for 2025–2026.

name: Association of Tax Authorities of Islamic Countries
description: Intergovernmental organization and OIC affiliated organ established in Putrajaya, Malaysia, to improve tax and zakat policies and administrations across member states. Provides a forum for discussion, research, and cooperation among Islamic countries' tax authorities, and conducts annual seminars, workshops, and training courses on tax information exchange and zakat administration.
notes: Founded in Putrajaya, Malaysia, on 15 October 2003 by eleven Islamic countries including Pakistan. Became an OIC affiliated organ through resolution 7/38-ORG adopted at the 38th session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Astana, Kazakhstan, on 28–30 June 2011. Permanent secretariat is in Khartoum, Sudan. ATAIC is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

other_names.name: Association of Tax Authorities of Islamic Countries
Association des autorités fiscales des pays islamiques
伊斯兰国家税务当局协会

name: Intra-European Organisation of Tax Administrations
description: Non-profit intergovernmental organisation that provides European tax administrations a platform for exchanging experiences and best practices on practical tax administration issues. Organises workshops and fora, publishes guidance for members, and promotes cooperation with international and regional partners including CIAT, the European Commission, the IMF, and the OECD.
notes: IOTA was established at the Conference of Tax Administrations of Central and Eastern Europe and Baltic Countries (CEEB), held in Warsaw on 28–30 October 1996, by the tax administrations of Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, and Slovakia. The organisation has since expanded to 43 full members and one associate member (Republic of Korea, from July 2021). The Secretariat is based in Budapest. Memberships of the Federal Tax Service of Russia and the Ministry of Taxes and Duties of Belarus were terminated in June 2023. IOTA is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

other_names.name: 歐洲內部稅務管理組織

provenance.note: membership_count counts national tax administrations; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: African Tax Administration Forum
description: Pan-African intergovernmental forum launched in Kampala on 19 November 2009, when 30 African tax commissioners signed the ATAF Agreement. Provides a platform for cooperation among African tax authorities through technical assistance, capacity building, research, and policy dialogue to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation and Africa's voice in global tax discussions.
notes: ATAF was conceived at a Pretoria conference in August 2008 and formally established in Kampala, Uganda, on 19 November 2009, when 30 African tax commissioners signed the founding agreement. Membership has grown from 25 countries at inauguration to 45 as of May 2026, when the Republic of Congo acceded as the 45th member; Algeria joined in 2024 and hosted the 2025 Annual Meetings in Algiers. ATAF is governed by a General Assembly, Council, and Secretariat in Pretoria, and is a founding member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

name: East African Revenue Authorities Forum
description: Cooperative forum of the revenue administrations of East African Community (EAC) partner states, inaugurated at the first Commissioners General meeting in 1999. Convenes biannually on a rotating basis to harmonise tax administration, share intelligence, and coordinate regional responses to common challenges such as cross-border tax evasion and digital economy taxation.
notes: EARAF brings together the Commissioners General of the EAC partner states' revenue authorities for biannual meetings (EARACG), supported by the East African Revenue Authorities Technical Committee (EARATC) and the Technical Committee on Integrity (EARATCI). Meetings rotate among member revenue authorities; the Zanzibar Revenue Board also participates alongside the mainland Tanzania Revenue Authority. Key outputs include the annual Regional Comparative Revenue Report and coordinated initiatives on customs harmonisation, domestic tax system integration, and anti-corruption measures. EARAF works closely with the EAC Secretariat and the African Tax Administration Forum (ATAF).

name: Cercle de Réflexion et d'Échange des Dirigeants des Administrations Fiscales
description: Francophone non-profit association founded in Yaoundé in 1982 that facilitates dialogue and exchange among senior officials of tax administrations from 30 French-speaking member countries across four continents. Promotes multilateral international cooperation through annual conferences, director seminars, working groups, and thematic meetings, and develops practical tax guidance through peer learning and best-practice sharing.
notes: CREDAF was initially named "Centre de Rencontres et d'Études des Dirigeants des Administrations fiscales" and adopted its current name in 2018 during the general assembly in Haiti. The organization was created in Yaoundé in 1982; founding members were Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Chad, Djibouti, France, Côte d'Ivoire, Lebanon, Mali, Morocco, Niger, Senegal, Togo, and Tunisia. CREDAF groups senior officials from 30 French-speaking member countries across four continents, plus Revenu Québec as associate member since 2020. CREDAF is a founding member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO) and an Addis Tax Initiative (ATI) supporting organisation. It has cooperation agreements with CIAT, OECD, UNDP, OIF, FERDI, and other partners.

other_names.name: Cercle de Réflexion et d'Échange des Dirigeants des Administrations Fiscales
Circle of Reflection and Exchange of Tax Administration Leaders

provenance.note: membership_count counts national tax administrations; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: West African Tax Administration Forum
description: Forum of the tax administrations of all 15 ECOWAS member states, established at an inaugural meeting in Abuja, Nigeria, on 12 September 2011. Coordinates regional tax policy, promotes harmonisation of tax laws and transparency, and supports capacity building to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation across West Africa.
notes: WATAF was formally established through adoption of its Agreement by the General Assembly of member states. Benin, Ghana, The Gambia, Liberia, and Nigeria were the original signatories at the inaugural Abuja meeting in September 2011. The forum now comprises all 15 ECOWAS member states and is governed by a General Assembly, a six-member Council, and a Secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary in Abuja. WATAF is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

other_names.name: Forum des Administrations Fiscales d'Afrique de l'Ouest
Fórum da Administração Fiscal da África Ocidental

name: Pacific Islands Tax Administrators Association
description: Regional forum for Pacific Island tax administrations, initiated in May 2003 at a seminar in Tonga organized by the Pacific Financial Technical Assistance Centre (PFTAC). Provides a platform for cooperation, information exchange, and policy coordination, and promotes international standards and best practices suited to Pacific Island countries through capacity building and professional development.
notes: PITAA was initiated in May 2003 during a seminar in Tonga attended by eight Pacific Island tax representatives and organized by PFTAC. The Secretariat is based in Suva, Fiji, and is governed by an Executive Committee reporting to annual Heads meetings. PITAA is a member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

name: Inter-American Center of Tax Administrations
description: Intergovernmental organization established in 1967 to support national governments in enhancing the development and institutional strengthening of tax administrations. Provides specialized technical assistance for modernization and strengthening of tax administrations, promotes international cooperation, and facilitates the exchange of experiences and best practices among tax administrations across the Americas and partner countries worldwide.
notes: CIAT comprises 42 member and associate member countries across four continents: 32 from the Americas, five European full members (France, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, and Spain), four African countries (Angola, Kenya, Morocco, and Nigeria), and one Asian country (India). Angola, India, Morocco, and Nigeria hold associate member status. The organization organizes annual events such as the General Assembly (April) and the Technical Conference (October). CIAT is a founding member of the Network of Tax Organizations (NTO).

provenance.note: membership_count counts national tax administrations; unit classified 2026-08, count value from earlier enrichment

name: Network of Tax Organizations
description: Global network of regional and international tax organisations, founded in Ottawa in May 2018, that provides a forum for cooperation and coordination among member organisations to strengthen tax administrations through peer learning and best-practice sharing. Through its ten member organisations, the NTO represents over 180 national tax administrations worldwide and supports effective domestic revenue mobilisation.

includes.name: Association of Tax Authorities of Islamic Countries
Cercle de Réflexion et d'Échange des Dirigeants des Administrations Fiscales
Study Group on Asia-Pacific Tax Administration and Research

notes: NTO was established in May 2018 in Ottawa, Canada, when ten regional and international tax organisations signed a memorandum of understanding. Governance comprises the NTO Assembly (heads of member secretariats), a five-member NTO Council (ATAF, CATA, CIAT, IOTA, and WATAF as of 2025), and a member-led Secretariat supported by the International Tax Compact (ITC) in Bonn. CATA chairs the NTO Council for 2025–2026. The network represents over 180 national tax administrations through its member organisations.

name: Civil law system
description: Legal system originating in continental Europe.

name: Bijuridical law system
description: The bijuridical law system is a legal system that is used in countries that have both civil law and common law.

name: Common law system
description: The common law system is a legal system that is used in countries that have both civil law and common law.

name: Islamic law system (Sharia)
description: The Islamic law system (Sharia) is a legal system that is used in countries that have both civil law and common law.

name: Quadrilateral Security Dialogue
description: Informal strategic security dialogue among Australia, India, Japan, and the United States, initiated in 2007 by Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe with support from Australian, Indian, and US leaders. The grouping coordinates diplomatic and security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific, including joint Malabar naval exercises and leader-level summits. Australia withdrew from the dialogue in 2008; all four countries revived the Quad at the 2017 ASEAN Summit in Manila. Not a formal treaty alliance and widely characterized as a consultative forum rather than a collective defense pact.
notes: First convened in 2007 with inaugural ministerial talks in Manila and parallel Malabar naval exercises. Australia stepped back in 2008 under Prime Minister Kevin Rudd; India, Japan, and the United States continued bilateral and trilateral security cooperation. Revived in November 2017 at the ASEAN Summit; held first leader-level virtual summit in March 2021. Operates without a secretariat or treaty charter; "Quad Plus" meetings have occasionally included additional partners on specific issues such as COVID-19 response.

name: NorthSeal
description: Joint security platform established following the Joint Declaration on cooperation regarding protection of infrastructure in the North Sea, signed on 9 April 2024 by six North Sea countries. Led by Belgium, NorthSeal enables maritime information bodies to monitor suspicious ship movements in real time, exchange threat data, and coordinate responses to sabotage, espionage, and other hybrid threats against critical underwater infrastructure such as pipelines, data cables, and offshore energy installations. NATO participates as an optional partner with access to shared information.
notes: Originated at the North Sea Summit in Ostend on 24 April 2023; joint declaration signed 9 April 2024. Belgium invested €1 million and developed the platform through Belgian Secure Communications (BSC). Operational launch followed a brief test phase on 15 January 2025. France, which has North Sea coastline, has not yet joined. NATO is included as an optional partner in the information exchange.

name: Alliance of Sahel States
description: Confederation and mutual defence alliance of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger in the Sahel. The Liptako-Gourma Charter, signed on 16 September 2023 during the Nigerien crisis, established a mutual defence pact after ECOWAS threatened military intervention following Niger's 2023 coup; Mali and Burkina Faso pledged to defend Niger, averting an ECOWAS intervention. Leaders signed a confederation treaty on 6 July 2024 in Niamey to deepen political and economic integration, including a rotating presidency, joint infrastructure, and a proposed monetary union. The United Force of the Alliance of Sahel States (FU-AES), a 5,000-strong joint military unit integrating air, land, and intelligence capabilities, was inaugurated in December 2025 with headquarters in Niamey. All three members withdrew from ECOWAS on 29 January 2025 after serving the required one-year notice. The bloc succeeded the Mali–Niger–Burkina track of the dissolved G5 Sahel.
notes: Mutual defence pact signed 16 September 2023 (Liptako-Gourma Charter); confederation treaty signed 6 July 2024 in Niamey. Rotating one-year presidency; Assimi Goïta (Mali) held the first term from July 2024, succeeded by Ibrahim Traoré (Burkina Faso) in December 2025. Members announced ECOWAS withdrawal on 28 January 2024 and completed exit on 29 January 2025. Joint AES passports circulated from January 2025. FU-AES joint force headquarters in Niamey; inaugural ceremony in Bamako, December 2025. All three states are military juntas that expelled Western military forces and deepened security cooperation with Russia from 2024 onward.

name: United Nations Command
description: Multinational military command established in 1950 to support South Korea during the Korean War and to uphold the Korean Armistice Agreement. The UNC enforces the armistice, facilitates diplomacy with North Korea, and integrates multinational forces during crises or conflicts on the Korean Peninsula.

name: G5 Sahel
description: Regional security and development alliance of Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger; dissolved in December 2023 after successive member withdrawals.
notes: Mali withdrew in May 2022; Burkina Faso and Niger withdrew in November 2023. Chad and Mauritania announced dissolution on 6 December 2023. The Mali–Niger–Burkina track continued via the Alliance of Sahel States (AES).

name: Combined Communications Electronics Board
description: Five-nation joint military communications-electronics (C-E) organization coordinating coalition C-E matters referred by member nations. The CCEB is the sponsoring authority for Allied Communications Publications (ACPs) and directs working groups on operational, procedural, and technical interoperability among Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Evolved from the wartime Combined Communications Board (1942); renamed the Combined Communications-Electronics Board in 1972 when New Zealand became a full member. Part of the Washington-based Multifora alongside ABCANZ Armies, AUSCANNZUKUS, and the Technical Cooperation Program.

other_names.name: Združeni odbor za komunikacije in elektroniko

notes: Established as the Combined Communications Board (CCB) in 1942 among the United Kingdom and United States during World War II; Canada became a full member in 1951, Australia in 1969, and New Zealand in 1972 when the body was renamed the Combined Communications-Electronics Board. The CCB was reduced after October 1949 with NATO's formation but UK–US coordination continued; CCEB interoperability activities are coordinated with NATO and the U.S. Military Communications Electronics Board. The U.S. representative is the Joint Chiefs of Staff Director for C4 Systems (J-6).

name: North Atlantic Treaty Organization
description: Intergovernmental military alliance between 32 member states.

other_names.name: Organisation du traité de l'Atlantique nord
Organização do Tratado do Atlântico Norte

name: UKUSA Agreement
description: Multilateral treaty for cooperation in signals intelligence (SIGINT) among Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Signed on 5 March 1946 by the United Kingdom and the United States, it formalized wartime BRUSA intelligence sharing and became the legal foundation of the Five Eyes alliance. Canada joined in 1948; Australia and New Zealand in 1956. The agreement governs exchange of intercepted communications, cryptanalysis, traffic analysis, and related intelligence products among participating signals-intelligence agencies.

other_names.name: United Kingdom – United States of America Agreement

notes: Evolved from the 1943 BRUSA Agreement and signed in Washington on 5 March 1946. Extended to Canada (1948), Australia and New Zealand (1956). Full treaty text was declassified and published jointly by GCHQ and the NSA on 25 June 2010. Underpins the Five Eyes (FVEY) intelligence community; related Five Eyes defence bodies include TTCP, AUSCANNZUKUS, and ABCANZ Armies.

name: Agreement on Strategic Partnership and Mutual Support
description: Bilateral treaty between Azerbaijan and Turkey signed in Baku on 16 August 2010, establishing strategic partnership and mutual assistance in military-political, military-technical, humanitarian, and economic cooperation. Each party pledges to support the other using all available means in the event of military attack or aggression. The agreement entered into force on 25 October 2011 after ratification by both parliaments and renews automatically every ten years unless a party withdraws.

other_names.name: Agreement on Strategic Partnership and Mutual Support
توافق‌نامه مشارکت راهبردی و حمایت متقابل
Acordo de Parceria Estratégica e Apoio Mútuo
Соглашение о стратегическом сотрудничестве между Турцией и Азербайджаном

notes: Signed in Baku by Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Abdullah Gül. Ratified by the National Assembly of Azerbaijan on 21 December 2010 and by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey on 2 February 2011. Registered with the United Nations by Turkey on 29 July 2013 (UN Treaty Series No. 51060).

name: Ukraine Defense Contact Group
description: Informal multinational forum coordinating military assistance to Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Also known as the Ramstein group or Ramstein format, the contact group convenes defense ministers and senior officials from NATO allies and partner countries at recurring meetings—often at Ramstein Air Base or NATO headquarters—to align equipment donations, training, production, and sustainment. It is not a treaty-based alliance; participation is established by attendance at group meetings. Capability coalitions formed within the group coordinate specialized support in areas such as air defense, armor, artillery, drones, and maritime security.

other_names.name: Groupe de contact sur la défense de l'Ukraine
Контактна група з питань оборони України

notes: No official static membership roster exists; countries are treated as participants when represented at one or more meetings. The inaugural session on 26 April 2022 at Ramstein Air Base drew about 39–41 countries. Argentina joined at the 23rd meeting on 13 June 2024. As of 2025, press reports cite roughly 50–57 participating states plus the European Union. The United States chaired through early 2025; Germany and the United Kingdom co-chair from 2025. Ukraine attends as aid recipient rather than a coalition member. Additional countries have provided military aid without publicly confirmed UDCG attendance.

name: Major non-NATO ally

includes.name: Taiwan
includes.note: Treated as MNNA under U.S. law without formal designation

includes.name: Afghanistan
includes.note: Revoked July 2022 after Taliban takeover

description: United States statutory designation (22 U.S.C. § 2321k) for close allies outside NATO, conferring enhanced defense cooperation benefits such as priority access to excess defense articles, cooperative research and development, and participation in certain U.S. defense programs.

name: Peninsula Shield Force
description: Joint military force of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), established in 1984 and permanently based at King Khalid Military City near Hafar al Batin in Saudi Arabia. The force integrates infantry, armour, artillery, and combat support contingents contributed by all six GCC member states for collective defence and crisis intervention in the Arabian Peninsula. Renamed the Unified Military Command of the GCC at the Al-Ula summit on 5 January 2021 to reflect deeper military integration; the legacy name Peninsula Shield Force remains widely used. Deployments include the 1991 liberation of Kuwait, the 2003 Kuwait defence build-up, and the 2011 Bahrain intervention.

other_names.name: Unified Military Command of the Gulf Cooperation Council
Fuerza del Escudo de la Península

notes: Created by the GCC in 1984 as a joint intervention force of initially 10,000 troops; permanent base at King Khalid Military City near Hafar al Batin. Renamed Unified Military Command at the GCC summit in Al-Ula on 5 January 2021. Any PSF deployment requires participation from all GCC member states per force doctrine. Notable operations include Kuwait liberation (1991), pre-Iraq War Kuwait defence (2003), and the March 2011 Bahrain deployment (Saudi Arabia and UAE troops; Kuwait and Oman did not send forces).

name: European Defence Agency
description: EU agency responsible for supporting member states in improving their defense capabilities and promoting European defense cooperation.

name: Inter-American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance
description: Hemispheric collective security treaty signed in Rio de Janeiro on 2 September 1947 and in force from 3 December 1948, establishing that an armed attack against any American state shall be considered an attack against all parties. Known as the Rio Pact or TIAR (Tratado Interamericano de Asistencia Recíproca), it was the first post-war mutual security agreement in the Americas and provided the regional defense framework alongside the OAS. Invoked during the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) and after the September 11 attacks (2001). Several Latin American states withdrew in the 2000s and 2010s; as of 2024 eighteen parties remain.
notes: Signed at Rio de Janeiro on 2 September 1947; entered into force 3 December 1948 after ratification by two-thirds of signatories (23 total signatories, 18 current parties). Cuba was suspended from treaty rights and obligations in 1962. Mexico denounced the treaty in September 2002 and ceased to be a party in September 2004. Bolivia, Ecuador, and Nicaragua withdrew in 2012–2014. Venezuela denounced the treaty in May 2013; the opposition-led National Assembly approved reincorporation in 2019 amid the presidential crisis. Uruguay briefly denounced the treaty in 2019 but withdrew its denunciation in March 2020. Trinidad and Tobago acceded in 1967 and The Bahamas in 1982. Canada is not a party.

name: Finabel
description: European land-forces organisation promoting cooperation and interoperability among member states' armies through harmonisation of concepts, doctrines, and procedures. Founded in 1953 as FINBEL by France, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands (renamed FINABEL when West Germany joined in 1956), Finabel is governed by member states' army chiefs of staff and produces studies, equipment agreements, and procedural conventions via working groups. Membership is open to EU member states; the permanent secretariat is in Brussels. Finabel complements NATO and EU military structures and operates by consensus among equal member states.
notes: Originally FINBEL (France, Italy, Belgium, Luxembourg, Netherlands); renamed FINABEL after West Germany joined in 1956. French was the official language until English became the working language across all levels in 2011.

name: Regional Security System
description: International defence and security arrangement for the Eastern Caribbean, established when Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Dominica, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines signed a memorandum of understanding on 29 October 1982 to provide mutual assistance on request in national emergencies, maritime policing, search and rescue, and threats to national security. Saint Kitts and Nevis joined after independence in 1983 and Grenada in 1985; juridical status was conferred by a treaty signed at St. George's, Grenada, on 5 March 1996. Headquartered at the Paragon Centre adjacent to Grantley Adams International Airport in Barbados, the RSS conducts counter-narcotics operations, disaster relief, and regional security coordination; Guyana acceded in September 2022, extending the system's reach to mainland South America.

other_names.name: 地域安全保障システム

notes: The 1982 MOU was signed by four OECS members together with Barbados; the system acquired treaty status on 5 March 1996. The RSS participated in the 1983 Grenada intervention (Operation Urgent Fury) alongside US forces. Since 2001 it cooperates with the CARICOM Regional Task Force on Crime and Security; the United States and Canada provide training and equipment support under the Caribbean Basin Security Initiative. Guyana signed the Instrument of Accession on 14 September 2022.

name: Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition
description: Intergovernmental counter-terrorist military alliance of Muslim-majority countries established to coordinate and support military operations against terrorism.

name: Nordic Defence Cooperation
description: Voluntary intergovernmental defence cooperation framework among Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden, established by memorandum of understanding signed in Helsinki on 4 November 2009. NORDEFCO succeeded parallel Nordic arrangements NORDSUP, NORDAC, and NORDCAPS and coordinates policy through Nordic ministers of defence and joint committees on strategic development, capabilities, training and exercises, operations, and human resources. Participation is voluntary and members may cooperate bilaterally or among all five; the organization is not a mutual-defence pact or integrated command structure, though members have added enhanced operational coordination agreements since 2021.
notes: Helsinki Declaration signed 4 November 2009; presidency rotates among member states while Nordic ministers of defence meet twice yearly. Five cooperation areas (COPAs) cover strategic development, capabilities, human resources and education, training and exercises, and operations, with Acquisition & Life Cycle Support (ALCS) screening armaments cooperation. Enhanced operational cooperation statements were signed for southern Nordic states (Denmark, Norway, Sweden, 2021) and northern Nordic states (Finland, Norway, Sweden, updated 2022); Denmark, Iceland, and Norway issued security assurances to Finland and Sweden during their 2022 NATO accession process.

name: European Intervention Initiative
description: Joint military initiative among 13 European countries operating outside NATO and EU institutional frameworks, launched with a letter of intent signed in Paris on 25 June 2018. EII aims to develop a shared strategic culture through strategic foresight, intelligence sharing, scenario planning, operational support, and lessons learned, with a light permanent secretariat hosted by France. Participation is voluntary and not all members need join every operation; the United Kingdom and Denmark participate despite not being in EU CSDP.
notes: Proposed by Emmanuel Macron in September 2017; first ministerial meeting in Paris November 2018. Finland joined November 2018; Norway, Sweden, and Italy joined at the Hilversum ministerial meeting on 20 September 2019 when Terms of Reference were signed. Operates alongside but outside CSDP and PESCO; eight participants launched the EMASoH maritime security operation in the Strait of Hormuz from late 2019.

name: ABCANZ Armies
description: Formal program of the American, British, Canadian, Australian, and New Zealand armies (plus the United States Marine Corps and Royal Marines) that optimizes coalition interoperability and standardization of training and equipment among Five Eyes land forces.

other_names.name: American, British, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand Armies' Program
美英澳新加五国陆军合作计划

notes: Established in 1947 among the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada; Australia joined in 1963; New Zealand was an observer from 1965 and became a full member in 2006. The United States Army hosts the permanent Program Office.

name: Organization of the Eurasian Law Enforcement Agencies with Military Status
description: Intergovernmental cooperation organization of gendarmerie and other military-status law enforcement agencies from Turkic states, established in Ankara on 25 January 2013. The acronym TAKM derives from the founding participants Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, and Mongolia. Member agencies coordinate training, operations, and institutional exchange; the organization is often described as a Eurasian counterpart to FIEP (Association of European and Mediterranean Police Forces and Gendarmeries with Military Status). Mongolia declined to sign the foundation agreement and withdrew in 2014; Kazakhstan subsequently applied for membership amid plans to reorganize the body on a new basis.

other_names.name: Organization of the Eurasian Law Enforcement Agencies with Military Status
سازمان اجرای قانون و وضعیت نظامی اوراسیا
Avrasya Askeri Statülü Kolluk Kuvvetleri Teşkilatı

notes: Established at a founding ceremony in Ankara on 25 January 2013 with Turkey, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, and Mongolia as initial participants. In 2014 Mongolia refused to sign the foundation agreement and quit; Kazakhstan applied for membership, leading to plans to reestablish the organization on a new basis. Headquarters hosted by the Turkish Gendarmerie General Command in Ankara.

name: Five Eyes Air Force Interoperability Council
description: Formal military organization comprising the air forces of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. AFIC enhances interoperability among these Five Eyes nations' air forces by standardizing doctrine, operational procedures, materiel, and equipment across various air power functions. Originally established as the Air Standards Coordinating Committee (ASCC) in 1948, it was restructured as the Air and Space Interoperability Council (ASIC) in 2005 and renamed AFIC in 2017.

other_names.name: המועצה לפעילות הדדית של חיל האוויר
Совет по интероперабельности воздушных и космических войск
Five Eyes Air Force Interoperability Council

notes: Formed in 1948 as the Air Standards Coordinating Committee (ASCC) by Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States; the Royal Australian Air Force joined in 1964 and the Royal New Zealand Air Force in 1965. Restructured and renamed the Air and Space Interoperability Council (ASIC) in 2005; realigned as the Five Eyes Air Force Interoperability Council (AFIC) in 2017. Notable for maintaining NATO-style reporting names for Soviet, Russian, and Chinese aircraft. Pentagon-based Management Committee coordinates day-to-day operations. Part of the Washington-based Five Eyes defence interoperability community alongside ABCANZ Armies, AUSCANNZUKUS, the Combined Communications Electronics Board, and TTCP.

name: AUKUS
description: Trilateral security partnership announced on 15 September 2021 among Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States to promote a free and open Indo-Pacific that is secure and stable. AUKUS operates through two pillars. Pillar 1 focuses on Australia acquiring nuclear-powered attack submarines, including the jointly developed SSN-AUKUS class and interim Virginia-class acquisitions, and on rotational basing of US and UK nuclear-powered submarines in Australia. Pillar 2 covers collaborative development of advanced capabilities in undersea systems, quantum technologies, artificial intelligence and autonomy, advanced cyber, hypersonic and counter-hypersonic weapons, and electronic warfare. Unlike ANZUS, AUKUS is not a mutual defence treaty but a technology and capability partnership; nuclear propulsion sharing builds on the long-standing US–UK Mutual Defence Agreement framework.
notes: Announced jointly by Australian prime minister Scott Morrison, British prime minister Boris Johnson, and US president Joe Biden on 15 September 2021. Australia cancelled its French Attack-class submarine contract the same day in favour of nuclear propulsion cooperation under AUKUS. The Exchange of Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information Agreement (ENNPIA) entered into force on 8 February 2022. Pillar 2 expansion talks have considered Japan and New Zealand as potential partners; no additional full members have joined. Related Five Eyes and anglosphere defence bodies include ANZUS, FVEY, TTCP, and AUSCANNZUKUS. No single headquarters location.

name: Southeast Asia Treaty Organization
description: Cold War collective defense alliance established by the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty (Manila Pact), signed in Manila on 8 September 1954 by Australia, France, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The organization was formally instituted on 19 February 1955 in Bangkok, with headquarters there. Modeled partly on NATO but without joint commands or standing forces; internal disagreements limited collective military action, though SEATO membership provided a rationale for large-scale U.S. involvement in Vietnam. Pakistan withdrew on 7 November 1973; France ended financial support in 1975; the alliance was phased out and formally dissolved on 30 June 1977.

other_names.name: Organización del Tratado del Sureste Asiático
Organisation du traité de l'Asie du Sud-Est
Organização do Tratado do Sudeste Asiático
องค์การสนธิสัญญาป้องกันภูมิภาคเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้
Tổ chức Hiệp ước Đông Nam Á

notes: The Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty was signed in Manila on 8 September 1954; SEATO was formally established at the first Council of Ministers meeting in Bangkok on 19 February 1955. Only the Philippines and Thailand were Southeast Asian members; Cambodia, Laos, and South Vietnam were covered as protocol states under Geneva Agreement restrictions but were not full members. Pakistan gave notice of withdrawal on 8 November 1972 and ceased membership on 7 November 1973; France withdrew financial support in 1975. A final exercise was held on 20 February 1976 before dissolution on 30 June 1977.

name: Warsaw Pact
description: Cold War collective defense alliance of Soviet-aligned states.

name: Eurocorps
description: Multinational army corps headquarters in Strasbourg, founded by France and Germany in 1992 and declared operational in 1995. Six framework nations (Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, Poland, and Spain) place the corps at the disposal of the European Union and NATO; NATO certified it in 2002 as one of nine High Readiness Land Headquarters. Five associated nations (Austria, Greece, Italy, Romania, and Turkey) contribute personnel under separate arrangements. Governed since 2009 by the Treaty of Strasbourg (signed 22 November 2004).
notes: Framework nations hold full membership under the Treaty of Strasbourg; associated nations contribute staff without framework-nation status. Poland became the sixth framework nation in 2022 after earlier associate participation. Austria was an associated nation from 2002 to 2011 and rejoined in 2021. The United Kingdom and the Netherlands participated as associated nations from 1999 to 2002; Finland (2002–2006) and Canada (2003–2007) were later associated nations. Commander rotates among framework nations.

name: Five Eyes
description: Multinational intelligence and military alliance comprising Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Rooted in the 1946 UKUSA Agreement for signals intelligence (SIGINT) cooperation, the Five Eyes community expanded over time to include significant military cooperation, joint exercises, technology sharing, and interoperability initiatives across air, land, and naval forces.
notes: The Five Eyes label describes the core anglosphere intelligence community underpinned by the UKUSA Agreement (1946). Canada joined in 1948; Australia and New Zealand in 1956, completing the five-member core. Related Five Eyes defence bodies include TTCP, AUSCANNZUKUS, ABCANZ Armies, and AFIC. Extended intelligence sharing groups include Nine Eyes and Fourteen Eyes.

name: Permanent Structured Cooperation
description: Voluntary EU framework established by Council Decision (CFSP) 2017/2315 on 11 December 2017 for willing member states to jointly plan, develop, and invest in shared defence capabilities. Twenty-five states activated PESCO in December 2017; Denmark became the 26th participant on 23 May 2023. Malta remains the only EU member state outside PESCO, citing constitutional neutrality.
notes: Malta is the sole EU member state not participating in PESCO. Denmark joined after abolishing its CSDP opt-out in a 2022 referendum; Council Decision (CFSP) 2023/1015 confirmed Danish participation on 23 May 2023.

name: Technical Cooperation Program
description: Long-standing intergovernmental program for cooperation on defence science and technology among Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Established bilaterally between the UK and US in 1957 following the Declaration of Common Purpose; Canada joined immediately to form the Tripartite Technical Cooperation Program, Australia in 1965, and New Zealand in 1969. TTCP coordinates multilateral technical panels on aerospace, land, maritime, C3I, sensors, and related priority areas among Five Eyes defence research communities.
notes: Began as UK–US bilateral cooperation in 1957; expanded to Canada (Tripartite), then Australia (1965) and New Zealand (1969). TTCP Principals are supported by deputies based in Washington. Part of the broader Five Eyes defence science and technology community alongside ABCANZ Armies, AUSCANNZUKUS, and the Combined Communications Electronics Board.

name: International security assistance force
description: NATO-led security mission in Afghanistan, 2001–14.

other_names.name: قوات المساعدة الدولية لإرساء الأمن في أفغانستان
Fuerza Internacional de Asistencia para la Seguridad
Force internationale d'assistance et de sécurité
Força Internacional de Assistência para Segurança
駐阿富汗國際維和部隊

name: African Standby Force
description: Multidisciplinary peacekeeping force established by the African Union to respond swiftly to crises across Africa. The ASF comprises military, police, and civilian components organized into five regional standby brigades (Eastern Africa, North Africa, West Africa/ECOWAS, Central Africa, and Southern Africa). It is designed for deployment in various scenarios including humanitarian assistance, peacekeeping, and intervention in member states experiencing grave circumstances.

name: Collective Rapid Reaction Force
description: Joint combined-arms task force comprising independent military units contributed by Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) member states, established by agreement signed at the Moscow summit on 4 February 2009. Mandated to counter limited military aggression against CSTO members and to conduct operations against terrorism and drug trafficking. Belarus acceded on 20 October 2009 after Armenia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan signed at the founding summit; first joint exercises followed in October 2009 at the Matybulak firing range in Kazakhstan.
notes: Agreement on creation signed 4 February 2009 by Armenia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, and Tajikistan; Belarus joined 20 October 2009. Operates under the CSTO Joint Staff in Moscow. Contributing units include Russian airborne and spetsnaz formations, Kazakh air assault and special operations elements, the Belarusian 103rd Guards Airborne Brigade, the Armenian 12th Peacekeeping Brigade, a Kyrgyz infantry battalion under the Scorpion 25th Special Forces Brigade, and a Tajik infantry battalion under the Mobile Forces.

name: AUSCANNZUKUS
description: Naval Command, Control, Communications, and Computers (C4) interoperability organization comprising Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Originated from 1960 dialogue between Admirals Arleigh Burke and Louis Mountbatten to align naval communications policies ahead of new equipment; matured into the current five-nation body when New Zealand became a full member in 1980. AUSCANNZUKUS fosters knowledge sharing and C4 interoperability among Five Eyes navies through a supervisory board, C4 Committee, and subordinate working groups, increasing operational effectiveness through standardized procedures, equipment, and systems for combined naval operations. Also used as a security caveat in the UKUSA/Five Eyes community.

other_names.name: 澳新美英加五国海军合作计划
澳新美英加五國海軍合作計劃

notes: Originated from UK–US naval communications dialogue in 1960; New Zealand became a full member in 1980, completing the five-nation organization. name: Five Power Defence Arrangements
description: Consultative defence arrangement established in 1971 among Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand, Singapore, and the United Kingdom following the UK's withdrawal of forces east of Suez. The five powers agree to consult immediately in the event of external armed attack or threat against Malaysia or Singapore, but the arrangement carries no binding commitment to intervene militarily. Headquarters Integrated Area Defence System (HQIADS) at RMAF Butterworth coordinates joint air, land, and maritime exercises including the annual Exercise Bersama Lima. Unlike integrated alliances such as NATO, the FPDA has no standing combined forces or mutual-defence treaty obligation.

notes: Established after termination of the Anglo-Malayan Defence Agreement when the United Kingdom completed its east-of-Suez withdrawal on 1 November 1971. The 16 April 1971 Joint Communiqué set the consultative framework; HQIADS at RMAF Butterworth (command rotates among member states) also supports UK personnel at Sembawang, Singapore. Annual FPDA Defence Ministers' Meeting and Defence Chiefs' Conference coordinate policy; official website launched at the 12th FDMM in May 2024.

name: Arctic Coast Guard Forum
description: Independent, informal, operationally driven forum that unites the coast guard agencies of the eight Arctic states to foster safe, secure, and environmentally responsible maritime activity in the Arctic. Established on 30 October 2015 and modeled on the North Atlantic and North Pacific Coast Guard Forums, the ACGF coordinates search and rescue, environmental protection, and maritime safety among member coast guards without treaty obligations. Membership mirrors the Arctic Council states; the rotating two-year chairmanship also follows Arctic Council chairmanship cycles. The forum is separate from the Arctic Council but maintains a statement of cooperation with it.
notes: Eight Arctic states participate through their coast guard or equivalent maritime safety agencies (Canada — Canadian Coast Guard; Denmark — Joint Arctic Command; Finland — Finnish Border Guard; Iceland — Icelandic Coast Guard; Norway — Norwegian Coast Guard; Russian Federation — Russian Coast Guard (FSB); Sweden — Swedish Coast Guard; United States — U.S. Coast Guard). Chairmanship rotates among members every two years in parallel with Arctic Council chair cycles. Live exercises include Arctic Guardian 2017 (Iceland) and Polaris 2019 (Finland); a 2018 simulator exercise was held in Turku, Finland. The forum builds on earlier Arctic SAR (2011) and oil-spill preparedness (2013) agreements among the same states.

name: International Maritime Security Construct

name: Central Treaty Organization
description: Cold War mutual defense alliance formed as the Baghdad Pact on 24 February 1955 by Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. Renamed the Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) in August 1959 after Iraq withdrew following the 1958 revolution; headquarters moved from Baghdad to Ankara in 1958. Modeled partly on NATO but without a unified military command; the United States participated in CENTO military committees from 1958 without full treaty membership. Dissolved on 16 March 1979 after Iran and Pakistan withdrew during the Iranian Revolution.
notes: Originally the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO); Iraq and Turkey signed the Baghdad Pact on 24 February 1955, with the United Kingdom (5 April), Pakistan (23 September), and Iran (3 November) acceding the same year. Iraq withdrew on 24 March 1959 after the 14 July 1958 revolution; the pact was renamed CENTO on 19 August 1959. Iran withdrew on 11 March 1979, Pakistan on 12 March 1979, and the United Kingdom and Turkey on 16 March 1979 when the alliance was formally disbanded.

description: International association of national gendarmeries and police forces with military status, founded in 1994 by France, Italy, and Spain and named FIEP after Portugal joined in 1996. Work is organized through a Senior Council of force commanders, a rotating annual presidency, and four commissions on human resources, service organization, new technologies and logistics, and international affairs. name: Australia, New Zealand, United States Security Treaty
description: Collective security treaty signed in San Francisco on 1 September 1951 and in force from 29 April 1952 among Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. The parties commit to maintaining capacity to resist armed attack, consulting on Pacific security matters, and acting to meet common danger in accordance with constitutional processes. Unlike NATO, ANZUS has no integrated command structure or standing forces; Australia and the United States conduct extensive bilateral exercises and operate joint facilities. New Zealand remains a treaty party but US treaty obligations toward New Zealand were suspended in 1986 over nuclear ship access; bilateral AU–US and AU–NZ cooperation continues under the treaty framework.
notes: Signed at San Francisco on 1 September 1951; entered into force 29 April 1952 ([1952] ATS 2). New Zealand's anti-nuclear port policy led the United States to suspend its ANZUS obligations toward New Zealand in 1986; the treaty remains in force between Australia and the United States and between Australia and New Zealand. Annual Australia–US Ministerial (AUSMIN) consultations replaced trilateral ANZUS Council meetings after 1985.

Belgium joined in 2003 and Spain in 2005. Other European states may participate in individual programmes as non-member participating states or observers without full membership.

name: Camp David Principles
description: Trilateral security partnership announced at Camp David, Maryland, on 18 August 2023 among Japan, the Republic of Korea, and the United States. The Camp David Principles establish a framework for enhanced collective security in the Indo-Pacific, including a commitment to consult on regional challenges, annual joint military exercises, real-time ballistic missile defence information sharing, and a trilateral security cooperation framework. The pact implements a formal casus foederis in which a threat to one member constitutes a threat against all, but does not mirror NATO Article 5—collective response must be discussed. Related US-led Indo-Pacific security bodies include AUKUS and the Quad.
notes: Announced jointly by US president Joe Biden, Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida, and South Korean president Yoon Suk Yeol at Camp David on 18 August 2023—the first trilateral leaders' summit hosted at the presidential retreat since 2015. The summit produced the Camp David Principles, a joint leaders' statement, and a Commitment to Consult. The first Indo-Pacific Dialogue under the framework was held in Washington, D.C., on 5 January 2024. No permanent headquarters; coordination occurs through annual trilateral meetings and working-level dialogues.

name: Baltic Naval Squadron
description: Trilateral Baltic naval cooperation project among Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, inaugurated in August 1998 to improve interoperability, mine countermeasures capability, and readiness for NATO-led operations. Each state contributes ships on rotation and staff for one-year assignments; Estonia hosts the BALTRON staff and communications training centre. Supporting nations signed a 1998 memorandum of understanding to assist development of the squadron as a mine countermeasures force aligned with NATO standards.
notes: Intergovernmental agreement on establishment signed in Riga on 16 April 1998; inauguration ceremony held at Tallinn Naval Base on 28 August 1998. Twelve supporting nations signed a June 1998 memorandum of understanding to assist development of BALTRON. In 2015 Estonia withdrew its permanent ship contribution while remaining in the framework; Latvia and Lithuania continue rotating mine countermeasures units. Related Baltic defence cooperation projects include BALTBAT, BALTNET, and BALTDEFCOL.

name: Individual Partnership Action Plan

IPAPs coordinated bilateral assistance from Allies and international institutions and were periodically reviewed with NATO. Eight countries concluded IPAPs between 2004 and 2015. In March 2021 the North Atlantic Council adopted the "One Partner, One Plan" concept, progressively replacing IPAPs with Individually Tailored Partnership Programmes (ITPPs) as NATO's primary tool for deepening bilateral partner cooperation; the IPAP framework was phased out by 2023.

name: INOGATE (INterstate Oil and GAs Transportation to Europe)
description: EU-funded international energy co-operation programme between the European Union, the littoral states of the Black and Caspian seas and their neighbouring countries, operational from 1996 to 2016. Initially focused on oil and gas pipeline transportation from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to the EU, it evolved after the 2004 Baku Initiative and 2006 Astana Declaration into a broader energy partnership covering energy security, market convergence with EU internal energy market principles, sustainable energy development, and investment attraction. Its Technical Secretariat in Kyiv was discontinued in April 2016.
notes: Partner countries were Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan; Turkey was a partner country but not a beneficiary, and the Russian Federation held observer status only. Funded by the Tacis Regional Cooperation Programme until 2006 and thereafter by the European Neighbourhood and Partnership Instrument (ENPI). The coordinating Technical Secretariat was based in Kyiv with regional offices in Tbilisi and Tashkent. After the programme closed in 2016, EU regional energy cooperation with the 11 partner countries continued through international bodies such as the International Energy Agency, the Energy Community Secretariat and the Energy Charter.

description: EU-backed intergovernmental transport programme linking Europe, the Black Sea basin, the South Caucasus, and Central Asia through road, rail, maritime, and aviation corridors. Launched at a Brussels conference in May 1993, its cornerstone is the Basic Multilateral Agreement on International Transport for Development of the Europe-the Caucasus-Asia Corridor (MLA), signed in Baku on 8 September 1998 by twelve states. The Intergovernmental Commission coordinates corridor development, customs harmonisation, infrastructure investment, and working groups on maritime transport, aviation, road and rail, transport security, and transport infrastructure.

other_names.name: 歐洲–高加索–亞洲運輸走廊計劃

The programme was originally financed by the European Commission through Tacis and later ENPI instruments; the Permanent Secretariat in Baku has been hosted by Azerbaijan since its inauguration in February 2001.

name: China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway
description: International railway project under construction linking Kashgar in western China to Andijan in eastern Uzbekistan via Kyrgyzstan. The 532-kilometre corridor spans 158 km in China, 305 km in Kyrgyzstan, and 69 km in Uzbekistan, crossing the Torugart Pass and requiring a break-of-gauge facility at Makmal. A strategic component of China's Belt and Road Initiative, the line is designed to reduce overland transit times between China and Europe and improve Central Asian connectivity. Construction began in 2025 with completion expected by 2029.
notes: The three governments signed a trilateral agreement to proceed in June 2024; project financing was finalised in December 2025. The line will initially be single-track and non-electrified, with electrification and dual-gauge conversion planned in a second phase. Standard gauge (1,435 mm) applies in China and Russian gauge (1,520 mm) in Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. Estimated cost was reported at US$4.7 billion in 2024, funded through Chinese concessional loans, multilateral development financing, and domestic contributions from Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan.

name: International Patient Summary
legal_status: Global health informatics standards initiative coordinated through the Joint Initiative Council
description: Global health informatics initiative developing a minimal, non-exhaustive, specialty-agnostic clinical dataset for unplanned and cross-border patient care. Coordinated through the Joint Initiative Council on Global Health Informatics Standardisation (JIC) among HL7, CEN/TC 251, ISO/TC 215, IHE, and SNOMED International, the International Patient Summary (IPS) is specified in ISO 27269 and implemented through HL7 FHIR and CDA implementation guides. The work evolved from the European Patient Summary and the epSOS large-scale pilot, and is adopted nationally through programmes such as the G7 International Patient Summary Roadmap, MyHealth@EU cross-border services, and national patient summary deployments in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, and the United States.
notes: IPS is a standards ecosystem rather than a treaty-based organization; includes lists countries with documented national or cross-border IPS implementation initiatives per the G7-IPS roadmap (December 2021), the IPS Implementation Registry, and European eHealth Network patient-summary programmes building on epSOS. G7 adopters (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, United Kingdom, United States) committed to open, interoperable patient-summary standards in 2021. Additional documented deployments include Australia, Brazil, Haiti, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, and Oman. European participants reflect continuing cross-border patient-summary infrastructure aligned with MyHealth@EU and CEN TS 17288. Major EHR vendors including Epic and MEDITECH announced IPS support from 2024.
