The United States manages the program as the sponsoring DoD bilateral partner.

name: Trans-Asian Railway

secretariat.note: Coordinates implementation of the Intergovernmental Agreement on the Trans-Asian Railway Network under the Asian Land Transport Infrastructure Development programme

description: ESCAP-led programme to create an integrated freight and passenger railway network across Asia with links to Europe and the Middle East. Planning began under the Asian Land Transport Infrastructure Development project in 1992; the Intergovernmental Agreement on the Trans-Asian Railway Network was adopted by ESCAP in April 2006, opened for signature in Busan in November 2006, and entered into force on 11 June 2009. The network comprises four main corridors — Northern, Southern, Southeast Asian, and North–South — spanning roughly 125,500 km of railway lines across 28 member countries, with coordinated development of lines of international importance, break-of-gauge transfer facilities, and interoperability standards. Sometimes called the Iron Silk Road.

other_names.name: ทางรถไฟสายเอเชีย

notes: Twenty-eight ESCAP member states are designated as Trans-Asian Railway network countries in Agreement annexes; 22 were parties to the Intergovernmental Agreement as of 2025. Armenia, Azerbaijan, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, and Singapore participate in the network but had not deposited instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval, or accession by mid-2025. Japan and the Philippines are listed as potential future members. ESCAP coordinates the network alongside the Asian Highway Network and dry ports of international significance.

name: Eastern Partnership
description: Joint EU initiative launched at the Prague summit on 7 May 2009 as the Eastern dimension of the European Neighbourhood Policy, bringing the European Union and its member states together with six post-Soviet Eastern European countries to deepen political association, economic integration, and sectoral cooperation. The partnership promotes shared values of democracy, rule of law, and human rights while supporting reforms, connectivity, trade, mobility, and civil-society engagement through bilateral and multilateral tracks, including association agreements, the EaP Civil Society Forum, and EURONEST.
notes: Belarus joined as a full partner at the 2009 Prague launch but suspended its participation on 28 June 2021; the EU continues limited engagement with Belarusian civil society. Five partner countries — Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine — remain active participants. Ukraine and Moldova are on EU accession paths; Georgia's EU trajectory depends on democratic reforms. Regional cooperation platforms include EURONEST, CORLEAP, and the EaP Civil Society Forum. Poland and Sweden co-authored the 2008 proposal that led to the initiative.

name: Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation Program
description: Asian Development Bank–hosted regional cooperation program linking eleven countries across Central Asia, the Caucasus, South Asia, and adjoining parts of East Asia through coordinated infrastructure investment and policy dialogue. Launched in 1997 among Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan, and the Xinjiang region of China, it has expanded through successive accessions to cover Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Mongolia, Pakistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan. CAREC prioritises six multimodal transport corridors, energy connectivity, trade facilitation, and customs harmonisation under the CAREC 2030 strategic framework, mobilising development finance from ADB and partner institutions including AIIB, EBRD, IMF, IsDB, UNDP, and the World Bank.

other_names.name: برنامج التعاون الاقتصادي الإقليمي لآسيا الوسطى
中亚区域经济合作项目
Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation Program
Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation Program

notes: Georgia participated as an observer at the 14th Ministerial Conference in 2015 before becoming the eleventh member in 2016. ADB placed its regular assistance to Afghanistan on hold effective 15 August 2021 and has supported the Afghan people through a special financing arrangement with the United Nations since 2022. The CAREC Institute, owned and managed by member countries, provides knowledge and capacity-building services; its physical base opened in Urumqi, Xinjiang, in 2015.

name: Belt and Road Initiative
recognition_status: Chinese government-led infrastructure and connectivity initiative announced by President Xi Jinping in 2013; countries join by signing bilateral Memoranda of Understanding with China
description: Major infrastructure and economic development initiative launched by China in 2013, focusing on connectivity and cooperation between countries along the ancient Silk Road routes and beyond. The initiative encompasses transport infrastructure projects including railways, roads, ports, and pipelines, as well as energy, telecommunications, and economic cooperation. Countries join by signing bilateral Memoranda of Understanding with China. As of May 2025, 150 countries maintain active BRI cooperation agreements; Italy exited in December 2023 and Panama in February 2025.

other_names.name: Iniciativa de la Franja y la Ruta

notes: Membership is tracked via bilateral MoU signatures rather than a single treaty instrument. MoU dates and membership status are compiled from official Chinese sources, press releases, and independent research; Austria, Niger, and the Russian Federation appear on some BRI country lists but independent confirmation of a full bilateral MoU is limited or disputed. Italy (joined 2019-03) did not renew its MoU and exited in December 2023; Panama (joined 2017-06) exited in February 2025. Some MoUs may have expired after initial five-year terms without public renewal.

name: Visa Waiver Program
legal_status: U.S. government program administered by the Department of Homeland Security in consultation with the Department of State
description: U.S. government program, administered by the Department of Homeland Security in consultation with the Department of State since 1986, that permits eligible citizens of 42 designated countries to travel to the United States for business or tourism for up to 90 days without a visa. Participating countries must grant reciprocal visa-free travel to U.S. citizens and nationals. Travelers must obtain pre-travel authorization through the Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA). DHS conducts biennial national-level risk assessments of each participating country and may suspend or terminate designation when security interests require it.
notes: Taiwan eligibility applies only to individuals with unrestricted right of permanent abode on Taiwan who hold an electronic passport bearing a personal identification (household registration) number. United Kingdom eligibility applies only to British citizens with unrestricted right of permanent abode in England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Channel Islands, and the Isle of Man; British overseas citizens and dependent territories citizens are excluded. Argentina and Uruguay were former participants (terminated 2002 and 2003 respectively). Romania was designated in January 2025 but the designation was rescinded in May 2025 before implementation.

name: China-Europe Land-Sea Express Line
description: Multimodal logistics corridor and Belt and Road Initiative component linking Chinese ports to Central and Eastern Europe via maritime shipping to Piraeus in Greece and overland rail and trucking through the Balkans. China, Serbia, Hungary, and North Macedonia agreed in 2014 to develop the corridor; COSCO Shipping fully launched scheduled services in 2017 after acquiring Piraeus container terminals from 2008. The route integrates with European networks including the Orient-East Med Corridor and the Budapest–Belgrade railway, shortening transit to Central Europe by up to 7–10 days compared with northern European ports. In 2022 the corridor handled about 181,000 TEUs on more than 2,600 train trips, serving inland European destinations including Austria, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Romania, Slovakia, and Spain.
notes: The corridor depends on COSCO Shipping's majority stake in Piraeus Port (concession from 2008, majority ownership from 2016). Weekly rail services from Piraeus connect to multiple inland European stations; the Budapest–Belgrade upgrade, expected by 2026, anchors the Balkan rail segment. The line complements the China–Europe Railway Express as a third major China–Europe trade channel.

name: Smart Open Services for European Patients
legal_status: EU ICT Policy Support Programme large-scale pilot
description: European Union co-funded large-scale eHealth pilot (2008–2014) that developed, tested, and evaluated cross-border services for exchanging patient summaries and electronic prescriptions (ePrescriptions) among national healthcare systems. Involving 25 participating nations — 22 EU member states plus Norway, Switzerland, and Turkey — and about 50 beneficiary organisations, epSOS built interoperability specifications, governance frameworks, and a National Contact Point infrastructure tested through 16 live pilot operations from April 2012. Results informed subsequent European initiatives including the eHealth Network, EXPAND, OpenNCP, MyHealth@EU, and the International Patient Summary standards work.

other_names.name: Smart Open Services for European Patients
Smart Open Services für europäische Patienten
Services ouverts intelligents pour les patients européens
Servicios abiertos inteligentes para pacientes europeos

notes: Participating nations comprised 22 EU member states plus three non-EU countries (Norway, Switzerland, Turkey). Turkey joined in the project's second phase from January 2011. Pilot operation of patient-summary and ePrescription services began on 13 April 2012. The project was co-funded under the ICT Policy Support Programme (ICT PSP) with an EU contribution of approximately €18 million. Sweden coordinated the consortium. Follow-on work continued through the EXPAND project and the OpenNCP open-source community before cross-border patient-summary standards evolved into the International Patient Summary (IPS) initiative.

name: EU-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Comprehensive bilateral free trade agreement signed on 9 July 2023; entered into force on 1 May 2024 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Comprehensive free trade agreement between the European Union and New Zealand, signed on 9 July 2023 and entered into force on 1 May 2024. Upon entry into force, 91% of New Zealand's goods exports to the EU had their duties removed, with this figure set to rise to 97% after seven years. All tariffs on EU exports to New Zealand were eliminated. The agreement includes enforceable commitments to the Paris Climate Agreement and core ILO standards, and protects EU geographical indications for wines, spirits, and traditional food products.

other_names.name: New Zealand-European Union Free Trade Agreement

provenance.source: New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade
WTO Regional Trade Agreements Information System

name: United States-Singapore Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Bilateral free trade agreement signed on 6 May 2003; entered into force on 1 January 2004 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Bilateral trade agreement between the United States and Singapore, signed on 6 May 2003 and implemented on 1 January 2004. The first U.S. free trade agreement with an Asian nation, it eliminated tariffs on all U.S. goods immediately while the U.S. phased out tariffs on Singaporean goods over up to 10 years. The agreement provides substantial access to services and investment markets and includes provisions on intellectual property, government procurement, and e-commerce.

name: Pacific Alliance
recognition_status: Regional integration initiative established by the Lima Declaration on 28 April 2011; Framework Agreement signed on 6 June 2012; four member states (Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru); Singapore is the first associated state after its free trade agreement entered into force on 3 May 2025; Costa Rica admitted as a membership candidate in December 2024; Panama is an official membership candidate
description: Latin American regional integration initiative and trade bloc comprising Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru, established by the Lima Declaration on 28 April 2011 and consolidated through the Framework Agreement signed on 6 June 2012. Aims at deep integration toward free movement of goods, services, capital and people, with strategic orientation toward the Asia-Pacific region. Singapore became the first associated state when the Pacific Alliance–Singapore free trade agreement entered into force on 3 May 2025. Costa Rica and Panama are official candidates for full membership.
notes: Full member count is four. membership_count reflects founding members plus associated state (Singapore) and membership candidates (Costa Rica, Panama). Observer states are tracked in the trade-bloc record PACALL.

name: EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Comprehensive partnership agreement between the European Union and the four founding Mercosur member states (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay), signed on 17 January 2026; the interim Trade Agreement (iTA) entered provisional application on 1 May 2026 after Mercosur parties completed domestic ratification; full Partnership Agreement (EMPA) awaits consent of the European Parliament and ratification by all EU member states
description: Comprehensive partnership agreement between the European Union and the four founding Mercosur member states, signed on 17 January 2026 in Paraguay. The interim Trade Agreement (iTA) entered provisional application on 1 May 2026, establishing a WTO-consistent free trade area while the full Partnership Agreement (EMPA) undergoes ratification. Upon full implementation, the agreement will eliminate tariffs on approximately 91% of EU exports to Mercosur and 92% of Mercosur exports to the EU, with tariff dismantling over up to 15 years for sensitive products. The agreement includes enforceable commitments on the Paris Climate Agreement, labour standards, and deforestation, and protects EU geographical indications.
notes: Negotiations began in 2000; a first agreement in principle on the trade pillar was reached on 28 June 2019 and an improved political agreement on 6 December 2024. The signed package comprises the EU-Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA, including political, cooperation, and trade pillars) and a separate interim Trade Agreement (iTA) covering trade matters only; the iTA will be repealed once the EMPA enters fully into force. Bolivia, which became a full Mercosur member in 2024, is not a party to this agreement. Venezuela remains suspended from Mercosur and is not a party.

name: China-Nicaragua Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Bilateral free trade agreement signed on 31 August 2023; entered into force on 1 January 2024 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Bilateral free trade agreement between China and Nicaragua, signed on 31 August 2023 and entered into force on 1 January 2024. Approximately 60% of goods in bilateral trade became exempt from tariffs upon implementation, with tariffs on more than 95% of goods set to be gradually reduced to zero. The agreement includes provisions on service trade, investment, digital economy, and environmental standards. It is China's first FTA to open cross-border service trade and investment through a negative list.

other_names.name: 中国-尼加拉瓜自由贸易协定

provenance.source: Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China

name: Australia-United Kingdom Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Comprehensive bilateral free trade agreement signed on 17 December 2021; entered into force on 31 May 2023 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Comprehensive free trade agreement between Australia and the United Kingdom, signed on 17 December 2021 and entered into force on 31 May 2023. The first trade agreement negotiated entirely anew by the UK since leaving the European Union, it eliminates tariffs on over 99% of Australian goods exported to the UK and creates significant opportunities for services, digital trade, innovation, and youth mobility. It also includes provisions for mutual recognition of professional qualifications.

provenance.source: Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

name: South Asian Free Trade Area
recognition_status: Free trade agreement signed at the 12th SAARC summit in Islamabad on 6 January 2004; entered into force on 1 January 2006 after ratification by all seven original SAARC contracting states; notified to the WTO on 21 April 2008 under the Enabling Clause; superseded the SAARC Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA)
description: The South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) is a framework agreement among SAARC member states to promote and sustain mutual trade and economic cooperation through progressive tariff liberalization. Signed at the 12th SAARC summit in Islamabad on 6 January 2004, it entered into force on 1 January 2006 after ratification by all seven original contracting states, superseding the SAARC Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA). The agreement established a staged trade liberalization programme with differentiated timelines for least developed and non-least developed countries, sensitive lists, rules of origin, and institutional arrangements including the SAFTA Ministerial Council. Afghanistan joined SAARC in April 2007 and ratified the SAFTA protocol on 4 May 2011, becoming the eighth participating state.

other_names.name: Accord de libre-échange de l'Asie du Sud
Área de Libre Comercio de Asia del Sur

notes: Afghanistan was not a SAARC member when SAFTA was signed in January 2004 and joined the agreement after acceding to SAARC in April 2007 and ratifying the SAFTA protocol on 4 May 2011. India and Pakistan completed ratification in 2009. SAFTA was notified to the WTO on 21 April 2008.

name: United States-Korea Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Bilateral free trade agreement signed on 30 June 2007, renegotiated and signed in December 2010; entered into force on 15 March 2012 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Bilateral trade agreement between the United States and the Republic of Korea, signed on 30 June 2007 and entered into force on 15 March 2012 after renegotiation and ratification by both legislatures. The agreement eliminated tariffs on over 95% of bilateral trade in consumer and industrial products within five years and covers manufactured goods, agriculture, services, investment, intellectual property, and labor and environmental standards.

name: Central American Integration System
description: Economic and political organization of Central American states.

name: European Free Trade Association
description: International trade organization and free trade area.

name: Central European Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Multilateral free trade agreement originally signed in Kraków on 21 December 1992 by Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia; the current CEFTA 2006 framework was signed on 19 December 2006 in Bucharest after Central European members acceded to the European Union, extending the agreement to Western Balkan and Moldovan parties
description: The Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) is a multilateral free trade agreement linking countries in Southeastern Europe. Originally signed in Kraków on 21 December 1992 by Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia, it expanded to include Slovenia, Romania, Bulgaria, Croatia, and North Macedonia before Central European members left upon joining the European Union. The CEFTA 2006 agreement, signed on 19 December 2006 in Bucharest, re-established the pact for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia, creating a regional free trade zone aligned with WTO rules and EU legislation. The agreement liberalises trade in goods and services, harmonises customs and trade-related policies, and supports the participating economies' European integration agendas.

other_names.name: اتفاقية التجارة الحرة في أوروبا الوسطى

notes: The original 1992 agreement entered into force on 1 March 1993 for Poland and Hungary and on 1 July 1994 overall. Slovenia joined in 1996, Romania in 1997, Bulgaria in 1999, Croatia in 2003, and North Macedonia in 2006. Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia left CEFTA upon acceding to the European Union. Kosovo was represented by UNMIK until October 2024, when it began representing itself directly at CEFTA meetings. The CEFTA 2006 agreement entered into force on 26 July 2007 for Albania, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, and North Macedonia; on 24 October 2007 for Serbia; and on 22 November 2007 for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

name: Central America-European Union Association Agreement
recognition_status: Comprehensive association agreement signed on 29 June 2012 in Tegucigalpa between the European Union and six Central American countries; the trade pillar was provisionally applied from August–December 2013; entered fully into force on 1 May 2024 after completion of ratification by all EU member states and Central American parties
description: Comprehensive association agreement between the European Union and six Central American countries, signed on 29 June 2012 in Tegucigalpa and entered fully into force on 1 May 2024. The agreement establishes political dialogue, cooperation, and a WTO-consistent free trade area. The trade pillar was provisionally applied from August–December 2013, eliminating most tariffs on industrial goods and fisheries and liberalising agricultural trade with asymmetric treatment favouring Central America. Upon entry into force, the EU removed 99% of tariff lines on industrial products and fisheries; Central America committed to duty-free access on all industrial products and fisheries by 2025.

other_names.name: Acuerdo de Asociación entre Centroamérica y la Unión Europea
Accord d'association entre le Système d'intégration centraméricain et l'Union européenne

notes: Negotiations were launched in October 2007 and concluded in May 2010. The European Parliament gave its consent on 11 December 2012. The trade pillar was provisionally applied from 1 August 2013 (Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama), 1 October 2013 (Costa Rica, El Salvador), and 1 December 2013 (Guatemala). Belgium was the last EU member state to ratify, on 17 January 2024, enabling full entry into force on 1 May 2024. Belize and the Dominican Republic are SICA members but are not parties to this agreement. Following Brexit, the United Kingdom and the six Central American parties signed a continuity agreement on 18 July 2019, which entered into force on 1 January 2021.

provenance.source: WTO Regional Trade Agreements Information System

name: G3 Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Third-generation free trade agreement registered with ALADI as Economic Complementation Agreement (ACE) No. 33; entered into force on 1 January 1995. Venezuela formally notified withdrawal on 25 May 2006; withdrawal took effect on 19 November 2006 after the 180-day notice period. The agreement remains in force bilaterally between Colombia and Mexico.
description: Regional free trade agreement among Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela, signed on 13 June 1994 and registered with ALADI as ACE No. 33. It entered into force on 1 January 1995, creating a market of roughly 149 million consumers. The agreement liberalized trade in goods and services over ten years and covered investment, government procurement, competition rules, and intellectual property. Venezuela withdrew effective 19 November 2006; Colombia and Mexico continue to apply the treaty bilaterally.

name: Greater Arab Free Trade Area
recognition_status: Pan-Arab free trade agreement adopted at the Arab League summit in Amman on 19 February 1997 following the 1981 Agreement to Facilitate and Develop Trade Among Arab Countries; entered into force on 1 January 1998; member states agreed in March 2001 to accelerate tariff reduction and eliminated most customs duties among participants by 1 January 2005; supervised by the Arab League Economic and Social Council
description: The Greater Arab Free Trade Area (GAFTA), also known as the Pan-Arab Free Trade Area (PAFTA), is a regional free trade agreement among Arab League states to reduce and eliminate customs duties and trade barriers on intra-Arab commerce. Adopted at the Amman Arab League summit on 19 February 1997 and building on the 1981 Agreement to Facilitate and Develop Trade Among Arab Countries, the pact entered into force on 1 January 1998. Member states originally agreed to cut customs duties by 10% annually; in March 2001 they accelerated liberalization, and most tariffs among participants were eliminated by 1 January 2005. GAFTA is supervised by the Arab League Economic and Social Council and covers 18 of the League's 22 member states.

other_names.name: Área Árabe de Libre Comercio Ampliada
Area Araba Allargata di Libero Scambio

notes: Fourteen states founded GAFTA on 19 February 1997: Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia, and the United Arab Emirates. Jordan, Palestine, and Yemen are current members but are not listed among those fourteen founders in the agreement's primary historical accounts; Algeria acceded in 2009 as the eighteenth member. Comoros, Djibouti, Mauritania, and Somalia remain candidates. Distinct from the Council of Arab Economic Unity (CAEU), though both operate under the Arab League umbrella.

name: Southern African Development Community Free Trade Area
recognition_status: Regional free trade area established under the SADC Protocol on Trade, signed on 24 August 1996 in Maseru and in force from 1 September 2000; tariff phase-down began in 2001 and minimum FTA conditions (85% of intra-regional trade at zero duty) were met in August 2008, with maximum tariff liberalisation on sensitive products completed by January 2012 for most members
description: The Southern African Development Community Free Trade Area (SADC FTA) is the intra-regional trade liberalisation framework of the Southern African Development Community. Established under the SADC Protocol on Trade signed in August 1996, it entered into force in September 2000 and achieved minimum free trade area conditions in August 2008 when 85% of intra-regional trade reached zero duty. Thirteen of sixteen SADC member states currently implement the FTA; Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Comoros remain outside pending accession.

other_names.name: Zone de libre-échange de la Communauté de développement de l'Afrique australe
Área de Livre Comércio da Comunidade para o Desenvolvimento da África Austral

notes: Angola submitted an updated tariff offer in February 2021 but has not yet acceded to the FTA. The Democratic Republic of the Congo and Comoros are SADC members that have not yet implemented the Protocol on Trade in Goods. Seychelles acceded to the trade protocol on 25 May 2015. Madagascar acceded in 2006 with an extended tariff phase-down schedule. SACU members completed tariff liberalisation in January 2007; most other members completed sensitive-product phase-downs by January 2012.

name: Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership
recognition_status: Free trade agreement signed on 15 November 2020 at the virtual ASEAN Summit hosted by Vietnam; entered into force on 1 January 2022 for the first ten ratifying parties. Negotiations were launched at the 2012 ASEAN Summit in Cambodia. India participated in negotiations but withdrew in November 2019; the agreement remains open to accession by India and other Asia-Pacific economies from 1 July 2023 onward.
description: Multilateral free trade agreement among fifteen Asia-Pacific economies, signed on 15 November 2020 and entered into force on 1 January 2022 for the first ten ratifying parties. Combines ASEAN's existing FTAs with Australia, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea into a single framework covering about 30% of global GDP and population, making it the world's largest free trade agreement by economic size. Indonesia and the Philippines completed ratification in 2023; India participated in negotiations but withdrew before signing.

other_names.name: 地域的な包括的経済連携協定
区域全面经济伙伴关系协定

provenance.source: Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

name: Trans-Pacific Partnership

acronyms.value: 泛太平洋戰略經濟夥伴

recognition_status: Multilateral free trade agreement signed on 4 February 2016 in Auckland by twelve Pacific Rim economies; never entered into force after the United States withdrew its signature on 23 January 2017. Evolved from the 2005 Trans-Pacific Strategic Economic Partnership (P4) and was superseded by the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).
description: Multilateral free trade agreement among twelve Pacific Rim economies, signed on 4 February 2016 in Auckland, New Zealand. Evolved from the 2005 Trans-Pacific Strategic Economic Partnership (P4) among Brunei, Chile, New Zealand, and Singapore. Japan and New Zealand completed domestic ratification, but the agreement never entered into force after the United States withdrew its signature on 23 January 2017, making the required ratification threshold unreachable. Remaining signatories negotiated the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which entered into force in December 2018.

other_names.name: 跨太平洋伙伴关系协定

Australian Government Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

name: China-Ecuador Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Bilateral free trade agreement signed on 11 May 2023; entered into force on 1 May 2024 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by both parties
description: Bilateral free trade agreement between China and Ecuador, signed on 11 May 2023 and entered into force on 1 May 2024. Approximately 90% of traded products are exempt from tariffs, with about 60% enjoying immediate zero tariffs upon implementation. Major Ecuadorian exports such as bananas, shrimp, fish, and fish oil see China's import tariffs gradually reduced to zero. Ecuador became China's 27th free trade partner and its fourth in Latin America, after Chile, Peru, and Costa Rica.

other_names.name: 中国-厄瓜多尔自由贸易协定

provenance.source: Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China

name: United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement
recognition_status: Trilateral free trade agreement signed on 30 November 2018; entered into force on 1 July 2020 after completion of domestic ratification procedures by all three parties, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)
description: Regional free trade agreement among Canada, Mexico, and the United States, signed on 30 November 2018 and entered into force on 1 July 2020, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). The agreement modernizes rules of origin for automobiles, strengthens labor and environmental standards, adds chapters on digital trade and anticorruption, and creates a more level playing field for North American workers, farmers, and businesses.

other_names.name: الاتفاقية بين الولايات المتحدة والمكسيك وكندا
Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá
美國-墨西哥-加拿大協定

name: United States-Costa Rica Free Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Bilateral market-access schedules under the Dominican Republic-Central America-United States Free Trade Agreement (CAFTA-DR); Costa Rica signed the U.S.-Central America FTA on 28 May 2004, approved the agreement in a national referendum on 7 October 2007, and completed implementing legislation on 14 November 2008; entered into force for Costa Rica on 1 January 2009
description: Bilateral trade relationship between the United States and Costa Rica under the CAFTA-DR framework. Costa Rica was the last CAFTA-DR party to implement the agreement, following a national referendum in October 2007 and adoption of implementing legislation in November 2008. The agreement entered into force for Costa Rica on 1 January 2009, eliminating tariffs on most bilateral trade in goods and services and establishing disciplines on investment, intellectual property, government procurement, labor, and the environment.

other_names.name: Tratado de Libre Comercio entre Estados Unidos y Costa Rica

name: ASEAN Free Trade Area
recognition_status: Agreement on the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) Scheme for the ASEAN Free Trade Area signed in Singapore on 28 January 1992; tariff-reduction schedules under CEPT began on 1 January 1993; notified to the WTO on 30 October 1992 under the Enabling Clause; superseded in part by the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) in 2010 while the AFTA framework remains the basis for intra-ASEAN trade liberalization
description: The ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) is a regional free trade agreement among ASEAN member states to promote intra-regional trade and manufacturing through progressive tariff liberalization. The Agreement on the Common Effective Preferential Tariff (CEPT) Scheme for AFTA was signed in Singapore on 28 January 1992 by the six original ASEAN members, with tariff-reduction schedules beginning on 1 January 1993 under the CEPT mechanism. Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar acceded as they joined ASEAN in 1995 and 1997, and Cambodia completed accession in 1999. AFTA applies preferential tariff rates of 0–5% on qualifying goods originating within ASEAN, with differentiated timelines for the CLMV countries. The agreement was notified to the WTO in 1992 and was largely superseded by the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) in 2010, though the AFTA framework remains central to ASEAN economic integration.

other_names.name: Área de Libre Comercio de la ASEAN
Área de Livre Comércio da ASEAN
เขตการค้าเสรีอาเซียน
Khu vực Mậu dịch Tự do ASEAN

notes: The six founding signatories (Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand) signed the CEPT agreement on 28 January 1992. Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar were required to accede to AFTA as a condition of ASEAN membership in 1995 and 1997; Cambodia acceded in 1999. CLMV countries received extended tariff-reduction timelines. AFTA was notified to the WTO on 30 October 1992 under the Enabling Clause. The ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA), signed in 2010, largely superseded the CEPT framework while building on AFTA's tariff liberalization achievements.

name: PACER Plus
recognition_status: Development-centred regional free trade agreement signed in Nuku'alofa on 14 June 2017; entered into force on 13 December 2020 after eight ratifications; builds on the 2001 PACER framework agreement
description: The Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus (PACER Plus) is a development-centred free trade agreement among Australia, New Zealand, and Pacific island countries. Negotiations concluded in Brisbane on 20 April 2017 and the agreement was opened for signature in Nuku'alofa on 14 June 2017. It entered into force on 13 December 2020 after eight ratifications, establishing common trading rules for goods, services, investment, and temporary movement of natural persons, together with a development and economic cooperation framework. Australia and New Zealand bound all tariffs on Pacific island country imports at zero on entry into force; Pacific island parties committed to staged tariff liberalisation over extended periods.

other_names.name: Pacific Agreement on Closer Economic Relations Plus
Accord du Pacifique sur les relations économiques Plus

notes: Negotiations were concluded on 20 April 2017 by fourteen Pacific Islands Forum members (Australia, Cook Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Zealand, Niue, Palau, Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu). Fiji and Papua New Guinea did not sign. Eleven states signed on 14 June 2017; Nauru signed but has not ratified and is not a party. Tuvalu and Vanuatu ratified after the initial entry into force and became parties on 3 April 2022 and 11 October 2022 respectively. PACER Plus builds on the 2001 PACER framework agreement and the earlier SPARTECA arrangement.

name: Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa

name: C5+1 Diplomatic Platform
description: Diplomatic platform bringing together the United States and the five Central Asian states (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan) for annual foreign-minister summits since 2015. Established on 26 September 2015 during the UN General Assembly, the format addresses regional security, Afghanistan, counterterrorism, trade and transport connectivity, energy, and environmental cooperation; working groups cover economics, environment and energy, and security.
notes: Distinct from Central Asia plus Japan (CENAPJ). The first ministerial summit was held in Samarkand on 1 November 2015; leaders met at the White House on 6 November 2025 for the first presidential-level C5+1 gathering.

name: Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes
description: Multilateral forum hosted by the OECD that monitors and promotes the implementation of international tax transparency standards, including exchange of information on request (EOIR), the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) for automatic exchange of financial account information, and the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF). Members undergo peer reviews and receive capacity-building support to combat offshore tax evasion.
notes: Restructured in September 2009 to expand membership beyond OECD countries. Roster of 173 participants (172 tax jurisdictions plus the European Union), sourced from the OECD members page and cross-checked against Wikipedia and OECD plenary rosters. Recent joiners include Sri Lanka (September 2025), Nepal (March 2026), and Suriname (July 2026).

other_names.name: Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes
Forum mondial sur la transparence et l'échange de renseignements à des fins fiscales
Foro Global sobre Transparencia e Intercambio de Información Tributaria

provenance.source: OECD press releases and annual report 2025

name: Climate Vulnerable Forum

headquarters.note: Independent CVF-V20 Secretariat headquartered in Accra following the May 2024 charter in Ghana; New York and Washington liaison offices also operate

description: Global partnership of climate-vulnerable developing countries established by the Malé Declaration of 10 November 2009 to amplify their collective voice in international climate negotiations and to promote ambitious domestic and international climate action. Operating jointly with the Vulnerable Twenty (V20) Finance Ministers as CVF-V20, the forum now comprises 74 member states spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, Latin America, the Middle East, and the Pacific. Barbados holds the 2024–2026 presidency; the independent secretariat is headquartered in Accra, Ghana.
notes: The V20 Finance Ministers platform was launched in Lima in October 2015 as the finance-ministers arm of the CVF; CVF and V20 now share the same 74-country membership and operate jointly as CVF-V20. Four members (Cabo Verde, Gabon, Solomon Islands, and Somalia) joined in April 2025, raising membership from 70 to 74. Eleven founding governments adopted the 2009 Malé Declaration.

name: ASEAN Regional Forum
description: ASEAN-led intergovernmental security dialogue forum established at its first ministerial meeting in Bangkok on 25 July 1994. It promotes confidence-building, preventive diplomacy, and cooperative security among 27 participants across the Asia-Pacific, with the ASEAN chair also chairing the ARF and the ASEAN Secretariat hosting the ARF Unit.

other_names.name: 東南アジア諸国連合地域フォーラム

notes: Officially termed Participants rather than members. The 18 founding participants at the Bangkok inaugural meeting were the ASEAN-6, seven Dialogue Partners (including the EU), China and Russia as Consultative Partners, and Laos, Papua New Guinea, and Vietnam as Observers. Cambodia joined in 1995; India and Myanmar in 1996; Mongolia in 1998; DPRK in 2000; Pakistan in 2004; Timor-Leste in 2005; Bangladesh in 2006; Sri Lanka in 2007. The ARF Unit at the ASEAN Secretariat in Jakarta provides administrative support. Wikidata Q481014 previously linked here was a German local court and has been replaced with Q7886981.

name: Caribbean Aviation Safety and Security Oversight System
recognition_status: Treaty-based Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) designated as an institution of CARICOM under Article 21 of the Revised Treaty of Chaguaramas; recognized by ICAO as an RSOO for the Caribbean
description: Regional aviation safety and security oversight organization (RSOO) established by treaty among CARICOM member states to succeed the interim Regional Aviation Safety Oversight System (RASOS). CASSOS assists States Parties in meeting Chicago Convention obligations, harmonizes civil aviation safety and security regulations across the Caribbean, and coordinates shared technical inspectorate resources among national civil aviation authorities in accordance with ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices.

other_names.name: Caribbean Aviation Safety and Security Oversight System

notes: Evolved from the 2001 Association of Civil Aviation Authorities of the Caribbean (ACAAC) and its interim Regional Aviation Safety Oversight System (RASOS), which operated from the Jamaica Civil Aviation Authority site in Kingston. The binding Agreement Establishing CASSOS was signed in Castries, Saint Lucia on 9 May 2008 and entered into force on 3 July 2008; CASSOS was formally launched in February 2009 at the CARICOM Secretariat in Georgetown, Guyana. Governed by a Board of Directors composed of directors general of member civil aviation authorities. Belize participated in ACAAC but is not a CASSOS States Party; it cooperates through ACSA (COCESNA). Bahamas, although a CARICOM member, is not listed among ICAO RSOO member states for CASSOS.

name: Central American Agency of Aviation Safety
recognition_status: Division of COCESNA recognized by ICAO as a Level 2 Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) for Central America
description: Regional aviation safety oversight organization (RSOO) established as a division of the Central American Corporation for Air Navigation Services (COCESNA). Inaugurated on 1 September 2000, ACSA harmonizes civil aviation safety oversight across the six COCESNA member states, providing audits, inspections, and technical assistance in air operations, airworthiness, aerodromes, and related areas. Services are ISO 9001:2015 certified and directed to civil aviation authorities and aviation service providers in the region.

other_names.name: Central American Agency of Aviation Safety

notes: Created by the COCESNA Governing Council on 15 December 1999 and ratified by the Council of Transport Ministers of COCESNA states on 12 May 2000; formally inaugurated on 1 September 2000. Legal domicile is Costa Rica, although ACSA operates administratively as a COCESNA division headquartered in Tegucigalpa, Honduras. Governed by a Technical Board composed of the civil aviation authorities of COCESNA member states under the administrative supervision of COCESNA General Management. Also referred to as the Central American Agency for Aeronautical Safety.

name: Unité Régionale de Supervision de la Sécurité et de la Sûreté de l'Aviation Civile de l'UEMOA
recognition_status: Specialized institution of UEMOA recognized by ICAO as a Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) for West Africa; transitional unit within the UEMOA Commission pending full operationalization of ACSAC

secretariat.organization: UEMOA Commission, Department of Community Spatial Planning and Transport (DATC)

description: Regional aviation safety and security oversight organization (RSOO) established as a unit within the UEMOA Commission's Department of Community Spatial Planning and Transport (DATC). Created on 3 November 2020 to succeed the ICAO-led COSCAP-UEMOA programme and security audit programme pending full operationalization of the Agence Communautaire de Supervision de la Sécurité et de la Sûreté de l'Aviation Civile (ACSAC), URSAC assists UEMOA member states in fulfilling Chicago Convention obligations, harmonizes civil aviation safety and security regulations, and provides oversight assistance including airport certification and inspector training.

other_names.name: Unité Régionale de Supervision de la Sécurité et de la Sûreté de l'Aviation Civile de l'UEMOA
UEMOA Regional Unit for Civil Aviation Safety and Security Oversight

notes: UEMOA established ACSAC by Additional Act No. 07/2013/CCEG/UEMOA of 24 October 2013, transforming the COSCAP-UEMOA programme (operational from 2006) into a community agency with both safety and security oversight functions. Operationalization of ACSAC was delayed by hosting arrangements and financing; the UEMOA Commission created URSAC on 3 November 2020 within the DATC transport department to continue COSCAP activities until ACSAC becomes fully operational. All eight UEMOA member states are also ASECNA states and therefore participate in AAMAC; a 2014 tripartite MOU with AAMAC and ASSA-AC confines AAMAC to ANS oversight while assigning ACSAC/URSAC and ASSA-AC other safety areas. Mauritania participated in the predecessor COSCAP-UEMOA arrangement and remains on ICAO's RSOO membership list, although UEMOA's ACSAC transition now excludes Mauritania, which also participates in MENA and AAMAC. In June 2018 UEMOA agreed a regional levy of 260 CFA francs per international passenger to fund the RSOO, pending implementation; the Commission continues interim financing.

name: East African Community Civil Aviation Safety and Security Oversight Agency
recognition_status: Regional Safety and Security Oversight Organization (RSOO) institution of the East African Community, established under the Protocol on the Establishment of CASSOA and the EAC Civil Aviation Safety and Security Oversight Agency Act, 2009; recognized by ICAO as an RSOO for East Africa
description: Regional aviation safety and security oversight organization (RSOO) established as an autonomous, self-accounting institution of the East African Community to harmonize civil aviation safety and security regulations among partner states and assist them in meeting Chicago Convention obligations. EAC-CASSOA coordinates shared oversight resources, develops harmonized regulations and technical guidance materials, supports ICAO USOAP and USAP audit preparation, and promotes capacity building for national civil aviation authorities across the EAC region.

includes.name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

other_names.name: East African Community Civil Aviation Safety and Security Oversight Agency
Civil Aviation Safety and Security Oversight Agency

notes: The EAC Council of Ministers approved establishment of CASSOA on 18 April 2007; operations commenced on 1 June 2007 initially at the East African Community Secretariat in Arusha, Tanzania, before the headquarters moved to Entebbe, Uganda (Plot 41/43 Circular Road, P.O. Box 873). The Protocol on the Establishment of CASSOA was signed at the 5th Extraordinary Summit of EAC Heads of State in Kampala on 18 June 2007. CASSOA derives its mandate from Article 92 of the EAC Treaty and operates under the CASSOA Act of 2009. Governance rests with the EAC Council of Ministers, a Board of Directors comprising directors general of partner civil aviation authorities plus nominated aviation experts, and an Executive Director appointed by the Council. Membership expanded from the original three EAC partner states (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda) as the Community admitted Burundi, Rwanda, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Somalia.

name: Pacific Aviation Safety Office
recognition_status: Regional Aviation Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) recognised by ICAO; sole international organisation responsible for regional regulatory aviation safety oversight under the Pacific Islands Civil Aviation Safety and Security Treaty (PICASST); member of the Council of Regional Organisations of the Pacific (CROP)
description: Intergovernmental regional aviation safety oversight organisation providing quality aviation safety and security services for Pacific member states. PASO is the sole international organisation responsible for regional regulatory aviation safety oversight for the ten PICASST signatories, and works as an ICAO-recognised Regional Aviation Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO). Headquartered in Port Vila, Vanuatu under a hosting agreement with the Vanuatu Government, it conducts audits, inspections, and regulatory assistance to harmonise civil aviation frameworks and ensure compliance with ICAO standards.
notes: Concept emerged from a Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in 2002. The Pacific Islands Civil Aviation Safety and Security Treaty (PICASST) was signed on 7 August 2004 in Apia, Samoa, with Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, and Vanuatu as original signatories; the treaty entered into force on 11 June 2005. PASO as an organisation was created in 2007 with Asian Development Bank support, and its office was established in Vanuatu under a hosting agreement with the Vanuatu Government; a renewed indefinite hosting agreement was signed in May 2018. Member of CROP and the only CROP agency permanently based in Vanuatu. Tonga withdrew on 7 April 2006 but rejoined on 24 August 2006. Works closely with CASA Australia, the Civil Aviation Authority of Fiji, and CAANZ.

name: Banjul Accord Group Aviation Safety Oversight Organisation
recognition_status: Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) of the Banjul Accord Group, recognized by ICAO; evolved from the ICAO Cooperative Development of Operational and Continuing Airworthiness Programme (COSCAP-BAG)
description: Regional aviation safety oversight organization (RSOO) established by the seven Banjul Accord Group member states to harmonize civil aviation safety regulations, pool regional inspector resources, and provide audit, quality assurance, and training support across West Africa. BAGASOO evolved from the ICAO-led COSCAP-BAG programme and was formally established by the BAGASOO Agreement signed on 30 June 2009. It promotes implementation of ICAO standards and the Global Aviation Safety Plan (GASP) and develops tools such as SIMCA (Safety Information Management for Civil Aviation) for member civil aviation authorities.

other_names.name: Banjul Accord Group Aviation Safety Oversight Organisation

notes: The BAGASOO Agreement was signed on 30 June 2009 by the Ministers responsible for Civil Aviation of the seven Banjul Accord Group member states and annexed to the BAG international legal instrument. BAGASOO is governed by a Board of Directors composed of the Directors General of member civil aviation authorities, with the Executive Director as member and secretary. Technical divisions cover Administration, Legal, Training and Support, and aviation specialty areas including flight operations, personnel licensing, airworthiness, air navigation services, and aerodromes. A Passenger Safety Charge levy intended to fund operations from 2012 was not implemented by member states; BAGASOO has pursued alternative revenue sources and cooperation with ECOWAS and ICAO regional programmes.

name: European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation
recognition_status: Intergovernmental organization established under the EUROCONTROL International Convention relating to Cooperation for the Safety of Air Navigation (signed 13 December 1960, entered into force 1 March 1963); 42 member states plus 2 Comprehensive Agreement States (Israel and Morocco); European Community accession protocol signed in 2002
description: Intergovernmental organization advancing safe and seamless civil and military air traffic management across the pan-European network. EUROCONTROL supports member states and aviation stakeholders including air navigation service providers, airspace users, airports, and manufacturers through operations, service provision, concept development, research, performance monitoring, and network management. Established by the Brussels Convention of 13 December 1960 (in force 1 March 1963), it operates the Maastricht Upper Area Control Centre and coordinates Single European Sky initiatives with the European Union while maintaining independent intergovernmental governance through the Permanent Commission and Provisional Council.

other_names.name: 欧洲空中航行安全组织

notes: Originally founded by six states (Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom). The Maastricht Upper Area Control Centre (MUAC) was established in 1972 for upper airspace over Benelux and parts of Germany. Iceland became the 42nd member state in 2025. Israel and Morocco participate as Comprehensive Agreement States. Additional sites include the Innovation Hub in Brétigny-sur-Orge, France, and the Aviation Learning Centre in Luxembourg. Employs approximately 2,000 officials with an annual budget exceeding €1 billion.

name: African Civil Aviation Commission
recognition_status: Specialized agency of the African Union for civil aviation; executing agency of the Yamoussoukro Decision (empowered 2007) and the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM)
description: African Union specialized agency for civil aviation across the continent, headquartered in Dakar. Established on 17 January 1969 at an ICAO and OAU conference in Addis Ababa, AFCAC coordinates safety, security, air transport, and regulatory harmonization among member states. Empowered in 2007 as executing agency of the Yamoussoukro Decision and SAATM, and works with ICAO on SARPs implementation through initiatives such as the AFI-CIS safety oversight scheme.

includes.name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

notes: Constitution provisionally effective until 20 states ratified on 12 January 1972; revised constitutions adopted in 2001 and 2009, with the 2009 constitution taking effect in April 2021. Governed by a Plenary (member states, meets every three years), an elected Bureau (President and five Vice Presidents by AU region), and a Secretariat headed by the Secretary General. Membership is open to AU or UN Economic Commission for Africa member states; all AU members except Western Sahara are AFCAC members. Empowered as executing agency of the Yamoussoukro Decision by the AU Assembly in 2007.

name: Arab Civil Aviation Organization
recognition_status: Specialized Arab organization affiliated with the League of Arab States; membership is limited to League of Arab States member states
description: Specialized Arab organization affiliated with the League of Arab States that coordinates civil aviation policy, safety, and development among its 22 member states. Established in Rabat when its founding agreement entered into force on 7 February 1996, replacing the Civil Aviation Council of Arab States. Works with ICAO on standards implementation and maintains a cooperation agreement signed in 1999.
notes: Also known as the Arab Civil Aviation Commission (ACAC). Replaced the Civil Aviation Council of Arab States (agreement in force since 14 October 1967). First General Assembly held on 5 June 1996. Governed by a General Assembly, Executive Council, and General Directorate with five technical committees (Environment, Air Transport, Air Navigation, Air Safety Standards, and Aviation Security) plus a Financial Oversight Committee.

name: Banjul Accord Group Accident Investigation Agency
recognition_status: Independent regional accident investigation organization (RAIO) established under the Banjul Accord Group; investigations are conducted upon delegation by member states in compliance with ICAO Annex 13 standards
description: Regional accident investigation organization (RAIO) established by the seven Banjul Accord Group member states to conduct independent investigations into aircraft accidents and serious incidents upon delegation by a State of Occurrence in the BAG sub-region. BAGAIA operates in compliance with ICAO Annex 13 standards, promotes harmonized accident investigation regulations among member states, and provides accident investigation training and technical support. The Office of the Commissioner is located in Praia, Cabo Verde.

other_names.name: Banjul Accord Group Accident Investigation Agency

notes: The BAGAIA Agreement was signed by the Ministers of Transport of the seven Banjul Accord Group member states in 2009. Governed by the BAG Council of Ministers, a Commissioner, and a Commission, BAGAIA conducts delegated investigations free of charge in accordance with its founding statutes. The Commissioner is supported by a Technical Support/Training Director, an Administrative/Account Manager, and a Legal Adviser, with investigative teams drawn from qualified investigators across BAG member states. As of 2024, Engr. Charles Irikefe Erhueh serves as Commissioner.

name: SADC Aviation Safety Organisation
recognition_status: Subsidiary organisation of SADC established under the principle of subsidiarity through the SASO Charter; recognized by ICAO as a Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) for Southern Africa
description: Subsidiary organisation of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and ICAO-recognized Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) for Southern Africa. Established under the principle of subsidiarity through the SASO Charter, SASO promotes the safe and efficient use and development of civil aviation across the SADC region. Its secretariat in Mbabane, Eswatini, assists member states in meeting ICAO safety oversight obligations, harmonises aviation safety standards through SADC Generic Regulations and Procedures, and provides advisory, certification, surveillance, regulatory, and training support to national civil aviation authorities.

includes.name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

other_names.name: Organisation de la sécurité aérienne de la SADC
Organização de Segurança da Aviação da SADC

notes: SADC Ministers of Transport and Meteorology approved an Interim SASO (iSASO) secretariat in October 2013, pending Council of Ministers approval of the SASO Charter. The MoU and Eswatini Hosting Agreement were signed in May 2015; COSCAP-SADC staff relocated to Eswatini in November 2015 to operationalise the organisation. On 2 May 2023 the Democratic Republic of the Congo became the 12th charter signatory, marking transition from interim to full SASO status. Governed by the Civil Aviation Committee (strategic planning) and the Committee of Ministers responsible for Civil Aviation (policy, budget, and Executive Director appointment). The Flight Safety Working Group supports domestication of SADC Generic Regulations and Procedures. As of 31 October 2024, 12 of 16 SADC member states had signed the SASO Charter.

name: International Air Transport Association
legal_status: trade association incorporated under Canadian federal law
recognition_status: Non-governmental trade association whose members are airlines operating scheduled and non-scheduled air services that maintain IATA Operational Safety Audit (IOSA) registration
description: Global trade association representing over 370 member airlines from more than 120 countries, together carrying about 85% of scheduled international air traffic. IATA develops industry standards for safety, security, and financial systems; operates settlement systems such as the Billing and Settlement Plan; advocates for airline interests with governments and international organisations; and provides training, consulting, and regulatory compliance support. Founded in Havana on 19 April 1945 as the successor to the International Air Traffic Association (1919).
notes: Founded in Havana on 19 April 1945 with 57 member airlines from 31 nations; incorporated under a Special Act of the Parliament of Canada on 18 December 1945 with head office in Montreal. Successor to the International Air Traffic Association founded at The Hague in 1919. Governed by an Annual General Meeting of member airlines, a Board of Directors (31 airline CEOs plus the Director General as of June 2026), nine Industry Committees, three Steering Groups, and six Traffic Conferences. The includes roster tracks countries represented by member airlines rather than sovereign membership.

name: European Network of Civil Aviation Safety Investigation Authorities
recognition_status: Independent network established under Regulation (EU) No 996/2010 comprising the civil aviation safety investigation authorities of all EU Member States; Iceland, Kosovo, Norway, and Switzerland participate as observers

secretariat.organization: SIA-Secretary (rotating among member authorities, supported by the European Commission)

description: European network of civil aviation safety investigation authorities established following the entry into force of Regulation (EU) No 996/2010 to improve the quality, independence, and harmonization of aviation safety investigations across Europe. ENCASIA brings together the heads of national safety investigation authorities from EU Member States to share best practices, coordinate mutual support through the European Mutual Support System (EMSS), conduct peer reviews, develop training initiatives, and advise EU institutions on accident investigation and prevention. Its website is hosted by the European Commission and its work programmes are funded through EC grants co-funded by members.

other_names.name: European Network of Civil Aviation Safety Investigation Authorities

notes: Established in January 2011 following the entry into force of Regulation (EU) No 996/2010 on the investigation and prevention of accidents and incidents in civil aviation; Rules of Procedure were formally approved on 19 January 2011. Governed by the heads of member safety investigation authorities (SIAs), who elect a Chair and Deputy Chair for three-year terms. Seven working groups address communication, cooperation, the European Mutual Support System (EMSS), planning and resources, peer reviews, safety recommendations, and ICAO matters. Peer reviews play an essential role in supporting implementation of Regulation 996/2010 in Member States. Funded through European Commission grants co-funded by members. The United Kingdom participated until departing after Brexit in 2020; Switzerland joined as an observer the same year. Observers include Iceland, Kosovo, Norway, and Switzerland. Plenary meetings are typically held in Brussels; the ENCASIA website is hosted by the European Commission.

name: Central American Corporation for Air Navigation Services
recognition_status: Specialized body of the Central American Integration System (SICA) with exclusive rights to provide air traffic control, aeronautical telecommunications, navigation aids, and aeronautical information services across the Central American flight information region
description: Intergovernmental regional organization and specialized body of the Central American Integration System (SICA) that provides integrated air navigation services across the Central American flight information region (FIR), covering approximately 2.6 million km² of continental and maritime airspace. Established on 26 February 1960, COCESNA holds exclusive rights to air traffic control, aeronautical telecommunications, navigation aids, aeronautical information management, and related meteorological support for its six member states. Services are delivered through the Central American Air Navigation Agency (ACNA), created on 1 June 2001, which operates the Central American Area Control Centre (CENAMER ACC) from Tegucigalpa, Honduras.

other_names.name: Central American Corporation for Air Navigation Services
Corporación Centroamericana de Servicios de Navegación Aérea

notes: Established on 26 February 1960 by Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua under the Constitutive Agreement; Belize joined in 1966. Governed by a Board of Directors composed of representatives of member civil aviation authorities. Provides air navigation services through ACNA (Agencia Centroamericana de Navegación Aérea), created on 1 June 2001, which operates the CENAMER ACC and maintains technical offices in all six member states. Related COCESNA units include ACSA (aviation safety oversight), ICCAE (training), and AIM. Recipient of the ICAO Edward Warner Award in October 1976 for coordinated air navigation and communications services. Headquarters located 150 m south of Toncontín International Airport, Tegucigalpa, Honduras.

name: Latin American Civil Aviation Commission
recognition_status: Consultative international organization whose recommendations require approval by each member state; statutory treaty registered with the United Nations (registration No. 20170, vol. 1241, 22 July 1981); Mexico is depositary state of the Multilateral Treaty establishing LACAC

secretariat.location: Av. Víctor Andrés Belaúnde 147, San Isidro, Lima, Peru
secretariat.head: Secretary
secretariat.organization: Secretariat of the Latin American Civil Aviation Commission

description: Regional consultative intergovernmental organization comprising 22 Latin American and Caribbean states, formally known as Comisión Latinoamericana de Aviación Civil (CLAC). Established on 14 December 1973 at the Second Conference of Aeronautical Authorities of Latin America in Mexico City and operational from 21 October 1975, LACAC provides civil aviation authorities a framework to coordinate air transport policy, operational safety, aviation security and facilitation, airport management, training, and environmental matters. Recommendations are non-binding and subject to approval by each member state. The Secretariat has been headquartered in Lima, Peru since 2007; Mexico serves as depositary state of the founding treaty. LACAC cooperates closely with ICAO under a Mutual Cooperation Agreement (2005) and administers a Multilateral Open Skies Agreement among member states.
notes: Statute approved at the Second Conference of Aeronautical Authorities of Latin America in Mexico City on 14 December 1973; entered into force on 21 October 1975 upon ratification by 12 member states. First Assembly held in Buenos Aires in August 1974 with 16 subscribing states. Governed by an Assembly (ordinary sessions at least every two years), an Executive Committee (President and Vice Presidents elected by the Assembly), and a Secretariat organized by the Executive Committee. Secretariat headquarters selected in 2005 (Lima, Peru over proposals from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and Venezuela); Headquarters Agreement with Peru signed in 2006; financial autonomy phase began in 2007. ICAO provided Secretariat services under a 1978 Modus Vivendi until the 2005 Mutual Cooperation Agreement; finances managed under the ICAO Technical Cooperation Bureau Regional Project scheme. Membership limited to South America, Central America including Panama, Mexico, and Caribbean states.

name: Eastern Caribbean Civil Aviation Authority
recognition_status: OECS institution under the Treaty of Basseterre (1982); multistate civil aviation authority established by agreement signed 21 October 2003 and given legal effect through national legislation in participating states by October 2004
description: OECS institution and multistate civil aviation authority providing safety and security oversight for Eastern Caribbean ICAO Contracting States. Established in October 2004 after OECS aviation ministers signed the founding agreement in October 2003, ECCAA evolved from the Directorate of Civil Aviation – Eastern Caribbean States (dating to 1957). Headquartered in Saint John's, Antigua and Barbuda, it regulates civil aviation across six participating states in accordance with ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs), harmonizes regulations and policies, and conducts inspection, investigation, monitoring, and licensing.
notes: Evolved from the Directorate of Civil Aviation – Eastern Caribbean States, first led by a UK-appointed director in 1957; administered by Antigua and Barbuda until 1968, then by the West Indies Associated States Council of Ministers, and recognized as an OECS institution in 1982. Agreement establishing ECCAA signed 21 October 2003 at St Georges, Grenada; ECCAA commenced operations in October 2004 when participating states enacted implementing legislation. Operates outstations serving additional OECS territories including Anguilla, Montserrat, and the British Virgin Islands.

name: Agence de Supervision de la Sécurité Aérienne en Afrique Centrale
recognition_status: Specialized institution of CEMAC (UEAC) recognized by ICAO as a Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) for Central Africa
description: Regional aviation safety oversight organization (RSOO) and specialized institution of the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC). Created on 25 April 2007 and established as a CEMAC specialized institution in July 2012, ASSA-AC succeeded the COSCAP CEMAC/São Tomé & Príncipe programme hosted by Chad from 2008 to 2012. It harmonizes civil aviation safety regulations across the six CEMAC member states, certifies and supervises air operators, maintenance and training organizations, and international aerodromes in accordance with ICAO standards.

other_names.name: Agence de Supervision de la Sécurité Aérienne en Afrique Centrale
Central African Aviation Safety Supervision Agency

notes: Created by CEMAC Additional Act No. 15/07-CEMAC-162-CCE of 25 April 2007 and elevated to a specialized institution by the CEMAC Heads of State Conference in July 2012; operational since December 2012. Governed under the supervision of the CEMAC Ministers Committee for Aviation, assisted by a Steering Committee, and directed by a Director General. Funded through CEMAC community import tax and Commission subventions. A 2014 tripartite MOU with AAMAC and ACSAC (URSAC) assigns ASSA-AC safety oversight in PEL, OPS, AIR, AIG, ANS, and AGA while confining AAMAC to ANS oversight. An ECCAS initiative to expand membership to all 11 central African states has stalled; ASSA-AC remains limited to the six CEMAC member states.

name: European Union Aviation Safety Agency
recognition_status: EU agency established under Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (Basic Regulation); all EU Member States participate automatically, and EFTA states Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland participate under Article 129 with management board observer status but without voting rights
description: Agency of the European Union responsible for civil aviation safety and environmental protection across Europe. EASA proposes and develops aviation safety rules and standards, certifies aircraft, parts, and equipment, approves and oversees aviation organisations, and provides oversight and support to national civil aviation authorities in shared competence areas such as air operations and air traffic management. Its jurisdiction covers all EU Member States and participating EFTA countries. Created as the European Aviation Safety Agency in 2002 and renamed the European Union Aviation Safety Agency in 2018, it took over core functions of the Joint Aviation Authorities and reached full functionality in 2008.

other_names.name: Agence européenne de la sécurité aérienne
Agência Europeia para a Segurança da Aviação

notes: Legally established by Regulation (EC) No 1592/2002 adopted on 15 July 2002 as the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA); began operations on 28 September 2003 and assumed product certification responsibilities from national authorities on 28 September 2003. Reached full functionality in 2008 after taking over core Joint Aviation Authorities functions. Renamed the European Union Aviation Safety Agency under Regulation (EU) 2018/1139. Governed by a Management Board, Executive Director, and Board of Appeal. The United Kingdom participated until leaving EASA at the end of the Brexit transition on 31 December 2020. Cooperates internationally through bilateral agreements and the Pan-European Partners (PANEP) initiative with Eastern Partnership states.

name: Autorités Africaines et Malgaches de l'Aviation Civile
recognition_status: Treaty-based Regional Safety Oversight Organization (RSOO) established by the 17 ASECNA member states; recognized by ICAO as an RSOO for the Africa and Indian Ocean (AFI) region
description: Regional aviation safety oversight organization (RSOO) established by treaty on 20 January 2012 among the 17 African and Malagasy states that are members of ASECNA. AAMAC harmonizes civil aviation regulations, audits national civil aviation authorities, and provides certification and surveillance services to maintain uniform safety standards. Governed by a Council and Executive Secretariat, it operates within the ASECNA air navigation framework and focuses on air navigation services (ANS) safety oversight.

other_names.name: Autorités Africaines et Malgaches de l'Aviation Civile
African and Malagasy Civil Aviation Authorities

notes: Originated from a 2001 study on strengthening civil aviation authorities in ASECNA member states; a memorandum of understanding was adopted in Dakar on 20 December 2001, with internal regulations adopted in 2003. The binding treaty was signed in N'Djamena on 20 January 2012. Although not attached to a regional economic community, AAMAC operates within the ASECNA air navigation service provider framework. A 2014 tripartite MOU with ACSAC (URSAC) and ASSA-AC confines AAMAC to ANS oversight; Council resolution 2015 CDA34-08 further focused activities on ANS regulation harmonization, audits, and provider certification. description: Regional association of supreme audit institutions in the Caribbean, established on 7 August 1988 in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago. Promotes exchange of ideas and experience in government auditing, training and continuing education, technical assistance, and comprehensive auditing among member SAIs, and raises audit consciousness across the region. One of seven regional organisations of INTOSAI; the General Secretariat is hosted by the Auditor General's Department of Jamaica in Kingston.
notes: Governed by an Executive Council of six members elected every three years at the Plenary. The Regional Institutional Strengthening Committee (RISC) provides training and capacity-building support to member SAIs. As of 2025, following the XIII CAROSAI Congress in Nassau, the Chair is held by the Bahamas (Brenda Neely), the incoming Chair is Saint Lucia (from 2028), and the General Secretariat remains with the Auditor General's Department of Jamaica (Pamela Monroe Ellis, Secretary-General since 2016). Saint Maarten and Belize serve on the Executive Council; Trinidad and Tobago conducts CAROSAI's audit; and Suriname represents CAROSAI on the INTOSAI Governing Board.

other_names.name: Caribbean Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions

name: Organisation of Rice Exporting Countries
recognition_status: Proposed Mekong-region rice-export coordination forum announced by Thailand on 30 April 2008; Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam agreed in principle; abandoned in June 2008 after opposition from the Philippines and the Asian Development Bank
description: Proposed coordination forum of five Mekong-region rice-exporting states announced by Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej in April 2008. The five countries — Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam — agreed in principle to cooperate on rice trading amid rising global prices, with leaders stressing regional food stability rather than an OPEC-style price cartel. The Philippines, the world's largest rice importer, and the Asian Development Bank opposed the plan; Thailand dropped the proposal in June 2008 and OREC was never formally established.

other_names.name: Organisation des pays exportateurs de riz
Tổ chức các quốc gia xuất khẩu gạo

notes: Thailand floated the idea on 30 April 2008 as a five-nation Mekong grouping sometimes compared to OPEC; Cambodia's Prime Minister Hun Sen said OREC would aim to ensure food stability and not hoard rice or raise prices during shortages. Regional ASEAN partners and the ADB warned that a rice cartel would worsen food security. No treaty, secretariat, or headquarters was ever established.

name: Western Central Atlantic Fishery Commission
recognition_status: FAO Article VI (1) statutory body established by FAO Council Resolution 4/61 (1973); statutes amended by the FAO Council at its 74th Session (December 1978) and 131st Session (November 2006); membership open to coastal States in the area of competence and to States whose vessels fish there that notify the FAO Director-General; secretariat provided by FAO

headquarters.note: Secretariat provided by FAO at the Subregional Office for the Caribbean (SLC)

description: FAO regional fishery body for the Western Central Atlantic (FAO Statistical Area 31 and the northern part of Area 41), established in 1973 under Article VI of the FAO Constitution. WECAFC promotes conservation, management, and development of living marine resources and addresses shared fisheries problems among its 34 members — coastal States of the Wider Caribbean and distant-water fishing States and the European Union that notify FAO of membership. It is an advisory body (not an RFMO with binding measures) that coordinates with CRFM and OSPESCA; its secretariat is hosted at FAO's Subregional Office for the Caribbean in Bridgetown.

other_names.name: Comisión de Pesca del Atlántico Centro-Occidental
Commission des pêches pour l'Atlantique Centre-Ouest

Distant-water members include Guinea, Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Spain. France, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom participate in respect of their Caribbean territories and dependencies. Statutes were last amended by the FAO Council in November 2006.

name: Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
recognition_status: Intergovernmental commission established by the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CAMLR Convention), adopted in Canberra on 20 May 1980 and in force from 7 April 1982; part of the Antarctic Treaty System; Australia is depositary; secretariat headquartered in Hobart, Tasmania
description: Intergovernmental commission for the conservation of Antarctic marine living resources in the Southern Ocean, established when the CAMLR Convention entered into force on 7 April 1982. Part of the Antarctic Treaty System, CCAMLR uses an ecosystem-based management approach covering krill and other marine living resources south of the Antarctic Convergence. The Commission has 27 Members (26 states and the European Union) that set conservation measures by consensus, plus 10 Acceding States that are Contracting Parties but do not participate in decision-making or the budget. The secretariat is based in Hobart, Tasmania.

other_names.name: Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
Kommission zur Erhaltung der lebenden Meeresschätze der Antarktis
