notes: The CAMLR Convention was adopted in Canberra on 20 May 1980 and opened for signature from 1 August to 31 December 1980 by States participating in the Canberra conference; original signatories (founding Members) include Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Chile, France, Germany (FRG and GDR), Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, South Africa, the Soviet Union (succeeded by the Russian Federation), the United Kingdom, and the United States. Acceding States (Bulgaria, Canada, Cook Islands, Finland, Greece, Mauritius, Pakistan, Panama, Peru, and Vanuatu) have acceded to the Convention but are not Commission Members. Ecuador became a Commission Member on 19 October 2022. The Netherlands previously held Acceding State status before becoming a Member.

name: Fishery Committee for the Eastern Central Atlantic
recognition_status: FAO Article VI(2) advisory statutory body established by FAO Council Resolution 1/48 at the Forty-eighth Session (Rome, June 1967); statutes promulgated by the Director-General on 19 September 1967; statutes amended by FAO Council in 1992 and 2003; secretariat housed at the FAO Regional Office for Africa in Accra

headquarters.note: Secretariat housed at the FAO Regional Office for Africa; no independent premises

description: FAO Article VI advisory fishery committee promoting sustainable utilization of living marine resources in the eastern central Atlantic (largely FAO Statistical Area 34), from Cape Spartel on the Moroccan coast to near the Congo River mouth, including high seas and national waters. Established by FAO Council Resolution 1/48 in June 1967, CECAF reviews stock status, promotes collection and exchange of fishery data, establishes the scientific basis for conservation measures, and issues management recommendations without binding regulatory powers. Membership comprises coastal African FAO members bordering the Atlantic from Cape Spartel to the Congo, plus other FAO members and the European Union selected by the Director-General for fishing, research, or related interest in the area.

other_names.name: Fishery Committee for the Eastern Central Atlantic
Comité des Pêches pour l'Atlantique Centre-Est
Comité de Pesca para el Atlántico Centro-Oriental

notes: CECAF replaced the inactive Regional Fisheries Commission for Western Africa. A Scientific Sub-Committee was established in 1998 to provide science-based advice; working groups cover small pelagic, demersal, and artisanal fisheries. Ordinary sessions are normally biennial (22nd session, Libreville, September 2019). Membership is by Director-General selection rather than open accession; Angola later joined the coastal roster after independence-era exclusion from the original southern limit at the Congo mouth.

description: FAO Article XIV Regional Fishery Body promoting sustainable development and management of fisheries and aquaculture in the Asia-Pacific region. Originally established as the Indo-Pacific Fisheries Council in 1948, it was renamed the Indo-Pacific Fishery Commission in 1976 and the Asia-Pacific Fishery Commission in 1993–1994. APFIC functions primarily as a regional consultative forum; the Secretariat is hosted by the FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific in Bangkok. The Commission has 21 current member states; the Netherlands withdrew in 1974. At its 37th Session (Qingdao, June 2023) members adopted a resolution suspending Commission activities for five years until 2028, while officers remain incumbent and the Secretariat continues correspondence.

other_names.name: 亚洲太平洋渔业委员会

Acceptance dates for current and former parties are taken from the FAO Legal Office parties list; China's listed acceptance is the 1993 PRC deposit. name: Central America Fisheries and Aquaculture Organization
recognition_status: Specialized regional body of the Central American Integration System (SICA) established by the Act of San Salvador on 18 December 1995; attached to the SICA General Secretariat since 2000; coordinates regional fisheries and aquaculture policy across member states

description: Specialized regional fisheries and aquaculture body of the Central American Integration System (SICA), established by the Act of San Salvador on 18 December 1995. OSPESCA coordinates the definition, implementation, and monitoring of regional policies, strategies, and projects for the sustainable development of fisheries and aquaculture across its eight member states — Belize, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama. The organization harmonizes binding regulations on gear, bycatch, IUU fishing, and shared stocks such as Caribbean spiny lobster, and participates in the FAO Network of Regional Fishery Bodies as a regional advisory body.

other_names.name: Central America Fisheries and Aquaculture Organization
Organización del Sector Pesquero y Acuicola del Istmo Centroamericano

notes: The six Central American isthmus states founded OSPESCA through the 1995 Act of San Salvador; Belize acceded after joining SICA (1998), and the Dominican Republic became a full SICA and OSPESCA member in 2013. OSPESCA was attached to the SICA General Secretariat in 2000 and reorganized as a specialized regional directorate in 2015. Work is guided by the Fisheries and Aquaculture Integration Policy 2015–2025.

recognition_status: FAO Article VI-2 statutory body established by the FAO Council at its 56th session (Rome, 7–18 June 1971, Resolution 1/56) as the Committee for Inland Fisheries of Africa (CIFA); renamed Committee for Inland Fisheries and Aquaculture of Africa (CIFAA) by the FAO Council in 2007 following the Committee’s 14th session recommendation; secretariat provided by the FAO Regional Office for Africa

headquarters.note: Secretariat at FAO Regional Office for Africa (RAF)

Established in June 1971 as the Committee for Inland Fisheries of Africa (CIFA) and renamed in 2007 to reflect its aquaculture mandate, CIFAA convenes biennial sessions of its 37 African member states and links national programmes with continental partners such as NEPAD and the Aquaculture Network for Africa (ANAF). Ordinary sessions are normally biennial (e.g. 17th session Banjul 2017; 18th Bamako 2019; 20th Dakar 2024).

headquarters.note: Pohnpei, Federated States of Micronesia

description: Regional fisheries management organisation for highly migratory fish stocks (especially tunas and billfish) in the western and central Pacific Ocean, established when the WCPF Convention entered into force on 19 June 2004. The Commission comprises 26 Members (25 States plus Chinese Taipei as a fishing entity), seven Participating Territories, and annually renewed Cooperating Non-Members; it adopts binding conservation and management measures, runs a vessel monitoring system and regional observer programme, and draws scientific advice from the Pacific Community and the International Scientific Committee for Tuna and Tuna-like Species in the North Pacific Ocean.

notes: The Convention was opened for signature at Honolulu on 5 September 2000; New Zealand is depositary. Chinese Taipei participates as a Member fishing entity under the Arrangement for the Participation of Fishing Entities (bound from 2 November 2004). Participating Territories (American Samoa, French Polynesia, Guam, New Caledonia, Northern Mariana Islands, Tokelau, Wallis and Futuna) lack full voting rights. Cooperating Non-Member status is granted annually; the 2026 official roster lists Bahamas, Curaçao, Ecuador, El Salvador, Liberia, Panama, Thailand, and Vietnam. State observers include Brunei Darussalam, Mexico, Nicaragua, and the United Kingdom. The Commission’s first regular session was held in December 2004; the permanent secretariat in Pohnpei became operational in 2005.

name: Indian Ocean Tuna Commission

description: Regional fisheries management organisation under FAO Article XIV responsible for the conservation and management of tuna and tuna-like species in the Indian Ocean and adjacent seas. The Agreement establishing the Commission was approved by the FAO Council on 25 November 1993 and entered into force on 27 March 1996 upon the tenth instrument of acceptance. The Commission comprises 29 Contracting Parties — including the European Union and France in respect of its Indian Ocean territories — plus Cooperating Non-Contracting Parties; it adopts binding conservation and management measures, monitors compliance, and coordinates scientific stock assessment through its Scientific Committee and species working parties.

other_names.name: Commission des thons de l'océan Indien

notes: The ten original acceptances that brought the Agreement into force were Sri Lanka, Eritrea, Mauritius, India, the United Kingdom, Pakistan, Seychelles, the European Community, Madagascar, and the Republic of Korea (Korea deposited the tenth instrument on 27 March 1996). France participates as France (OT) in respect of its Indian Ocean overseas territories. The United Kingdom originally accepted in 1995 (including for British Indian Ocean Territory) and deposited a successor instrument as the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland on 22 December 2020 following Brexit-related membership changes. Former Contracting Parties are Belize (left end-2016), Vanuatu (left end-2015), Guinea (left end-2017), Sierra Leone (left early 2021), and founding member Eritrea (left end-2023). Liberia (since 2015) and Panama (since 2025) hold Cooperating Non-Contracting Party status. The Secretariat has operated in Victoria, Seychelles, since January 1998.

RECOFI replaced the former Gulf fisheries committee of the Indian Ocean Fishery Commission and maintains working groups on fisheries management and aquaculture.
notes: All eight Gulf and Sea of Oman coastal states signed the 1999 agreement; acceptance instruments were deposited between July 2000 and October 2008, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates triggering entry into force on 26 February 2001. Bahrain and Iraq were the last to accept; Kuwait participated in the first session in October 2001 before depositing acceptance in 2006. Subsidiary bodies include the Working Group on Fisheries Management and the Working Group on Aquaculture.

name: Generalized System of Preferences
recognition_status: Non-reciprocal preferential tariff framework established under UNCTAD in the 1960s; GATT Decision on Generalized System of Preferences adopted on 25 June 1971; made permanent through the 1979 GATT Enabling Clause (Decision of 28 November 1979), which permits WTO members to grant generalized, non-discriminatory, non-reciprocal tariff preferences to developing countries
description: The Generalized System of Preferences (GSP) is a WTO-authorized framework under which developed economies grant unilateral, non-reciprocal preferential tariff treatment to imports from designated developing and least developed countries. Conceived within UNCTAD in the 1960s and codified through the 1971 GATT waivers and the permanent 1979 Enabling Clause, GSP allows preference-granting countries to reduce import duties below most-favoured-nation rates for eligible products without requiring reciprocal concessions from beneficiaries. Each preference-granting economy operates its own national scheme with distinct product coverage, rules of origin, graduation thresholds, and beneficiary lists. Fifteen economies currently maintain GSP or GSP-equivalent schemes, including the European Union, Japan, Canada, Australia, Norway, Switzerland, New Zealand, Iceland, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Eurasian Economic Union members Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and the Russian Federation.

notes: Includes lists preference-granting economies operating national GSP schemes, not beneficiary developing countries. Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and the Russian Federation grant preferences through the Eurasian Economic Union Common System of Tariff Preferences (in force 2016). The United Kingdom replaced EU GSP coverage with the Developing Countries Trading Scheme (DCTS), which entered into force on 19 June 2023. The United States GSP authorization expired on 31 December 2020 and remained lapsed as of mid-2026, though the statutory framework persists and past lapses have been followed by retroactive renewals. Product coverage, graduation rules, and beneficiary eligibility differ across national schemes.

description: The South Pacific Regional Trade and Economic Cooperation Agreement (SPARTECA) is a non-reciprocal preferential trade arrangement signed in Tarawa on 14 July 1980 among Australia, New Zealand, and Pacific Islands Forum island countries. Australia and New Zealand grant duty-free and concessional access to products originating from participating island economies, subject to rules of origin requiring substantial manufacture in a beneficiary country. The agreement entered into force on 1 January 1981 and was registered with the United Nations on 14 July 1981. SPARTECA addressed unequal trade relationships in the South Pacific and has been particularly significant for textiles, clothing, and footwear exports. It remains in force alongside later Pacific regional arrangements including PACER and PACER Plus, with PACER Plus prevailing where provisions are inconsistent.

description: Interim Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 15 January 2009 between the European Union and the Central Africa Party, initially implemented with Cameroon. Negotiations for a comprehensive regional EPA with Central African countries were launched in 2003. The agreement provides duty-free, quota-free EU market access for Cameroon and a phased 15-year reduction of tariffs on approximately 80% of EU exports to Cameroon, covering trade in goods, aid for trade, institutional issues, and dispute settlement. Cameroon is currently the only Central African country that has signed and ratified the interim EPA; the agreement remains open to accession by other countries in the regional configuration.

other_names.name: Accord de partenariat économique UE-Afrique centrale
Acuerdo de Asociación Económica UE-África Central

notes: Regional EPA negotiations cover Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo (Brazzaville), Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and São Tomé and Príncipe. Angola, Burundi, and Rwanda are ECCAS members but not part of this EPA configuration. Chad, Central African Republic, DRC, and São Tomé and Príncipe currently trade with the EU under Everything but Arms; Congo (Brazzaville) under the GSP; Gabon and Equatorial Guinea are ineligible for GSP as upper-middle-income countries.

name: Global System of Trade Preferences among Developing Countries
recognition_status: Preferential trade agreement signed in Belgrade on 13 April 1988 among developing countries under the UNCTAD and Group of 77 framework; entered into force on 19 April 1989; notified to the GATT/WTO on 25 September 1989 under the Enabling Clause; UNCTAD serves as the agreement secretariat
description: The Global System of Trade Preferences among Developing Countries (GSTP) is an inter-regional preferential trade agreement negotiated within the UNCTAD framework by members of the Group of 77 to increase South-South trade through reciprocal tariff reductions. Signed in Belgrade on 13 April 1988, it entered into force on 19 April 1989 and was notified to the GATT/WTO under the Enabling Clause. As of 2026, 43 countries and Mercosur participate as contracting parties. UNCTAD serves as the agreement secretariat and supports the Committee of Participants, which oversees negotiation rounds including the São Paulo Round concluded in 2010.

other_names.name: Global System of Trade Preferences among Developing Countries
Sistema Global de Preferencias Comerciales entre Países en Desarrollo
Système global de préférences commerciales entre pays en développement
Sistema Global de Preferências Comerciais entre Países em Desenvolvimento

notes: Former participants include Colombia (withdrew 2017), Romania (withdrew upon EU accession in 2007), and Yugoslavia (until dissolution). Mercosur participates as a single contracting party alongside its member states Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. The São Paulo Round Protocol of December 2010 envisaged an across-the-board 20% tariff reduction but requires ratification by at least four signatories before entering into force; as of 2026 Argentina, Brazil, Cuba, India, Malaysia, and Uruguay have ratified.

name: India-MERCOSUR Preferential Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Preferential trade agreement between India and the four founding MERCOSUR member states, signed in New Delhi on 25 January 2004; annexes added 19 March 2005; entered into force 1 June 2009; notified to the WTO under the Enabling Clause on 23 February 2010
description: Preferential trade agreement signed in New Delhi on 25 January 2004 between India and the four founding MERCOSUR member states (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay). Annexes incorporating tariff concession lists and rules of origin were added on 19 March 2005; the agreement entered into force on 1 June 2009. Provides reciprocal preferential tariffs on approximately 450 product lines from each side, notified to the WTO under the Enabling Clause in February 2010. Parties have held ongoing negotiations to expand product coverage beyond the original lists.
notes: A Framework Agreement was signed on 17 June 2003. Annexes I–V (tariff offer lists, rules of origin, safeguard measures, and dispute settlement) were incorporated on 19 March 2005. Bolivia, which joined MERCOSUR as a full member in 2024, is not a party to this agreement. Expansion negotiations to broaden product coverage have been under discussion since 2009.

name: Commonwealth of Independent States Free Trade Area

acronyms.value: 獨立國家國協自由貿易區

recognition_status: Free trade agreement signed in Saint Petersburg on 18 October 2011 by eight Commonwealth of Independent States governments; entered into force on 20 September 2012 for the first ratifying parties; replaces the 1994 CIS free trade agreement and numerous bilateral arrangements among participants; Uzbekistan acceded via a separate protocol signed on 13 December 2013 that entered into force on 12 January 2014
description: The Commonwealth of Independent States Free Trade Area (CIS FTA) is a multilateral free trade agreement in goods signed in Saint Petersburg on 18 October 2011 by eight CIS governments and entered into force on 20 September 2012 for the first ratifying parties. It establishes a comprehensive free trade regime among participants, replacing the 1994 CIS free trade agreement and over one hundred prior bilateral and multilateral arrangements. Goods must carry a preferential certificate CT-1 or a declaration of origin to qualify for duty-free treatment under the 2009 CIS rules of origin. The treaty permits members to maintain other trade agreements and customs unions, and Eurasian Economic Union members apply a grandfather clause for pre-2015 third-country FTAs. Uzbekistan joined through a separate protocol signed in December 2013 rather than as an original signatory. Azerbaijan is the only full CIS member state that does not participate.

other_names.name: Commonwealth of Independent States Free Trade Area
Tratado de Libre Comercio de la Comunidad de Estados Independientes
Zone de libre-échange de la Communauté des États indépendants

notes: Russia suspended application of the CIS FTA with respect to Ukraine from 1 January 2016; Ukraine responded with reciprocal trade restrictions on Russia from 2 January 2016, but bilateral FTA provisions with other CIS FTA parties remain in effect. Uzbekistan applies the agreement under a separate protocol and, as of 2024, had not yet acceded to the 2009 rules of origin, continuing to apply the 1993 rules instead. A draft bill to denounce the treaty was introduced in the Verkhovna Rada in November 2022 but had not completed the denunciation process as of mid-2026. Azerbaijan is the only full CIS member that is not a party to the agreement.

name: EU-Eastern and Southern Africa Economic Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Interim Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 29 August 2009 in Grand Baie, Mauritius between the EU and Eastern and Southern Africa states; Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles, and Zimbabwe have provisionally applied it since 14 May 2012; Comoros signed in July 2017 and began provisional application on 7 February 2019; European Parliament consent in January 2013; open to accession by other ESA regional configuration countries; on 10 June 2026 the EU and four ESA states (Comoros, Madagascar, Mauritius, and Seychelles) concluded negotiations on an enhanced EPA, with Zimbabwe negotiations ongoing
description: Interim Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 29 August 2009 between the European Union and Eastern and Southern Africa states. Madagascar, Mauritius, Seychelles, and Zimbabwe began provisional application on 14 May 2012; Comoros joined on 7 February 2019. The agreement provides duty-free, quota-free EU market access for ESA partners, phased liberalisation of tariffs on EU imports (around 80–98% depending on the partner), rules of origin, fisheries, development cooperation, and dispute settlement, with a rendez-vous clause to deepen coverage to services, investment, and sustainable development. Negotiations to deepen the EPA launched in October 2019; on 10 June 2026 the EU and four ESA states concluded an enhanced comprehensive agreement, with Zimbabwe accession still under negotiation.

other_names.name: EU-Eastern and Southern Africa Economic Partnership Agreement
Accord de partenariat économique UE-Afrique orientale et australe
Acuerdo de Asociación Económica UE-África Oriental y Meridional

notes: ESA regional configuration covers Comoros, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Seychelles, Sudan, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Six states concluded the interim EPA at the end of 2007; Zambia did not sign. Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Malawi, and Sudan are Horn of Africa or mainland members outside the current applying group. On 10 June 2026 the EU concluded an enhanced EPA with Comoros, Madagascar, Mauritius, and Seychelles; Zimbabwe negotiations continue. Non-applying ESA LDCs trade with the EU under Everything but Arms pending accession.

name: SAARC Preferential Trading Arrangement
recognition_status: Preferential trade arrangement signed in Dhaka on 11 April 1993 by the seven SAARC member states; entered into force on 7 December 1995 after ratification by all contracting states; superseded by the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) on 1 January 2006
description: The SAARC Preferential Trading Arrangement (SAPTA) was a framework agreement signed in Dhaka on 11 April 1993 by the seven SAARC member states to promote intra-regional trade through reciprocal tariff concessions under a positive-list approach. It entered into force on 7 December 1995 after all contracting states completed ratification formalities. Four rounds of negotiations expanded product coverage to more than 6,500 tariff lines. SAPTA was envisaged as the first step toward deeper South Asian economic integration and was superseded by the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) on 1 January 2006, although SAPTA concessions remained available until completion of the SAFTA trade liberalization programme.
notes: Afghanistan joined SAARC in April 2007, after SAPTA had already been superseded by SAFTA, and was therefore not a contracting party to SAPTA. The agreement was signed at the seventh SAARC summit in Dhaka; Sri Lanka had first proposed a preferential trading arrangement at the sixth summit in Colombo in December 1991.

name: EU-Pacific Economic Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Interim Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 30 July 2009 in London between the EU and Pacific ACP states; not yet formally in force but provisionally applied by Papua New Guinea since 20 December 2009, Fiji since 28 July 2014, Samoa since 31 December 2018, and Solomon Islands since 17 May 2020; open to accession by other ACP Pacific states
description: Interim Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 30 July 2009 between the European Union and Pacific ACP states. The agreement establishes a framework for reciprocal trade in goods with asymmetric liberalisation favouring Pacific partners, including duty-free and quota-free EU market access, phased tariff reduction on EU imports, rules of origin with global sourcing provisions for fisheries, and technical and sanitary cooperation. It has not formally entered into force but is provisionally applied by Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Samoa, and Solomon Islands; accession remains open to the other Pacific ACP states in the regional configuration.
notes: Regional EPA configuration covers 15 ACP Pacific states — Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. Niue, Tonga, and Tuvalu have EU Council approval for accession (January 2025); Vanuatu, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Timor-Leste are in active accession processes. Cook Islands, Kiribati, Nauru, and Palau are in earlier stages of joining. Pacific LDCs not yet applying the EPA continue to trade with the EU under Everything but Arms.

name: Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement
recognition_status: Preferential trade agreement signed in Bangkok on 31 July 1975 as the First Agreement on Trade Negotiations among Developing Member Countries of ESCAP (Bangkok Agreement); entered into force on 17 June 1976; notified to the GATT/WTO under the Enabling Clause on 2 November 1976; renamed Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement (APTA) on 2 November 2005; amended agreement entered into force on 1 September 2006
description: The Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement (APTA), formerly known as the Bangkok Agreement, is the oldest preferential regional trade agreement among developing countries in the Asia-Pacific. Signed in Bangkok on 31 July 1975 under the auspices of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), it entered into force on 17 June 1976 and was renamed APTA on 2 November 2005. Seven participating states — Bangladesh, China, India, the Republic of Korea, Lao PDR, Mongolia, and Sri Lanka — exchange reciprocal tariff concessions through successive negotiation rounds covering goods, with framework agreements on trade facilitation, services, and investment. ESCAP's Trade, Investment and Innovation Division serves as the agreement secretariat.
notes: China acceded in April 2001, the first expansion since the original five participating states. Mongolia's accession terms were finalized in October 2013; it deposited its instrument of accession on 29 September 2020, becoming the seventh participating state. The third round of tariff concessions entered into force on 1 September 2006. Participating states are negotiating a fourth round to widen product coverage and deepen cooperation on trade facilitation, services, and investment.

name: Protocol on Trade Negotiations
recognition_status: Preferential trade agreement signed in Geneva on 8 December 1971 among developing countries under the GATT Enabling Clause framework; entered into force on 11 February 1973; notified to the GATT/WTO on 9 November 1971
description: Preferential trade agreement signed in Geneva on 8 December 1971 among developing countries to exchange reciprocal tariff concessions under the GATT Enabling Clause. One of the earliest South–South preferential trade arrangements; entered into force on 11 February 1973. Fifteen developing countries currently apply the agreement; four former participants (Greece, India, Romania, and Spain) have withdrawn.

other_names.name: Protocolo Relativo a las Negociaciones Comerciales entre Países en Desarrollo
Protocole concernant les négociations commerciales entre pays en voie de développement

notes: Serbia continues application as successor to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, an original signatory. Bangladesh acceded in 1976; Romania acceded in 1978 and withdrew in 2006. Greece withdrew effective 28 June 1980 upon accession to the European Economic Community. Spain ratified on 12 January 1973 and withdrew effective 6 February 1987. India notified withdrawal effective 29 March 1993.

name: EU-CARIFORUM Economic Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Full Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 15 October 2008 in Bridgetown, Barbados between the EU and 14 CARIFORUM states; provisionally applied since 29 December 2008; first comprehensive EU EPA covering goods, services, investment, and a Protocol on Cultural Cooperation; Haiti signed on 10 December 2009 but is not applying the agreement pending parliamentary ratification
description: Full Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 15 October 2008 between the European Union and 14 CARIFORUM states. The agreement provides duty-free, quota-free EU market access for all Caribbean products, phased liberalisation of EU exports to CARIFORUM over 15–25 years with permanent protection for the most sensitive goods, market access in services and investment, rules of origin with regional cumulation, a Protocol on Cultural Cooperation, and development cooperation provisions. It has been provisionally applied since 29 December 2008 and was the first comprehensive EU EPA to enter into force.
notes: CARIFORUM regional configuration covers 15 states — Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Barbados, Belize, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Grenada, Guyana, Haiti, Jamaica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, and Trinidad and Tobago. Fourteen states signed in October 2008 and provisionally apply the EPA; Haiti signed on 10 December 2009 but is not applying it pending parliamentary ratification and continues to trade with the EU under Everything but Arms. The agreement includes regional preference clauses for intra-Caribbean trade and cumulation with other ACP and EU overseas territories in the Caribbean.

name: EU-SADC Economic Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 10 June 2016 between the EU and the SADC EPA Group (Botswana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, and Eswatini); provisionally applied since 10 October 2016 by five parties and since 4 February 2018 by Mozambique; first fully operational regional EPA in Africa; repealed the trade component of the EU-South Africa TDCA; Angola participated in negotiations but did not sign and has an option to accede
description: Economic Partnership Agreement signed on 10 June 2016 between the European Union and the SADC EPA Group — Botswana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, and Eswatini. The agreement provides asymmetric market access with duty-free, quota-free EU entry for Botswana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, and Eswatini and enhanced access for South Africa beyond the former EU-South Africa TDCA, while SADC partners liberalise around 74–86% of tariff lines on EU imports. It covers trade in goods, development cooperation, sustainable development, and dispute settlement, and became the first fully operational regional EPA in Africa when Mozambique began applying it in February 2018.
notes: SADC EPA Group covers six Southern African states. Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa, and Eswatini form the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) and began provisional application on 10 October 2016; Mozambique joined on 4 February 2018. Angola participated in negotiations but did not sign; it submitted an accession request in February 2020. Other SADC members (Comoros, Democratic Republic of Congo, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Seychelles, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe) are outside this EPA configuration — Indian Ocean states trade under the EU-ESA EPA; most mainland members continue under Everything but Arms or GSP pending their own EPA tracks.

name: EU-West Africa Economic Partnership Agreement
recognition_status: Regional Economic Partnership Agreement initialled on 30 June 2014 between the EU and 16 West African states (ECOWAS members plus Mauritania), together with ECOWAS and UEMOA; not yet in force pending signature by all West African parties and ratification by two thirds of them; Nigeria has not signed. Interim stepping-stone EPAs with Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana were signed on 28 July 2016 and entered provisional application on 15 December 2016.
description: Regional Economic Partnership Agreement negotiated between the European Union and 16 West African states — the ECOWAS membership plus Mauritania — together with ECOWAS and UEMOA. Negotiations concluded in February 2014 and the agreement was initialled in Ouagadougou on 30 June 2014. The regional EPA has not entered into force; trade is governed by interim stepping-stone EPAs with Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, which provide duty-free, quota-free EU market access and phased tariff liberalisation on EU exports while preserving regional integration objectives aligned with the ECOWAS Common External Tariff.

other_names.name: Accord de partenariat économique UE-Afrique de l'Ouest
Acuerdo de Asociación Económica UE-África Occidental

notes: Regional EPA configuration covers Benin, Burkina Faso, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, and Togo. Mauritania is included in the West Africa EPA configuration but is not an ECOWAS member. Nigeria is the only regional party that has not signed the regional EPA. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana apply separate interim EPAs pending full regional implementation. Most other West African LDCs continue to trade with the EU under Everything but Arms until the regional EPA enters force.

name: Mesoamerican region
description: The Mesoamerican region (MAR) is a trans-national economic territory in the Americas recognized by the OECD and other development organizations. It comprises the seven Central American countries plus Mexico; OECD coverage of Mexico is limited to nine south-eastern states (Campeche, Chiapas, Guerrero, Oaxaca, Puebla, Quintana Roo, Tabasco, Veracruz, and Yucatán). The OECD designation gained prominence after the 2001 Puebla–Panama Plan (PPP) for regional integration across south-eastern Mexico and Central America.
notes: OECD economic territory, not a formal organization. Mexico is listed at country level although only nine south-eastern states fall within the MAR; the broader Puebla–Panama Plan also included Colombia, which is outside the OECD Mesoamerican region. The MAR loosely correlates with the pre-Columbian Mesoamerica culture area but is a modern economic label distinct from geographic groupings such as CENTRALAMER and MIDAMERICA.

name: Periphery countries
description: In world-systems theory, periphery countries are those that are less developed than the semi-periphery and core countries. These countries usually receive a disproportionately small share of global wealth and are often dependent on more developed states for capital, technology, and markets.
notes: Membership follows the periphery-country list in Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000), "Trade Globalization since 1795: Waves of Integration in the World-System" (American Sociological Review 65:77–95), as reproduced on Wikipedia. World-systems classifications overlap across sources and time periods; countries such as Chile, Greece, Hungary, Spain, Portugal, and Turkey appear in multiple tiers in different studies.

provenance.source: Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000) via Wikipedia

name: G33
description: G33 (also known as the Friends of Special Products in agriculture) is a coalition of developing countries established before the 2003 Cancún WTO ministerial conference to coordinate during the Doha Round agriculture negotiations. Dominated by India, the group seeks flexibility for developing countries to limit market opening in agriculture, advocating for a "special products" exemption from tariff cuts and a "special safeguard mechanism" to raise tariffs in response to import surges. Despite the "33" in its name — reflecting the original founding membership — the coalition had grown to 47 WTO members by 2021.

other_names.name: Friends of Special Products in agriculture

notes: WTO agriculture negotiating coalition formed ahead of the 2003 Cancún ministerial. Not to be confused with any G33 finance ministers group. Membership roster per WTO "Groups in the agriculture negotiations" (last updated April 2021); Wikipedia cites 48 members, while the WTO official list enumerates 47 WTO members. Distinct from the WTO G-20 (agriculture), G-10, and Cairns Group coalitions in the same negotiations.

name: Core countries
description: In world-systems theory, core countries (or the imperial core) are the industrialized capitalist and/or imperialist countries.
notes: Membership follows the core-country list in Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000), "Trade Globalization since 1795: Waves of Integration in the World-System" (American Sociological Review 65:77–95), as reproduced on Wikipedia. World-systems classifications overlap across sources and time periods; countries such as Chile, Greece, Hungary, Spain, Portugal, and Turkey appear in multiple tiers in different studies.

provenance.source: Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000) via Wikipedia

name: Middle America
description: Middle America is a subregion in the Northern Hemisphere tropics of the Americas. It usually comprises Mexico, the seven sovereign states of Central America, and the Caribbean island countries and dependent territories — per the Wikipedia regional definition.
notes: Informal geographic label, not an organization. Wikipedia lists 21 sovereign states and 18 Caribbean dependencies; Navassa Island (US) is omitted here because it has no Internacia country code. Colombia, Venezuela, and The Guianas are sometimes included in broader definitions; Bermuda is often grouped with the Caribbean but is excluded from the standard Middle America definition.

name: Next Eleven
description: Next Eleven (N-11) is an acronym for Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, South Korea, Turkey, and Vietnam — eleven large-population developing economies identified in December 2005 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill as the next set of countries with potential to follow the BRICs in influencing the global economy. The grouping was introduced in Global Economics Paper No. 134 ("How Solid are the BRICs?") as a framework to assess which other populous nations might achieve BRIC-like growth trajectories and rival the G7 over time.
notes: Coined by Jim O'Neill (Goldman Sachs) in Global Economics Paper No. 134 (December 2005) as a follow-on to the BRIC acronym. Selection criterion was large population plus potential for BRIC-like growth; Goldman Sachs judged only Mexico and perhaps South Korea capable of rivaling the BRICs in global importance, though several others have compelling potential. Five members overlap with CIVETS (Egypt, Indonesia, Turkey, Vietnam, plus Colombia and South Africa in CIVETS). Related but distinct from BRICS, CIVETS, E7, MINT, TIMBI, and VISTA groupings.

name: VISTA
description: VISTA is an acronym for Vietnam, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey, and Argentina — five emerging-market economies proposed in November 2006 by economist Takafumi Kadokura of the BRICs Economic Research Institute as a post-BRICs investment grouping. The term (a pun on the word "vista") highlights countries with strong trade, sourcing, and investment potential but has not achieved the same global recognition as BRICs, CIVETS, or the Next Eleven.

other_names.name: Vietnam, Indonesia, South Africa, Turkey, and Argentina

notes: Coined by Takafumi Kadokura (BRICs Economic Research Institute) on 6 November 2006 in Nikkei BP Online as a post-BRICs emerging-market framework. Chooses Argentina over Mexico (OECD member) and South Africa over Nigeria for Africa representation. Three members (Vietnam, Indonesia, Turkey) overlap with CIVETS; Indonesia also appears in MINT and TIMBI; South Africa joined BRICS in 2010. Related but distinct from N-11, CIVETS, MINT, TIMBI, and E7 groupings.

name: FATF blacklist
description: The FATF blacklist — officially called "High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action" — is a list maintained by the Financial Action Task Force of countries with significant strategic deficiencies in anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing, and counter-proliferation financing regimes. FATF calls on members and other jurisdictions to apply enhanced due diligence, and in the most serious cases countermeasures, to protect the international financial system. As of the October 2025 FATF plenary, the list comprises Iran, North Korea, and Myanmar.

other_names.name: القائمة السوداء لمجموعة العمل المالي الدولية
反洗钱金融行动特别工作组黑名单

notes: First published in June 2000 as the Non-Cooperative Countries or Territories (NCCT) list. North Korea and Iran are subject to FATF calls for countermeasures; Myanmar was moved from the grey list to the blacklist in October 2022 and remains subject to enhanced due diligence (not full countermeasures as of October 2025). Distinct from the FATF grey list ("Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring"), which tracks a separate roster of countries working to address strategic deficiencies.

name: Semi-periphery countries
description: In world-systems theory, semi-periphery countries are the industrializing, mostly capitalist countries that are positioned between the periphery and the core countries.
notes: Membership follows the semi-periphery country list in Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000), "Trade Globalization since 1795: Waves of Integration in the World-System" (American Sociological Review 65:77–95), as reproduced on Wikipedia. World-systems classifications overlap across sources and time periods; countries such as Chile, Greece, Hungary, Spain, Portugal, and Turkey appear in multiple tiers in different studies.

provenance.source: Chase-Dunn, Kawano, and Brewer (2000) via Wikipedia

name: PIGS
description: PIGS is a derogatory acronym for Portugal, Italy, Greece, and Spain — four Southern European EU economies grouped in financial commentary since the 1990s as the euro area integrated and their debt and growth profiles drew comparison. During the European sovereign-debt crisis of 2009–2014 the variant PIIGS (adding Ireland) and the reordering GIPSI or GIIPS became common; usage of the term was discouraged by the Financial Times and Barclays Capital in 2010 as offensive.
notes: Core membership is Portugal, Italy, Greece, and Spain (P-I-G-S). Ireland was added during the 2008–2014 debt crisis as PIIGS; Italy was sometimes dropped when Ireland was included. Karim Abadir coined GIPSI for the expected sequencing of crises. Extended variants PIGGS and PIIGGS add France or the United Kingdom. Widely regarded as derogatory and racist framing in academic and media commentary.

name: Landlocked developing countries
description: Landlocked developing countries (LLDCs) are developing countries without direct access to the sea. The United Nations recognizes 32 LLDCs — 16 in Africa, 12 in Asia, 2 in Europe, and 2 in South America — out of the world's 44 landlocked countries. UN-OHRLLS coordinates international support for the group; the Awaza Programme of Action (2024–2034) sets priorities on trade integration, transport connectivity, and structural transformation.
notes: UN classification maintained by UN-OHRLLS. Membership overlaps substantially with the Least Developed Countries (LDC) list but is not identical — several LLDCs are middle-income countries (e.g. Kazakhstan, Mongolia). European LLDCs (Moldova, North Macedonia) are generally more developed than African, Asian, and South American members due to regional market integration. Distinct from the broader set of all landlocked countries, which includes developed European states such as Austria and Switzerland.

name: CIVETS
description: CIVETS is an acronym for Colombia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Egypt, Turkey, and South Africa — six emerging-market economies identified for strong growth potential, coined in late 2009 by Robert Ward of the Economist Intelligence Unit as a second-wave counterpart to the BRIC grouping. The term was popularized by HSBC president Michael Geoghegan in 2010 and highlights countries with diverse economies, young growing populations, and relatively sophisticated financial systems.
notes: Coined by Robert Ward (Economist Intelligence Unit) in late 2009, inspired by Jim O'Neill's BRIC acronym. Popularized by Michael Geoghegan (HSBC) in April 2010 as "the new BRICs". Five of six members (all except Colombia and South Africa) overlap with Goldman's Next Eleven (N-11). Related but distinct from VISTA, MINT, and E7 groupings.

name: Middle East and North Africa
description: MENA (Middle East and North Africa) is a geographic and economic grouping with no single standardized definition. Internacia follows the World Bank MENA classification of 21 countries and territories — the six Gulf Cooperation Council members plus Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Malta, Morocco, Palestine, Syria, Tunisia, and Yemen. The label is widely used in academia, development finance, media planning, and business; alternative acronyms include WANA (West Asia and North Africa) and SWANA (South West Asia and North Africa).
notes: MENA has no fixed membership list across organizations. UNICEF, UNAIDS, IMF, and Pew Research use different rosters (e.g. some include Sudan or Somalia, some exclude Israel or Malta). This record uses the World Bank 21-country/territory set. Turkey, Cyprus, Mauritania, Sudan, Somalia, Afghanistan, and Pakistan appear in other MENA/WANA definitions but are excluded here. See also geographic records MIDDLEEAST and MAGHREB for narrower regional definitions.

name: Emerging and Growth-Leading Economies
description: EAGLE (Emerging and Growth-Leading Economies) is a dynamic grouping of emerging markets created by BBVA Research in 2010 for economies whose expected incremental GDP contribution over the next ten years exceeds the average of the G6 industrialized nations (G7 excluding the United States). Unlike fixed-acronym groupings such as BRIC or CIVETS, EAGLE membership is revised annually from growth forecasts; the 2015 roster comprised fourteen countries led by China and India. BBVA also maintains an EAGLEs Nest watch list for economies below the EAGLE threshold but above Italy's expected contribution.

other_names.name: Economías Emergentes que lideran el Crecimiento Global

notes: Coined by BBVA Research in November 2010 as a forward-looking alternative to static BRIC-style acronyms. The inaugural 2011 cohort had ten members (China, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Korea, Russia, Mexico, Egypt, Taiwan, Turkey); membership is re-evaluated each year from ten-year incremental-GDP forecasts. The 2015 EAGLEs roster listed fourteen countries; Egypt, Iran, and Malaysia appear in the Nest watch list rather than the core EAGLE group. Related but distinct from BRIC, CIVETS, E7, N-11, MINT, and VISTA groupings.

name: Southern Cone
description: The Southern Cone (Spanish Cono Sur, Portuguese Cone Sul) is a geographical and cultural subregion of the southernmost areas of South America, mostly south of the Tropic of Capricorn. The core countries are Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay; broader definitions also include Paraguay and Brazil's southern states (Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, and São Paulo).
notes: Informal geographic and cultural label, not an organization. Narrow definitions cover only Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay; Wikipedia and Wikidata also list Paraguay and Brazil at country level, while many geographic accounts treat only Brazil's four southernmost states as part of the cone.

name: E7
description: E7 (Emerging 7) is an acronym for Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Russia, and Turkey — the seven largest emerging-market economies grouped by PricewaterhouseCoopers economists John Hawksworth and Gordon Cookson in 2006 as an emerging-market counterpart to the advanced-economy G7. The term is widely used in long-term growth forecasting and macroeconomic research; the World Bank uses the closely related EM7 label for the same seven countries.
notes: Coined at PwC in 2006 as the emerging-market mirror of the G7. Membership matches the World Bank EM7 grouping (China, India, Brazil, Russia, Mexico, Indonesia, Turkey). Distinct from BRICS (which excludes Mexico and Turkey), TIMBI, MINT, and VISTA acronyms that overlap partially with the E7 roster.

name: Weimar Triangle
description: The Weimar Triangle is a regional alliance of France, Germany, and Poland established on 28–29 August 1991 in Weimar, Germany, by their foreign ministers. The format promotes cooperation on European and cross-border issues through summit meetings of leaders and ministers, parliamentary contacts, and military, scientific, and cultural exchanges. It was created to support Poland's transition from Communist rule and integration into Western European structures.
notes: Informal trilateral format without a permanent secretariat. Activity has fluctuated since the 1990s, with renewed summits after Brexit and Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The Weimar Battlegroup (EU battlegroup under Polish command, agreed 2011) is a related but distinct military cooperation project.

name: FATF grey list
description: The FATF grey list — officially called "Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring" — is a roster maintained by the Financial Action Task Force of countries and territories with strategic deficiencies in anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing, and counter-proliferation financing regimes that have committed to address them under agreed action plans. Unlike the FATF blacklist ("High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action"), the FATF does not call for enhanced due diligence measures against grey-list jurisdictions but encourages members to take the published information into account in risk analysis. As of the June 2026 FATF plenary, the list comprises 22 jurisdictions; Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq were added and Algeria and Namibia were removed.

other_names.name: 反洗钱金融行动特别工作组灰名单

notes: Evolved from FATF's February 2010 "Improving Global AML/CFT Compliance: on-going process" statements, reinvigorated after the 2008 G20 call for regular updates on jurisdictions with strategic AML/CFT deficiencies. Membership changes at each FATF plenary (typically February, June, and October). At the June 2026 plenary, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Iraq were added; Algeria and Namibia graduated after completing action plans. Distinct from the FATF blacklist (FATFBLACKLIST), which triggers calls for enhanced due diligence or countermeasures.

name: Failed States
description: Failed States (FAILEDS) maps to the "Alert" tier of the Fund for Peace Fragile States Index (FSI; formerly the Failed States Index) — countries scoring 90.0–120.0 on the 12-indicator composite, indicating the highest measured vulnerability to state collapse or conflict. A failed state is a state that has lost its ability to fulfill fundamental security and development functions, lacking effective control over its territory and borders. As of the 2024 FSI, 29 countries fall in the Alert category, led by Somalia, Sudan, and South Sudan.
notes: The Fund for Peace has published the Fragile States Index annually since 2005 (as the Failed States Index until 2014). Alert-tier membership (scores 90.0–120.0) changes each year as country scores shift; this roster reflects the 2024 edition. The index measures vulnerability, not an official designation — Alert countries are not necessarily experiencing active collapse. Distinct from the FSI Warning (60.0–89.9), Stable (30.0–59.9), and Sustainable (0.0–29.9) tiers.

name: Newly industrialized countries
description: NIC (newly industrialized country) is a socioeconomic classification applied by economists and political scientists to developing economies whose industrialization and export-led growth outpace other developing nations. There is no fixed official roster; Wikipedia's widely cited current list comprises Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, and Turkey — overlapping partially with G8+5, BRICS, E7, and MINT groupings.
notes: The term entered use around 1970 as the Four Asian Tigers (Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea) graduated to high-income status. Unlike formal organizations, NIC membership varies by author; Brunei, Mongolia, and Vietnam appear in some lists. Turkey and South Africa were classified among developed countries by the CIA World Factbook in 2008. Related but distinct from BRICS, E7, MINT, TIMBI, and VISTA acronyms.

name: Baltic States
description: The Baltic states or Baltic countries is a geopolitical term for the three sovereign states on the eastern coast of the Baltic Sea — Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. All three are members of NATO, the European Union, the Eurozone, the Baltic Assembly, and the OECD. Since regaining independence in 1991, they cooperate closely in foreign, security, energy, and transport policy.
notes: Informal geopolitical label, not an organization. After World War I the term sometimes also included Finland; since World War II it is generally limited to Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. It is distinct from broader "Baltic Sea countries" or "Baltic region" labels that may include other littoral states.

name: TIMBI
description: TIMBI is an acronym for Turkey, India, Mexico, Brazil, and Indonesia — five large emerging-market democracies proposed as a successor grouping to the BRICs by George Mason University professor Jack Goldstone in a December 2011 Foreign Policy article. The term highlights countries with favorable demographics, political openness, and strong growth potential relative to China and Russia.

other_names.name: Turkey, India, Mexico, Brazil, and Indonesia

notes: Coined by Jack Goldstone in Foreign Policy (2 December 2011) as an alternative to BRICs, emphasizing democratic emerging economies with growing labor forces. Related but distinct from MINT (Mexico, Indonesia, Nigeria, Turkey) and VISTA groupings.

name: The African Electrotechnical Standardization Commission
legal_status: subsidiary body of the African Energy Commission
recognition_status: Established under African Union auspices as a subsidiary body of AFREC following the 2008 Algiers ministerial declaration on energy

secretariat.organization: Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy, Egypt

description: Subsidiary body of the African Energy Commission (AFREC) under African Union auspices, established following the 17 February 2008 declaration of the Conference of African Ministers of Energy in Algiers. AFSEC harmonizes and develops electrotechnical standards and conformity assessment requirements to improve electricity access and support Africa's industrialization, drawing on internationally accepted standards including IEC publications. Headquarters in Cairo, Egypt since 2019 (hosted by Egypt's Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy), after relocating from a temporary secretariat in South Africa.
notes: AFSEC is one of the PAQI (Pan-African Quality Infrastructure) pillars and participates in AfCFTA technical-barriers-to-trade implementation. As of 2026 the secretariat lists 19 statutory members and 13 affiliate members; the homepage counter may lag updates. National electrotechnical committees represent each statutory member.

name: International Astronomical Union
recognition_status: International non-governmental scientific union founded at the 1919 Constitutive Assembly of the International Research Council in Brussels; member of the International Science Council (ISC); recognized by the United Nations as the international authority for astronomical nomenclature (UN Resolution 13, 1982)

headquarters.note: IAU Secretariat, Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris, 98-bis boulevard Arago

description: International non-governmental scientific union that promotes and safeguards astronomy in all its aspects — research, communication, education, and development — through international cooperation. Founded on 28 July 1919 in Brussels, the IAU comprises individual members (professional astronomers at Ph.D. level and beyond, organized into Divisions, Commissions, and Working Groups) and national members (organizations representing national professional astronomical communities). As of 2026 the Union has 85 National Members and more than 12,000 individual members spanning over 90 countries. The IAU is the internationally recognized authority for assigning designations to celestial bodies and their surface features, and organizes scientific meetings including triennial General Assemblies. Member of the International Science Council (ISC).
notes: National Members are organizations representing national professional astronomical communities; individual membership is open to professional astronomers worldwide and spans more countries than the National Member roster. Organizations may join on an interim or observer basis before attaining full National Member status. Seven countries were founding members at the 1919 Constitutive Assembly: Belgium, Canada, France, Greece, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

name: World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization

other_names.name: 世界人工智能合作组织

description: Independent intergovernmental organization established on 16 July 2026 in Shanghai to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence, with an orientation toward development and the Global South. Twenty-nine countries signed the founding agreement; headquarters are in Shanghai, China.

name: Indian Ocean Commission
recognition_status: Intergovernmental organization linking five African Indian Ocean nations, institutionalized by the Victoria Agreement (1984) and revised in March 2020; General Secretariat established in Mauritius in 1989
description: Intergovernmental organization created in 1982 in Port Louis, Mauritius, to promote regional cooperation among Comoros, Madagascar, Mauritius, Réunion (France), and Seychelles. Institutionalized by the Victoria Agreement (1984) and revised in 2020. Coordinates projects on maritime security, environmental management, fisheries, climate change adaptation, food security, public health, and regional connectivity. General Secretariat based in Ebène, Mauritius.
notes: Uses ID `COI` rather than `IOC` to avoid collision with the International Olympic Committee; the common English abbreviation is IOC while the French acronym is COI (Commission de l'Océan Indien). Réunion participates as a French overseas department. The Sovereign Order of Malta is also an observer (2017) but has no separate intblock record. Current Secretary-General is Edgard Razafindravahy (Madagascar, since July 2024). Chaired the Contact Group on Piracy off the Coast of Somalia (CGPCS) secretariat in 2018–2020.

name: Digital Nations
description: Collaborative network of the world's leading digital governments with a common goal of harnessing digital technology to improve citizens' lives. Members share world-class digital practices, collaborate to solve common problems, identify improvements to digital services, and support and champion the group's growing digital economies.
notes: Originally founded as Digital 5 (D5) in December 2014 by Estonia, Israel, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, and United Kingdom. Expanded to Digital 7 (D7) in February 2018 with the addition of Canada and Uruguay. Further expanded to Digital 9 (D9) in November 2018 with the addition of Mexico and Portugal. Renamed to Digital Nations (DN) in November 2019 when Denmark joined as the tenth member. The group meets twice per year to showcase accomplishments in countries' digital landscapes and co-create best practices.

name: European Travel Commission
recognition_status: Registered in Belgium as a non-profit international association (association internationale sans but lucratif); strategic partner of the European Commission for promoting Destination Europe in third-country markets
description: Non-profit international association representing 36 European national tourism organisations (NTOs) from 35 countries. Established in 1948 at Stalheim, Norway, to promote Europe as a tourist destination in long-haul markets outside Europe, ETC supports members through market intelligence, cooperative promotion programmes in overseas chapters, and advocacy on competitiveness, sustainability, connectivity, and destination management. Belgium is represented by Visit Flanders and Visit Wallonia; permanent Board seats are held by Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, and Spain.
notes: Full membership comprises 36 NTOs from 35 European countries; Belgium is represented by Visit Flanders and Visit Wallonia. Go Türkiye rejoined as a full member in 2024. An associate membership programme for private-sector organizations has operated since 2015. Overseas chapters promote Destination Europe in the United States, Canada, Brazil, China, Japan, and Australia.

name: International Development Law Organization
description: Global intergovernmental organization exclusively devoted to promoting the rule of law to advance peace and sustainable development. IDLO partners with governments and communities to reform laws and strengthen institutions, aiming to make justice systems fairer and more effective. The organization has experience working in more than 90 countries with diverse legal systems and holds United Nations Observer Status since 2001.

recognition_status: Affiliated body of the D-8 Organization for Economic Cooperation established under the Charter of Establishment and Management of D-8 Technology Transfer and Exchange Network; comprises national coordination organizations (NaCOs) from each D-8 member state with the secretariat hosted at Pardis Technology Park, Iran
description: Affiliated body of the D-8 Organization for Economic Cooperation that facilitates technology transfer among member countries, fulfills technology market functions, and pursues capacity building and information dissemination on technological capabilities, achievements, and needs of D-8 member countries. The network organizes technology transactions and creates coordination and synergism among member states through national coordination organizations (NaCOs), including instruments such as a databank of requests and offers, exhibition support, workshops, and business meetings.

name: Pacific Community
recognition_status: Established by the Canberra Agreement (signed 6 February 1947) as the South Pacific Commission; renamed Secretariat of the Pacific Community in 1997 and Pacific Community in 2016; founding member of the Council of Regional Organisations in the Pacific (CROP, 1988)
description: Intergovernmental development organisation owned and governed by 27 Pacific countries and territories, providing scientific and technical advice across more than 20 sectors including fisheries, public health, geoscience, statistics, education, and climate resilience. Founded in 1947 as the South Pacific Commission under the Canberra Agreement; headquarters in Nouméa, New Caledonia, with regional offices in Suva, Pohnpei, and Port Vila. Works in English and French and is a founding member of the Council of Regional Organisations in the Pacific (CROP).
notes: The Netherlands was a founding signatory of the 1947 Canberra Agreement but withdrew in 1962 after Dutch New Guinea was transferred. The United Kingdom withdrew on 1 January 1996, rejoined on 1 January 1998, withdrew again on 1 January 2005, and rejoined on 2 December 2021. Samoa joined as Western Samoa in 1965. SOPAC (South Pacific Applied Geoscience Commission) was integrated into SPC as the Applied Geoscience and Technology Division from 1 January 2011. Also known by the PC acronym since the 2016 rebrand.

name: Coalition for Rainforest Nations
recognition_status: Intergovernmental coalition of tropical forest countries formed on 10 May 2005 at Columbia University at the initiative of Papua New Guinea; secretariat hosted at Columbia University in New York; instrumental in launching the REDD+ framework under the UNFCCC and advancing forest-climate finance mechanisms including the World Bank Forest Carbon Partnership Facility and UN-REDD
description: Intergovernmental coalition of tropical forest countries that advances sustainable rainforest stewardship and climate action. Formed in May 2005 at Columbia University, CfRN unites developing rainforest nations to negotiate forest-related climate finance and capacity building, and was central to establishing REDD+ under the UNFCCC and Article 5 of the Paris Agreement.

other_names.name: Njikọ Maka Mba Ndị Dị n'Oké Osimiri

notes: Voluntary coalition of tropical forest countries; membership is not treaty-based. The secretariat was established at Columbia University in New York at the request of Papua New Guinea. CfRN provides technical assistance for national REDD+ readiness, greenhouse-gas inventories, and forest reference levels under the UNFCCC.

name: South-East Atlantic Fisheries Organisation

description: Regional fisheries management organisation responsible for the long-term conservation and sustainable use of living marine resources (excluding highly migratory stocks) in the high seas of the southeast Atlantic Ocean, outside the exclusive economic zones of Angola, Namibia, and South Africa and UK overseas territories in the region. The Secretariat is based in Swakopmund, Namibia.

name: Southern Indian Ocean Fisheries Agreement

The Agreement covers fish, molluscs, crustaceans, and other sedentary species, excluding highly migratory species and sedentary stocks under coastal-state jurisdiction. The Secretariat is headquartered in Le Port, Réunion.

Works in close cooperation with the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and holds colloquia, conferences, and symposia on contemporary maritime law issues.

Focuses on regional cooperation in asset disclosure, strengthening public institutions' resilience against corruption, promoting a culture of integrity, and improving asset recovery practices.

The Secretariat is based in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Five countries participate as observers in the Steering Group (Poland, Georgia, Slovenia, Ukraine, and Greece).

Established in 2017 with 14 founding corporate partners, the Forum hosts an annual summit in a different maritime capital each year and incubates industry initiatives including the Getting to Zero Coalition, Poseidon Principles, Sea Cargo Charter, All Aboard Alliance, and Neptune Declaration. Funded through partner contributions and grants; membership is held by organizations across the maritime value chain, not by countries.
notes: Membership is held by maritime companies, industry associations, and philanthropic funders — not sovereign states; country-level includes are therefore not applicable. The Forum was established in 2017 with 14 founding partners including A.P. Møller-Mærsk, Euronav, GasLog, PSA International, Trafigura, and Wan Hai Lines. description: Voluntary global partnership hosted by FAO that brings together governments, international organizations, and civil society to promote sustainable bioenergy for climate change mitigation, energy access, and food security. Colombia, Ghana, and Nigeria remain observers; Nigeria has been moving toward full membership. In February 2023, Malaysia, as chair, invited Thailand to join the organisation. The WCO develops international conventions and tools on commodity classification, valuation, rules of origin, revenue collection, supply chain security, trade facilitation, enforcement, and capacity building. It maintains the Harmonized System (HS) nomenclature and administers the technical aspects of the WTO Agreements on Customs Valuation and Rules of Origin. As of 2026 the WCO comprises 187 member customs administrations.

NPI acts as an International Searching Authority and International Preliminary Examining Authority under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and provides commercial prior-art search services, drawing on examiners from the Danish and Norwegian patent offices. The Board consists of the directors of the three member countries' national patent offices; the Institute is headquartered in Taastrup, Denmark.
notes: NPI also serves as PCT International Searching Authority and International Preliminary Examining Authority for applicants filing through the receiving offices of Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden; Sweden is not a Contracting Party to the establishing agreement.

name: Collaborative Inter-Governmental Scientific Research Institute
recognition_status: Multilateral treaty-based intergovernmental organization established under the Free Agreement for cooperation in scientific research and humanitarian use of micro-alga spirulina as food; registered with the United Nations Treaty Series (I-37542, volume 2151); treaty entered into force on 20 November 2000 upon ratification by two states

description: Intergovernmental organization established to promote scientific research, initiatives, and education in favor of international cooperation, with a focus on the humanitarian use of micro-alga spirulina as food to combat malnutrition. Governed by a General Council and Secretariat, with the Intergovernmental Institution for the Use of Micro-alga Spirulina (Spirulina Program) as an affiliated body. Based in Rome and Novara, Italy; treaty registered with the United Nations in 2001.
notes: Established through the "Free Agreement for cooperation in scientific research and humanitarian use of micro-alga spirulina as food." The founding agreement was signed in Kinshasa (24 August 2000) and Conakry (20 November 2000) by the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea. Italy was initially listed as a party but requested removal from the annexes of United Nations registration documents I-37542 and I-37543 in 2009. The organization maintains offices in both Rome and Novara, Italy.

name: Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization
recognition_status: Sole multilateral intergovernmental organization dedicated exclusively to the Amazon region
description: Intergovernmental organization of the eight Amazonian countries established to strengthen implementation of the Amazon Cooperation Treaty (1978). ACTO coordinates political and technical regional cooperation on forest protection, sustainable development, biodiversity, and climate preservation in the world's largest tropical rainforest and river basin. The Permanent Secretariat in Brasília, inaugurated in December 2002, plans regional projects and represents the Amazon at international forums.

notes: The Amazon Cooperation Treaty (ACT) was signed in Brasília on 3 July 1978 by the eight Amazonian countries and amended in 1998 to create ACTO as a permanent body with legal personality. ACTO replaced rotating pro tempore secretariats; the Permanent Secretariat has been based in Brasília since December 2002. Governance operates by consensus among member countries through the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Council and meetings of foreign ministers.

name: Baltic Marine Environment Protection Commission
recognition_status: Treaty-based regional sea convention established by the Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Baltic Sea Area (Helsinki Convention), originally signed on 22 March 1974 and updated on 9 April 1992; the current convention entered into force on 17 January 2000

headquarters.note: HELCOM Secretariat established in 1980

description: Intergovernmental organization and regional sea convention governing the Helsinki Convention on the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Baltic Sea Area. HELCOM brings together ten Contracting Parties — Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, Sweden, and the European Union — to prevent and eliminate pollution of the Baltic Sea from land, air, and sea sources, conserve habitats and biological diversity, and promote sustainable use of marine resources. The Commission meets annually at Head-of-Delegation level and holds ministerial meetings every few years; its Secretariat is headquartered in Helsinki.
notes: Russia remains a Contracting Party under the Helsinki Convention, but HELCOM has observed a strategic pause in regular meetings involving Russia since 4 March 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

name: European Committee for Standardization
recognition_status: Officially recognized European standards body by the European Union, European Free Trade Association, and the United Kingdom, alongside CENELEC and ETSI; recognized under Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 on European standardization
description: Public standards organization whose 34 national member bodies develop European Standards (EN) for all sectors except electrotechnical (CENELEC) and telecommunications (ETSI). Founded in 1961, CEN fosters the European single market and global trade by providing coherent sets of standards. Officially recognized by the EU, EFTA, and the United Kingdom as a European standards body under Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012.
notes: CEN operates the CEN/CENELEC Management Centre in Brussels jointly with CENELEC. Members are national standards bodies of all EU member states, three EFTA countries (Iceland, Norway, Switzerland), and the United Kingdom, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Türkiye. CEN also maintains affiliate and partner relationships with standards bodies in neighboring and partner countries. The Vienna Agreement (1991) governs cooperation with ISO to avoid duplication of standards.

name: ASEAN - Australia - New Zealand Free Trade Agreement

description: Regional free trade agreement among the ten ASEAN member states, Australia, and New Zealand. Signed at Cha-am, Thailand on 27 February 2009 and entering into force on 1 January 2010 for eight parties, with staggered entry for Thailand (12 March 2010), Laos and Cambodia (January 2011), and Indonesia (10 January 2012). Provides extensive tariff elimination, services and investment liberalization, intellectual property protection, and rules of origin governed through operational certification procedures. Described by Australian trade authorities as the highest-quality of ASEAN's free trade agreements with dialogue partners.

other_names.name: Agreement Establishing the ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area

notes: Negotiations concluded on 28 August 2008 in Singapore. All twelve parties signed on 27 February 2009. Entry into force required ratification by Australia, New Zealand, and at least four ASEAN member states. The agreement was notified to the WTO on 8 April 2010. An upgraded Second Protocol to AANZFTA entered into force on 21 April 2025.

description: Regional fisheries management organisation whose Contracting Parties cooperate to conserve and manage tuna and tuna-like species — including Atlantic bluefin, yellowfin, albacore, and bigeye tuna, swordfish, billfishes, and mackerels — across the Atlantic Ocean and adjacent seas. ICCAT sets catch limits and conservation measures, conducts scientific stock assessments through its Standing Committee on Research and Statistics (SCRS), and coordinates compliance monitoring. Four Cooperating Non-Contracting Parties (Bolivia, Chinese Taipei, Guyana, and Suriname) participate under Recommendation 21-24. The Secretariat is headquartered in Madrid.

Formed in October 1980 at the instigation of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision as the Offshore Group of Banking Supervisors (OGBS); renamed in March 2011 to reflect its expanded mandate beyond banking supervision. Holds two plenary meetings per year, promotes adoption of Basel Core Principles and FATF AML/CFT Recommendations among members, and has issued an international Standard for the Regulation of TCSPs backed by a multilateral memorandum of understanding and peer evaluations.

name: South Pacific Applied Geoscience Commission
recognition_status: Established by the Agreement establishing the South Pacific Applied Geoscience Commission (signed 10 October 1990 in Tarawa; entered into force 18 November 1990); operated as an independent regional body affiliated with the Pacific Community (SPC) until Regional Institutional Framework reform transferred its functions to SPC and SPREP; ceased as a separate organisation on 1 January 2011
description: Intergovernmental regional organisation that delivered applied geoscience services to Pacific members in three programme areas — Ocean and Islands (seabed resources, maritime boundaries, ocean monitoring), Community Lifelines (energy, water, sanitation, ICT), and Community Risk (hazard assessment and disaster risk management). Established by the 1990 Tarawa Agreement with 14 founding signatories; 12 further states and territories later acceded. Operated within the SPC institutional family until Pacific Islands Forum leaders endorsed Regional Institutional Framework reform in 2009; energy and ICT functions moved to SPC and climate-related functions to SPREP during 2010, and the remaining geoscience mandate integrated into SPC as the Applied Geoscience and Technology Division from 1 January 2011.

other_names.name: 南太平洋応用地地球科学委員会

notes: The 1990 Tarawa Agreement entered into force on 18 November 1990 (Australia from 3 February 1991). After accession by American Samoa, France, French Polynesia, Nauru, New Caledonia, Niue, the Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, Pitcairn Islands, Tokelau, the United States, and Wallis and Futuna, membership stood at 26. Partial function transfers to SPC and SPREP began 1 January 2010; core geoscience functions were integrated into SPC as the Applied Geoscience and Technology Division from 1 January 2011. Also known as Pacific Islands Applied Geoscience Commission (PIAGSC) in later branding.

description: Informal coalition of developing countries that coordinate common negotiating positions in United Nations and World Trade Organization fora. notes: The Like-Minded Group of Developing Countries (LMDC) is a negotiating bloc that coordinates positions in international organizations such as the United Nations and the World Trade Organization. The membership list provided here reflects the composition in UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change) negotiations. The group's composition may vary in different contexts. name: International Road Transport Union
description: Global road transport organisation representing bus, coach, taxi, and truck operators through national member associations and associate members. Founded in Geneva in 1948 to rebuild post-war European trade links, IRU administers the TIR customs transit system under United Nations mandate, advocates for road transport policy worldwide, and promotes professional standards through the IRU Academy. As of July 2026, IRU lists member organisations in 79 countries hosting active or associate members in its public directory.

other_names.name: Organización internacional del transporte por carretera

Headquartered in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, CAMES harmonizes university systems, runs quality-assurance and diploma-equivalence programmes, accredits academic titles, and supports regional academic cooperation through ministerial councils and thematic research programmes.

The Council of Ministers rotates presidency among member states.

EUCLID trains civil servants for its participating states and offers graduate programmes in diplomacy, sustainable development, international law, and related fields.
