name: Program on Forests
recognition_status: World Bank-hosted multi-donor partnership trust fund; partner of the Collaborative Partnership on Forests (CPF)
description: Multi-donor trust fund for sustainable forest management, poverty reduction, and forest governance. Established at the United Nations Development Programme in 1997 and hosted by the World Bank from 2002, PROFOR provided knowledge, tools, and analysis on livelihoods, finance, governance, and cross-sectoral forest issues for the Bank and partner countries. Eight bilateral donors and the European Union contributed approximately USD 52 million, supporting 273 projects before operations closed in June 2020 upon consolidation into the PROGREEN trust fund.
notes: Began at UNDP in 1997 and transferred to World Bank administration in 2002. The World Bank housed PROFOR's secretariat. Donors listed on the official website were DFID (United Kingdom), Swiss Development Cooperation, the European Union, GIZ on behalf of Germany, Finland's Department for International Development Cooperation, Japan's International Forestry Cooperation Office, Italy's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Dutch Ministry of Agriculture, Nature and Food Quality. Closed June 2020; successor trust fund PROGREEN focuses on integrated landscape management.

name: Partners in Population and Development
recognition_status: Intergovernmental alliance of developing countries launched at the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD); holds Permanent Observer Status at the United Nations and diplomatic status in Bangladesh
description: Southern-led intergovernmental alliance of 28 developing countries promoting South-South cooperation in reproductive health, family planning, population, and development. Launched at the 1994 ICPD in Cairo by ten founding members to support implementation of the Cairo Programme of Action; membership now spans Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Latin America, representing about 59% of the world population. Holds UN Permanent Observer status; the Secretariat is headquartered in Dhaka, Bangladesh, with regional offices in Kampala (Africa), Taicang (China), and New York (UN observer).
notes: Regional offices include the Africa Regional Office (Kampala, Uganda), Programme Office (Taicang, China), and UN Permanent Observer Office (New York, USA). Each member country designates a Partner Country Coordinator (PCC) and a board representative, typically the minister responsible for health or population.

name: Middle East and North Africa Financial Action Task Force
recognition_status: FATF-style regional body (FSRB) for anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing, and counter-proliferation financing; associate member of the Financial Action Task Force
description: Intergovernmental FATF-style regional body (FSRB) whose 21 member jurisdictions in the Middle East and North Africa commit to implementing the FATF Recommendations on anti-money laundering (AML), countering the financing of terrorism (CFT), and proliferation financing. Established at an inaugural Ministerial Meeting in Manama, Bahrain on 30 November 2004 by 14 founding governments; the Secretariat is hosted in the Kingdom of Bahrain. Voluntary and cooperative in nature, not based on an international treaty; conducts mutual evaluations, typology research, training and technical assistance, and coordinates regional AML/CFT cooperation within the FATF Global Network.

recognition_status: FATF-style regional body (FSRB) for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing; associate member of the Financial Action Task Force

Established in 1997 at a meeting in Thailand following regional symposia from 1993; the APG Secretariat is hosted in Sydney, Australia. Conducts mutual evaluations, coordinates technical assistance and training, researches money laundering and terrorist financing typologies, engages with the global FSRB network and FATF, and works with the private sector and international partners including the IMF, World Bank, UN, INTERPOL, and the Egmont Group.

description: Intergovernmental organization headquartered in Seoul that supports developing and emerging economies in planning and implementing green growth strategies that reconcile economic development with climate action and environmental sustainability. name: Commonwealth Foundation
recognition_status: Established by Commonwealth Heads of Government in 1966 and reconstituted as an international organisation in 1983; one of three Commonwealth intergovernmental agencies alongside the Commonwealth Secretariat and Commonwealth of Learning
description: Intergovernmental organisation serving as the Commonwealth's agency for civil society, established in 1966 and headquartered at Marlborough House in London. Funded by member governments, it supports NGOs, professional associations, faith-based groups, media, and trade unions through grants and programmes that strengthen participatory governance across the Commonwealth. Membership is voluntary and separate from membership of the Commonwealth of Nations.

other_names.name: Fundación de la Mancomunidad de Naciones

notes: Membership is voluntary and distinct from Commonwealth of Nations membership. As of 2026 the foundation reports 51 member governments plus Gibraltar as associate member; Fiji, Nauru, Singapore, Togo, and Tuvalu remain Commonwealth members that have not joined the foundation.

name: Financial Stability Board
recognition_status: International body established at the April 2009 G20 London Summit as successor to the Financial Stability Forum; incorporated as an association (Verein) under Swiss law in January 2013; Secretariat hosted by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel
description: International body that coordinates national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies to develop and promote effective regulatory, supervisory, and other financial sector policies. Established in April 2009 as the successor to the Financial Stability Forum at the initiative of G20 leaders; incorporated as a Swiss association (Verein) in January 2013 with its Secretariat hosted by the Bank for International Settlements in Basel. The Plenary — comprising representatives from 24 jurisdictions and 13 international financial institutions and standard-setting bodies — is the sole decision-making organ. Six Regional Consultative Groups extend outreach to approximately 70 additional jurisdictions.

includes.name: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
Committee on the Global Financial System
Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures

notes: Russian authorities remain listed as FSB members but have agreed not to participate in FSB meetings at present. The FSB Secretariat is hosted by the BIS in Basel; country membership covers 24 jurisdictions plus 13 international financial institutions and standard-setting bodies represented on the Plenary.

name: Pacific Salmon Commission
recognition_status: Regional fishery management organization (RFMO) established under the Pacific Salmon Treaty to implement cooperative salmon conservation and harvest-sharing between Canada and the United States
description: Bilateral treaty-based regional fishery management organization (RFMO) established by Canada and the United States to implement the 1985 Pacific Salmon Treaty, which entered into force on 18 March 1985. The Commission administers cooperative management of Pacific salmon stocks, setting harvest quotas and conservation measures for fisheries in Alaska, British Columbia, the Fraser River, the Columbia River, the Yukon River, and transboundary rivers. Each country appoints four Commissioners and four alternates representing commercial and recreational fisheries as well as federal, state, and tribal governments; decisions require consensus between the two national sections. The Secretariat is headquartered in Vancouver, British Columbia.
notes: The PSC succeeded the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission (1937–1985), which focused primarily on Fraser River sockeye restoration including fishways at Hells Gate. The 1985 Pacific Salmon Treaty was amended by the 1999 Agreement, which established Northern and Southern Restoration and Enhancement funds. Five regional Panels (Northern, Fraser River, Southern, Yukon, and Transboundary) provide technical recommendations to the sixteen-person Commission.

name: International Fertilizer Development Center
recognition_status: Independent non-profit public international organization designated by U.S. President Jimmy Carter in 1977 under the International Organizations Immunities Act; conceived at the urging of the U.S. Department of State following Henry Kissinger's 1974 UN General Assembly address and building on the Tennessee Valley Authority's National Fertilizer Development Center legacy
description: Science-based public international organization that develops and disseminates fertilizer technologies, soil fertility management practices, and market-system approaches to improve smallholder farmer productivity and food security. Founded in October 1974 and headquartered in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, with a Washington, D.C. office. Governed by an international board of individual experts rather than country delegates; as of 2024 maintains an operational presence in 31 countries across Africa and Asia while working with partners in over 100 developing countries historically.
notes: IFDC is not a treaty-based membership organization; governance rests with an international board of individual experts. The includes roster lists countries where IFDC maintained an operational presence as of 2024 (annual report "Our Reach" section), not formal member states. Headquarters country (US) is excluded because it hosts the secretariat rather than being a programme country.

name: World Federation of Trade Unions
recognition_status: International federation of trade unions founded on 3 October 1945 at the World Trade Union Conference in Paris; holds general consultative status with the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) since 1946 (UN ECOSOC profile code 462)

headquarters.note: Central Offices at 6 Florinis Street, Mosxato

description: International federation of national and sectoral trade unions founded on 3 October 1945 in Paris as a successor to the pre-war International Federation of Trade Unions. Headquartered in Athens since 2006, the WFTU coordinates class-oriented trade union affiliates and Trade Union Internationals (TUIs) across five continents. It holds ECOSOC consultative status and participates in ILO, UNESCO, and FAO forums. As of 2026 the federation reports representing more than 105 million workers through affiliates in 134 countries.
notes: Membership is institutional (national and sectoral trade union affiliates), not state-based; this record maps countries and territories with at least one WFTU-affiliated organization as identified from the official Presidential Council roster and published affiliate examples. French overseas departments and territories with CGT federations (GF, GP, MQ, NC, PM, RE) are listed separately where the WFTU source material references distinct affiliate bodies.

name: Nordic Council of Ministers
recognition_status: Official intergovernmental forum for Nordic government cooperation established by amendment to the Helsinki Treaty (13 February 1971, entered into force July 1971); complements the Nordic Council and operates under the treaty framework among Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden

headquarters.note: Ved Stranden 18

description: Official intergovernmental body for cooperation among Nordic governments, established in July 1971 to complement the Nordic Council. Ministers for Nordic Cooperation delegate sectoral ministerial councils (labour, culture, environment, health, education, and others) that coordinate policy and programmes across the region. The presidency rotates annually among members; the Secretariat is headquartered in Copenhagen. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden are High Contracting Parties to the Helsinki Treaty; the Faroe Islands, Greenland, and Åland participate in Nordic cooperation alongside the sovereign states.
notes: Complements the Nordic Council (NORDEN); both institutions share the Copenhagen secretariat complex. The Faroe Islands and Åland were included in Nordic ministerial cooperation via the 1971 Helsinki Treaty amendment; Greenland joined in 1984. In March 2026 the Nordic Ministers for Cooperation established a commission to revise the Helsinki Treaty to enable equal participation for the three autonomous territories.

name: International Nickel Study Group
description: Intergovernmental organization of nickel producing and consuming states that serves as the international commodity board for nickel. Promotes market transparency through exchange of information on production, usage, stocks, trade, and prices, and provides a forum for international cooperation on nickel-related issues. Has no provision for market stabilization or market intervention.
notes: Established 23 May 1990 under the Terms of Reference adopted at the 1986 United Nations Conference on Nickel. Secretariat is co-located in Lisbon with the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) and the International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG). Official membership is 14 member governments plus the European Union (15). India joined on 1 June 2025. Indonesia withdrew in 2006. Canada, China, and the United States participate as invited official observers but are not members.

name: International Association of Ports and Harbors
description: Global non-governmental alliance of port authorities and port-related businesses, founded in 1955 and headquartered in Tokyo. As of December 2024, IAPH represents some 190 regular member ports and 165 port-related associate members across 89 countries; member ports collectively handle well over 60% of world seaborne trade and over 60% of global container traffic. IAPH advocates for ports at the International Maritime Organization, World Customs Organization, and International Organization for Standardization, and leads industry initiatives on decarbonization, digitalization, and port risk and resilience.

name: International Social Tourism Organization
description: International non-profit organization founded in 1963 as the International Bureau of Social Tourism (BITS); renamed ISTO in September 2010. Promotes access to leisure, holidays, and tourism for all, emphasizing sustainable, solidarity, and responsible tourism that benefits local populations and respects natural and cultural heritage. Network of member organizations across governments, regional authorities, associations, and social tourism cooperatives.
notes: Membership is organizational, not state-based; includes lists countries where ISTO member organizations are located per the official member directory (106 countries as of July 2026). ISTO reports 182 member organizations across 44 countries on its website; the directory region filter reflects the broader geographic footprint of member entities.

Governance comprises the Assembly of Members, Board of Directors, and Executive Secretariat; legal domicile in Buenos Aires, Argentina, with the Executive Secretariat based in Guatemala City, Guatemala. Cooperates with ISO, IEC, and other regional standards organizations.

ICES was established in Copenhagen in 1902 and is governed by the 1964 ICES Convention. name: Asian Disaster Preparedness Center
description: Autonomous intergovernmental organization established in 1986 to strengthen disaster risk reduction and climate resilience across Asia and the Pacific through capacity building, technical assistance, and regional cooperation.
notes: Charter signed in 2005 by nine founding members and ratified by all by 2018, establishing ADPC as an autonomous intergovernmental organization governed by a Board of Trustees. The Regional Consultative Committee on Disaster Management (RCC) brings together national disaster management organizations from additional Asia-Pacific countries for coordination and knowledge sharing.

name: Regional Organization for the Protection of the Marine Environment
description: Intergovernmental organization established in 1979 to coordinate the eight member states' efforts to protect the marine and coastal environment of the ROPME Sea Area. Implements the Kuwait Regional Convention for Cooperation on the Protection and Development of the Marine Environment and the Coastal Areas and the Kuwait Action Plan, addressing marine pollution, environmental degradation, and conservation in the Persian Gulf region.
notes: Established following the Regional Conference of Plenipotentiaries held in Kuwait in April 1978, where eight coastal states signed the Kuwait Regional Convention. A UNEP interim secretariat administered programmes until the ROPME Secretariat was formally established in Kuwait on 1 January 1982. The ROPME Sea Area denotes the semi-enclosed sea surrounded by the member states. Milestones include the 1982 establishment of the Marine Emergency Mutual Aid Centre (MEMAC) and adoption of protocols on marine emergencies, hazardous wastes, land-based activities, and sea-based pollution. Part of the UNEP Regional Seas Programme.

name: North Pacific Marine Science Organization

secretariat.location: Institute of Ocean Sciences, Sidney, British Columbia, Canada

description: Intergovernmental organization established under a 1990 convention to promote and coordinate marine scientific research in the North Pacific Ocean and adjacent seas. Provides a mechanism for information and data exchange among scientists in member countries, with scientific work organized through committees on biological oceanography, fishery science, physical oceanography and climate, marine environmental quality, and human dimensions.
notes: Known as PICES (Pacific ICES), modeled after the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea. Convention entered into force on 24 March 1992 with initial members Canada, Japan, and the United States; China ratified in August 1992, Russia in December 1994, and the Republic of Korea in July 1995. Secretariat hosted at the Institute of Ocean Sciences in Sidney, British Columbia, Canada. Major programmes have included PICES/GLOBEC on climate change and carrying capacity (1995–2006) and FUTURE (Forecasting and Understanding Trends, Uncertainty and Responses of North Pacific Marine Ecosystems) from 2009.

name: Pax Silica
recognition_status: US-led non-binding economic-security initiative coordinated by the U.S. Department of State; partners join by signing the Pax Silica Declaration.
description: United States-led international initiative to secure supply chains for advanced technologies including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and critical minerals. Coordinated by the U.S. Department of State and launched with the non-binding Pax Silica Declaration at the inaugural Washington summit in December 2025; partners align policy and investment across connectivity, compute, advanced manufacturing, logistics, mineral processing, and energy.
notes: Motto "Securing the Silicon Supply Chain". The inaugural Pax Silica Summit was held in Washington, D.C. on 12 December 2025, with seven founding declaration signatories (Australia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, United Kingdom, United States). Later signatories joined through mid-2026, including the European Union. Canada, Estonia, and Taiwan participate as observers; Estonia signed the declaration while retaining observer status. The Netherlands joined on 17 December 2025 and has been described in some reporting as a non-signing partner at accession. Not a treaty organization or permanent secretariat; coordination sits with the U.S. Department of State.

name: Chip 4 Alliance
recognition_status: Informal US-led working group (also called Fab 4 or Chip 4); not a treaty organization or permanent secretariat. Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs refers to the grouping as the US-East Asia Semiconductor Supply Chain Resilience Working Group.
description: Informal US-led coordination forum among the United States, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan on semiconductor supply chain resilience, export controls, and technology security. Convened by Washington in response to pandemic-era chip shortages and intensifying US–China technology competition, the grouping held a preparatory working-level videoconference in September 2022 and its first senior-officials meeting on 16 February 2023. Members coordinate across complementary strengths in chip design (US), manufacturing (Taiwan and South Korea), and materials and equipment (Japan).

other_names.name: US-East Asia Semiconductor Supply Chain Resilience Working Group

notes: Also widely called Fab 4. The US convened the first working-level meeting in September 2022 after months of coordination; senior officials met by videoconference on 16 February 2023, hosted by the American Institute in Taiwan. The alliance has no founding treaty, charter, or standing secretariat. South Korea joined talks cautiously given its economic ties with China. China has criticized the initiative as a US-led effort to contain Beijing in the semiconductor sector.

name: Outer Space Treaty
recognition_status: Foundational United Nations space law treaty; adopted by General Assembly resolution 2222 (XXI) on 19 December 1966; opened for signature in London, Moscow, and Washington on 27 January 1967; entered into force on 10 October 1967; registered as UNTS vol. 610, No. 8843. Depositaries are the Governments of the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
description: Multilateral treaty establishing that outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes and is not subject to national appropriation. Prohibits placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on celestial bodies, assigns international liability for space activities, and requires registration of launched objects. Opened for signature on 27 January 1967 and entered into force on 10 October 1967; as of October 2025, 118 states are parties.

Eleven ratifications (Antigua and Barbuda, Belize, Cuba, Dominica, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nicaragua, Paraguay, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Venezuela) triggered entry into force on 27 October 2024 when Cuba deposited the eleventh instrument on 27 September 2024. APRSAF operates through five working groups and has no treaty-based membership; participation is open and voluntary.
notes: APRSAF is a conference forum, not a treaty organization with formal members. name: International Space Station
recognition_status: Multinational civil space station governed by the Space Station Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA), signed on 29 January 1998 in Washington by the United States, Russia, Japan, Canada, and eleven European Space Agency member states; entered into force on 27 March 2001.
description: Modular space station in low Earth orbit operated through a multinational partnership under the 1998 Intergovernmental Agreement. NASA, Roscosmos, JAXA, CSA, and ESA member states jointly design, assemble, operate, and use the station for peaceful scientific research; as of 2026, partner agencies have committed to operations through 2028–2030 with a planned controlled deorbit around 2031.
notes: The fifteen IGA signatories are the authoritative partner roster. European participation is coordinated collectively through ESA under the "European Partner" designation in the treaty, but each listed European state signed the IGA in its own right. Brazil participated in early programme planning via a bilateral NASA agreement but was never an IGA signatory and withdrew from ISS cooperation in 2015.

name: CFP Franc Zone

description: Monetary union of three French Pacific overseas collectivities—French Polynesia, New Caledonia and Wallis and Futuna—using the CFP franc (XPF). Created on 26 December 1945 alongside the CFA franc; pegged to the French franc until 1999 and to the euro since at F.CFP 1,000 = €8.38. Currency is issued by the Institut d'émission d'outre-mer (IEOM), which has operated since 1967.
notes: CFP originally stood for Colonies françaises du Pacifique; since 2022 officially denotes Collectivités françaises du Pacifique. Distinct territorial coin and banknote series existed until unified designs were introduced in 2014 (notes) and 2023 (coins). The New Hebrides used a separate CFP franc until 1969; Vanuatu replaced it with the vatu in 1982. France guarantees convertibility; IEOM headquarters are in Paris.

name: West African CFA Franc Zone
recognition_status: Regional monetary union of eight West African states using the West African CFA franc (XOF, ISO 4217 code 952); currency issued exclusively by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) for members of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA); pegged to the euro at €1 = F.CFA 655.957 with French Treasury convertibility guarantee; equal in value to but not interchangeable with the Central African CFA franc (XAF)
description: Monetary union of eight West African states using the West African CFA franc (XOF). Introduced in 1945 to replace the French West African franc; pegged to the French franc until 1999 and to the euro since then at €1 = F.CFA 655.957. Currency is issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) for members of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA), established under the West African Monetary Union treaty of 12 May 1962.
notes: CFA originally stood for Colonies françaises d'Afrique and now Communauté financière africaine. Guinea-Bissau adopted the franc in 1997, replacing the peso at 1 franc = 65 pesos. Of equal value to but not interchangeable with the Central African CFA franc (XAF). Strong institutional overlap with UEMOA; notes and coins bear the UEMOA legend. Bank of France prints CFA franc notes in Chamalières. France ended reserve-deposit requirements for the West African CFA franc in 2019–2020. ECOWAS and UEMOA have announced plans to replace the CFA franc with a common eco currency, targeting 2027.

name: Microstates and the European Union
recognition_status: Informal analyst grouping of five third-country European microstates (Andorra, Liechtenstein, Monaco, San Marino, Vatican City) defined by differentiated monetary and EU integration arrangements; not a formal organization or monetary union — Andorra, Monaco, San Marino, and Vatican City use the euro (EUR) under bilateral monetary agreements with the EU, while Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc (CHF) via Switzerland
description: Group of five third-country European microstates (Andorra, Liechtenstein, Monaco, San Marino, and Vatican City) with differentiated monetary ties to the European Union. Andorra, Monaco, San Marino, and Vatican City use the euro through bilateral monetary agreements and may issue limited euro coins; Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc.
notes: None are EU members. Andorra and San Marino are in customs unions with the EU; Monaco participates in the EU customs territory through France. Liechtenstein is in the European Economic Area via EFTA and in a customs union with Switzerland. Andorra, Monaco, and San Marino have pursued closer EU integration through association agreements; negotiations concluded with Andorra and San Marino in December 2023, with the Commission proposing signature in April 2024. Monaco negotiations were suspended in September 2023 over financial regulation disputes. In December 2025 the Council determined the Andorra and San Marino agreement has mixed competencies and requires approval in each EU member state's parliament. Luxembourg and Malta are sometimes classed as microstates but are full EU members and excluded from this grouping.

description: Monetary union of six Central African states using the Central African CFA franc (XAF). Currency is issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC) for members of the Economic and Monetary Community of Central Africa (CEMAC).

Of equal value to but not interchangeable with the West African CFA franc (XOF). Strong institutional overlap with CEMAC; notes and coins since 2006 bear the CEMAC legend. name: Eastern Caribbean Currency Union
recognition_status: Regional monetary union of eight Eastern Caribbean states and territories using the Eastern Caribbean dollar (XCD, ISO 4217 code 951); currency issued and supervised by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB) within the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States; pegged to the US dollar at EC$2.70 = US$1 since 7 July 1976
description: Monetary union of eight Eastern Caribbean states and territories sharing the Eastern Caribbean dollar (XCD, ISO 4217 code 951), issued and supervised by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank (ECCB). Established in 1983 to replace the Eastern Caribbean Currency Authority as a development of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States. The EC dollar has been pegged to the US dollar at EC$2.70 since 7 July 1976.
notes: Members are Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Lucia, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, Anguilla and Montserrat. British Virgin Islands, an OECS associate member, uses the US dollar and is not part of the union. One of four regional currency unions worldwide. Before 1976 the EC dollar was pegged to the British pound at EC$4.80 = £1.

name: Common Monetary Area
recognition_status: Regional monetary arrangement of four Southern African states; member currencies (LSL, NAD, SZL) pegged at par with the South African rand (ZAR, ISO 4217 code 710), which is legal tender throughout the area; foreign exchange regulations and monetary policy reflect the influence of the South African Reserve Bank (SARB); formalized as the Rand Monetary Area in December 1974 and restyled as the Multilateral Monetary Area (MMA) when Namibia joined in February 1992
description: Monetary union linking Lesotho, Namibia, South Africa and Eswatini. Enacted in July 1986, succeeding the Rand Monetary Area established in December 1974; member states issue national currencies (loti, Namibian dollar, lilangeni) pegged at par with the South African rand, which remains legal tender throughout the area.
notes: Closely associated with but distinct from the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), which includes Botswana in addition to all CMA members. Botswana declined to join the 1974 Rand Monetary Area and adopted the pula in 1976. Foreign exchange regulations and monetary policy reflect the influence of the South African Reserve Bank. Namibia joined in February 1992; the agreement was then restyled as the Multilateral Monetary Area (MMA), though the zone is still commonly called the CMA.

name: CFA Franc Zone
recognition_status: Umbrella currency arrangement comprising two juxtaposed monetary zones in fourteen African countries; West African CFA franc (XOF, ISO 4217 code 952) issued by BCEAO for eight UEMOA states and Central African CFA franc (XAF, ISO 4217 code 950) issued by BEAC for six CEMAC states; both pegged to the euro at €1 = F.CFA 655.957 with French Treasury convertibility guarantees; equal in value but not interchangeable; not a single monetary union
description: Umbrella designation for two distinct but equally valued CFA franc monetary zones in Africa—the West African CFA franc (XOF), issued by BCEAO for eight UEMOA states, and the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by BEAC for six CEMAC states. Created on 26 December 1945 alongside the CFP franc; both zones are pegged to the euro at €1 = F.CFA 655.957 with French Treasury convertibility guarantees. Not a single monetary union—the zones are juxtaposed and their currencies are not interchangeable.
notes: CFA originally stood for Colonies françaises d'Afrique; since independence it denotes Communauté Financière Africaine (West) or Coopération Financière en Afrique centrale (Central). France ended reserve-deposit requirements for the West African CFA franc in 2019–2020; Central African arrangements were unchanged. Bank of France prints CFA franc notes in Chamalières. West Africa plans replacement by the eco currency; ECOWAS targets 2027.

name: Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States
recognition_status: Treaty-based inter-governmental organisation for economic harmonisation and integration in the Eastern Caribbean, established by the Treaty of Basseterre (18 June 1981); seven protocol members form an economic union under the Revised Treaty of Basseterre (effective 21 January 2011) within the broader Caribbean Community (CARICOM) framework; eight members participate in the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (ECCU) using the Eastern Caribbean dollar
description: Inter-governmental organisation of Eastern Caribbean states and territories dedicated to economic harmonisation and integration, established by the Treaty of Basseterre on 18 June 1981. Seven independent and non-independent protocol members form an economic union under the Revised Treaty of Basseterre (effective 21 January 2011), operating within the broader Caribbean Community (CARICOM) framework. Eight members participate in the Eastern Caribbean Currency Union (ECCU), sharing the Eastern Caribbean dollar.
notes: Full members are Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Lucia and St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Associate members are Anguilla (from 1995), British Virgin Islands (from 1984), Martinique (from 2016), Guadeloupe (from 2019) and Saint Martin (from 2019). The OECS Commission is headquartered in Castries, Saint Lucia. Montserrat remained a protocol member but did not ratify the 2010 economic union treaty by the January 2011 deadline. Anguilla uses the Eastern Caribbean dollar through the ECCU; the British Virgin Islands uses the US dollar. Martinique, Guadeloupe and Saint Martin are French overseas departments and collectivity.

name: ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly
description: Regional inter-parliamentary body formally associated with ASEAN, established on 2 September 1977 in Manila as the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Organization (AIPO) by the parliamentary delegations of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand. Renamed AIPA at the 27th General Assembly in Cebu on 14 September 2006 and governed since 2007 by the AIPA Charter. Composed of national parliaments from all ten ASEAN member states, AIPA holds an annual General Assembly hosted in rotation by the presiding member parliament, maintains standing committees on political, economic, social, and organizational matters, and operates a permanent Secretariat co-located with the ASEAN Secretariat in Jakarta. Unlike the European Parliament, AIPA is an advisory transnational parliamentary conference without legislative or oversight powers over ASEAN; it promotes dialogue, disseminates ASEAN community policies, and coordinates parliamentary engagement with ASEAN summits and dialogue partners.
notes: Brunei participated as a special observer from 1993 and as a permanent observer before the Legislative Council was admitted as a full member at the 30th General Assembly in Pattaya on 4 September 2009. Myanmar participated as a special observer from 1997 and became a full member at the 32nd General Assembly in Cambodia on 20 September 2011. AIPA also maintains observer parliaments (including the European Parliament and other national legislatures) that are not modeled as country includes. Timor-Leste is scheduled to accede as the eleventh member parliament at the 47th General Assembly in Manila in October 2026.

name: CIS Interparliamentary Assembly
description: Consultative inter-parliamentary body of the Commonwealth of Independent States, established on 27 March 1992 in Almaty by agreement among the parliaments of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan. Regulated by the Convention on the Interparliamentary Assembly signed on 26 May 1995 and in force from 16 January 1996, the Assembly develops model legislation for voluntary adoption by member parliaments, harmonises national laws with CIS treaties, and coordinates parliamentary cooperation across the CIS. The Council of the Assembly, comprising parliamentary speakers, meets twice yearly; the permanent Secretariat is housed in the Tauride Palace in Saint Petersburg. The Assembly also conducts election observation through the International Institute for Monitoring of Democratic Development, Parliamentarism and Suffrage Protection (IIMDD IPA CIS).
notes: Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Moldova joined the 1992 agreement in 1993; Moldova became a full convention member on 2 June 1998 and formally withdrew on 8 February 2024 after denouncing the convention in July 2023. The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine acceded to the 1992 agreement in 1999 but never ratified the 1995 convention; Ukraine ceased cooperation in 2014 and formally withdrew from the 1992 agreement on 3 May 2023. The Georgian parliament left the Assembly in 2010 following the 2008 war with Russia. Turkmenistan is not a member. The National Assembly of Afghanistan held observer status from 2006 until 2021.

name: Parliamentary Assembly of Union of Belarus and Russia
description: Representative and legislative body of the Union State of Russia and Belarus, established by agreement of the heads of the parliaments of Russia and Belarus signed on 29 April 1996 in Saint Petersburg. Transformed from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Community of Russia and Belarus following the 1997 Union Charter. Under Article 70 of the 1999 Treaty on the Establishment of the Union State, it performs the functions of the Union State Parliament pending elections to a permanent House of Representatives. Comprises 72 deputies in equal delegations of 36 from each state's national parliament (Council of the Republic and House of Representatives of Belarus; Federation Council and State Duma of Russia). Drafts model legislation, harmonizes national laws, and holds plenary sessions twice yearly.
notes: Individual deputies are delegated by national parliamentary chambers and are not modeled as separate includes. Holds observer status in the CSTO Parliamentary Assembly (PA CSTO) since 2010. Maintains standing commissions, a scientific advisory council, and a Youth Chamber. Secretariat is based in Moscow with a representation office in Minsk.

description: Legislative and consultative body of the League of Arab States comprising four representatives from each of the 22 Arab League member states (88 seats total). Agreed at the 2001 Amman summit and formally established on 27 December 2002; inaugural sessions began at the League headquarters in Cairo in 2004. A permanent seat in Damascus was planned but sessions were suspended there in May 2012 and relocated to Cairo. Member states elect or appoint their representatives through national parliaments or direct suffrage according to each country's constitutional system.
notes: Membership mirrors the 22 Arab League member states (DZ, BH, KM, DJ, EG, IQ, JO, KW, LB, LY, MR, MA, OM, PS, QA, SA, SO, SD, SY, TN, AE, YE). Syria's Arab League membership has been suspended since November 2011 but remains listed as a member state. Turkey holds observer status in the Arab Parliament.

recognition_status: Official inter-parliamentary body for Nordic cooperation established at Copenhagen on 16 March 1952; inaugural session held on 13 February 1953. Operates under the Helsinki Treaty framework (1962) among Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden; the Faroe Islands, Greenland, and Åland participate as associate members with parliamentary representation alongside the sovereign states.
description: Official inter-parliamentary body for formal Nordic cooperation among the national and territorial parliaments of the region. Comprises 87 representatives elected by the member parliaments; sovereign states hold full membership and the autonomous territories of the Faroe Islands, Greenland, and Åland participate as associate members with their own delegations. Holds an ordinary session each autumn and a thematic session in spring. Complements the intergovernmental Nordic Council of Ministers (NCM), with which it shares the Copenhagen secretariat.
notes: Finland joined in December 1955 after parliamentary approval in October 1955. Representatives from the Faroe Islands and Åland were first included in 1970; Greenland joined in 1984. Working languages of the secretariat are Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish; Danish, Finnish, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish are official languages. Distinct from the West Nordic Council (VESTNORDISK), although members overlap and the bodies cooperate on selected issues.

name: West Nordic Council
description: Cooperative inter-parliamentary forum for Greenland, the Faroe Islands, and Iceland, established on 24 September 1985 in Nuuk as the West Nordic Parliamentarian Council of Cooperation (renamed in 1997). Each national parliament appoints six members; the annual general meeting rotates among the three territories and is the council's highest authority. Promotes West Nordic and North Atlantic interests, resource stewardship, and coordination with the Nordic Council and Arctic parliamentary cooperation.
notes: Distinct from the Nordic Council (NORDEN), although all West Nordic Council members are also Nordic Council members and the two bodies cooperate on selected issues. Greenland and the Faroe Islands participate as autonomous territories within the Danish Realm; Iceland is a sovereign state and former Danish possession.

Included in the CSTO Charter in December 2010 as the organization's statutory inter-parliamentary cooperation body. Holds annual plenary sessions and three permanent commissions on political issues and international cooperation, defense and security, and socio-economic and legal issues.
notes: Serbia and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Union of Belarus and Russia hold observer status. Afghanistan held observer status from April 2013 until the collapse of the Islamic Republic in 2021.

name: Interparliamentary Assembly of EurAsEC
description: Inter-parliamentary organ of the Eurasian Economic Community (EurAsEC), established by the Treaty on the Establishment of the EurAsEC signed on 10 October 2000 in Astana as the legal successor to the Interparliamentary Committee of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia. Composed of parliamentarians delegated by member-state parliaments, the Assembly harmonised national legislation with EurAsEC treaties, adopted model laws, and issued recommendations to the Interstate Council and Integration Committee. The Secretariat was based in Saint Petersburg. Uzbekistan participated after acceding to EurAsEC in January 2006 but suspended membership in October 2008. The Assembly ceased operations on 1 January 2015 when EurAsEC was dissolved upon the launch of the Eurasian Economic Union; the EAEU Treaty did not establish a successor parliamentary body.
notes: Uzbekistan joined EurAsEC on 25 January 2006 following merger with the Central Asian Cooperation Organisation and withdrew from EurAsEC bodies on 16 October 2008. Tajikistan remained a EurAsEC member but did not join the EAEU. Armenia and Kyrgyzstan joined the EAEU in 2015 but were never members of the EurAsEC Interparliamentary Assembly.

name: British–Irish Parliamentary Assembly
description: Deliberative inter-parliamentary body established in February 1990 as the British–Irish Inter-Parliamentary Body (BIIPB) by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and the Oireachtas to foster mutual understanding between elected representatives in Britain and Ireland. Enlarged in 2001 to include delegations from the Scottish Parliament, Senedd Cymru, the Northern Ireland Assembly, and the legislatures of the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey. Holds two plenary sessions each year, alternating between the UK and Ireland, and maintains four subject committees. Evolved from Strand 3 of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which encouraged elected institutions to develop inter-parliamentary links building on the BIIPB.
notes: BIPA comprises eight delegating legislatures. The Scottish Parliament, Senedd Cymru, and Northern Ireland Assembly appoint separate delegations (five full members and four associate members each since 2001) but are not modeled as distinct country includes because they are devolved legislatures within the United Kingdom. Each sovereign parliament and devolved or crown-dependency legislature also appoints associate members who may attend plenary sessions and committees in place of full members.

name: Mercosur Parliament
description: Consultative parliamentary institution of the Southern Common Market (Mercosur), established by the Constitutive Protocol signed on 9 December 2005 at Montevideo by the presidents of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. Held its first session on 7 May 2007, replacing the Joint Parliamentary Commission. Composed of national parliamentarians delegated by member-state legislatures; direct elections were introduced in Paraguay from 2008 with other states adopting them on a staggered schedule. Issues recommendations on Mercosur integration legislation without supranational lawmaking power. Headquarters in Montevideo.
notes: Venezuela acceded to Mercosur in July 2012 and holds a reduced delegation as an applying member; Mercosur suspended Venezuela from bloc decisions in December 2016 but Parlasur continues to seat Venezuelan parliamentarians. Bolivia became a full Mercosur member in July 2024. Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru participate as Mercosur associate states and may hold non-voting seats in the Parliament.

name: Andean Parliament
description: Deliberative and oversight body of the Andean Community, composed of 25 parliamentarians (five per participating state). Established by the Constitutive Treaty signed in La Paz on 25 October 1979 and in force since January 1984; exercises political control over the Andean Integration System without supranational legislative power. Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru are full members; Chile joined as a permanent associate participant in 2015 despite not being a full Andean Community member.
notes: Venezuela was a founding signatory but withdrew from the Andean Community and Parliament on 22 April 2006. Chile became a permanent parliament member in 2015. Spain, Mexico, and Panama are permanent observers (2011); Argentina (2016) and Turkey (2019) later joined as observers. Each member state maintains a national liaison office; the General Secretariat is in Bogotá. Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru hold direct elections for Andean parliamentarians; Bolivia selects representatives through its national legislature.

name: Conference of Parliamentarians of the Arctic Region
description: Biennial inter-parliamentary forum established at the first Arctic parliamentary conference in Reykjavik in 1993. Delegations are appointed by the national parliaments of the eight Arctic states and by the European Parliament. Indigenous peoples organizations with Arctic Council Permanent Participant status also take part, along with additional observers. Between conferences, cooperation is carried on by the Standing Committee of Parliamentarians of the Arctic Region (SCPAR), which began work in 1994 and meets several times each year. CPAR acts as a parliamentary forum for Arctic issues and participates in Arctic Council work as an observer.
notes: Indigenous peoples organizations participate as Permanent Participants mirroring Arctic Council Permanent Participant status; individual organizations are not modeled as country includes. Russian Federation delegates remain listed members but were not invited to SCPAR or CPAR meetings held after 2022 amid wider Arctic cooperation suspensions following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

name: Assembly of the Western European Union
description: Parliamentary assembly of the Western European Union (WEU), also known as the European Security and Defence Assembly. Established when the Modified Brussels Treaty entered into force in 1955, the Assembly held its first session on 5 July 1955 in Paris. Composed of delegations appointed by the national parliaments of WEU member states, it scrutinized security and defence cooperation under the treaty, issued recommendations to the WEU Council of Ministers, and monitored implementation of the mutual-defence commitment in Article V. After WEU operational tasks transferred to the European Union, the Assembly continued interparliamentary oversight of the Common Security and Defence Policy and briefly renamed itself the Interim European Security and Defence Assembly. Its final plenary session was held on 10 May 2011, following the collective decision to abolish the WEU.
notes: By the 2000s, delegations from 39 European countries — including WEU associate members, observers, and associate partners — had the right to send parliamentary delegations; only the ten full WEU treaty members are modeled here as includes. The Western European Union parent organization ceased to exist on 30 June 2011.

name: Parliamentary Assembly of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation
description: Inter-parliamentary consultative body of the Organization of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC), established on 26 February 1993 by the Declaration on the Establishment of the Parliamentary Assembly signed by nine founding parliaments. PABSEC promotes parliamentary understanding of BSEC objectives, supports legislative frameworks for regional economic and humanitarian cooperation, and strengthens parliamentary democracy. The General Assembly comprises 81 parliamentarians from thirteen member states; working languages are English, French, Russian, and Turkish. The International Secretariat is based in Istanbul.
notes: Greece joined in 1995, Bulgaria in 1997, Serbia and Montenegro in 2004 (membership inherited by Serbia after 2006), and North Macedonia in 2021. Belarus, France, and other observer parliaments have had observer status temporarily suspended at various times. Russia suspended budget contributions in December 2022; published sources also report suspended participation from 2023. PABSEC also grants observer status to inter-parliamentary organizations including the IPU, NATO PA, OSCE PA, and TURKPA, which are not modeled as country includes.

name: Baltic Assembly
description: Inter-parliamentary organization of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania established on 1 December 1990 in Vilnius to promote cooperation among the three Baltic national parliaments on economic, political, and cultural issues. Each parliament appoints twenty members (sixty total); decisions are advisory. Operational regulations were approved in Tallinn on 8 November 1991, and the organizational structure and rules were agreed on 13 June 1994. The Secretariat is based in Riga; working languages are Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian. Annual sessions rotate among the three capitals.
notes: Distinct from but cooperates with the Nordic Council, which holds periodic joint meetings with the Baltic Assembly. Helped establish the Baltic Council of Ministers as a governmental cooperation body. Maintains standing committees on budget and audit, economics, education, natural resources, and security and defence, and awards Baltic Assembly Prizes for Literature, the Arts, and Science.

The permanent secretariat is in Tehran; standing specialized committees cover political and foreign relations, economic affairs and environment, human rights and family affairs, and cultural and legal affairs.

name: Latin American and Caribbean Parliament
recognition_status: Regional permanent unicameral inter-parliamentary body founded in Lima on 10 December 1964; institutionalized by the Treaty of Institutionalization signed in Lima on 16 November 1987; permanent headquarters inaugurated in Panama City on 18 October 2013
description: Regional permanent unicameral inter-parliamentary assembly bringing together the national legislatures of Latin America and the Caribbean. Founded in Lima on 10 December 1964 by thirteen parliaments; institutionalized by the Treaty of Institutionalization ratified on 16 November 1987. Each member parliament sends twelve plenipotentiaries to the consultative assembly, which promotes democracy, integration, and human rights without supranational lawmaking power. Renamed Parlamento Latinoamericano y Caribeño in 2015.
notes: Thirteen parliaments founded PARLATINO at the Lima Constitutive Assembly (7–11 December 1964); Honduras joined in July 1965, Mexico and the Dominican Republic in December 1972, Cuba in June 1985, and Aruba and Suriname in August 1988. Bolivia and Ecuador are among the eighteen states that signed the 1987 institutionalization treaty. Curaçao and Sint Maarten represent the Dutch Caribbean after the 2010 dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles. The permanent headquarters in Panama City opened on 18 October 2013.

name: African Parliamentary Union
description: Continental interparliamentary organization bringing together national parliaments of Africa to promote democracy, peace, and parliamentary cooperation. Formerly the Union of African Parliaments.

name: Central American Parliament
recognition_status: Regional parliamentary organ of the Central American Integration System established by the Esquipulas II agreement; first formal session held on 28 October 1991 in Guatemala City
description: Regional parliamentary organ of the Central American Integration System (SICA), composed of 20 directly elected deputies from each member state plus ex officio former presidents and vice-presidents. Established by the Esquipulas II agreement; first formal session on 28 October 1991 in Guatemala City. Exercises political oversight and proposes integration legislation without supranational lawmaking power.
notes: Costa Rica signed the 1987 constitutive treaty but never ratified Esquipulas II and is not represented in PARLACEN despite participating in SICA. Panama ratified membership in 1994; a 2009 withdrawal law was declared unconstitutional and Panama returned in 2012. The Dominican Republic was an observer from 1996 and became a full member with elected delegates in 2010. El Salvador's Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional reform on 31 July 2025 to withdraw; the country will stop electing representatives starting with the 2027 legislative elections but remains a member until then.

name: Parliamentary Assembly of the Mediterranean
description: Inter-parliamentary organization established in 2005 by national parliaments of Euro-Mediterranean and Gulf countries, succeeding the Conference on Security and Cooperation in the Mediterranean (CSCM). Headquartered in San Marino (previously Malta), with additional offices in Naples. Comprises 31 member parliaments represented on equal footing, each with up to five delegates. Conducts regional parliamentary diplomacy through three standing committees and annual plenary sessions on political, economic, social, and human-rights issues. Holds UN observer status (General Assembly resolution A/RES/64/124, 2009) and permanent representations to LAS and UN agencies in Geneva, New York, and Vienna.
notes: Associate members include the Holy See and the Sovereign Order of Malta (neither modeled in includes — Order of Malta has no ISO country code). Partner states include Bahrain, Bulgaria, Georgia, Kuwait, Moldova, Saudi Arabia, Slovakia, Switzerland, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Observer states include Armenia and Azerbaijan. The Russian Federation is listed as a candidate member. Bahrain's parliament reported full membership in February 2025; PAM's published member list still classifies Bahrain among partner states as of mid-2026.

name: OACPS–EU Joint Parliamentary Assembly
description: Inter-parliamentary institution of the European Parliament and parliamentarians from Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States (OACPS) parties to the Samoa Agreement; successor to the ACP–EU Joint Parliamentary Assembly established under the Cotonou Agreement.
notes: Membership covers all 27 EU member states and 79 OACPS state parties to the EU–OACPS partnership. Cuba remains an OACPS member but does not participate because it is not party to the Cotonou or Samoa agreements. South Africa withdrew from the OACPS in September 2022.

The General Secretariat is permanently based in Baku. Hungary holds observer status. TURKPA holds annual plenary sessions (the first in Baku on 29 September 2009), maintains four permanent specialized commissions, and conducts election observation missions in member states. Inaugurated on 30 November 2001 in Arusha, Tanzania; membership follows EAC partner states.
notes: Each partner state nominates nine elected members. As of the Fifth Assembly (2022–2027), the body comprises 63 elected members plus nine ex-officio members. Burundi and Rwanda joined when they acceded to the EAC in 2009; South Sudan in 2016; the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2022; and Somalia in 2024.

name: Asia Pacific Parliamentary Forum
description: Regional inter-parliamentary forum established at the inaugural meeting in Tokyo on 13–15 January 1993, when delegates adopted the Tokyo Declaration as the founding charter. Initiated by former Japanese Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone, APPF brings together national parliament delegations from 28 member countries across Northeast Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania, and the Americas to discuss political, security, economic, social, and cultural issues of common concern. The forum meets annually with a rotating host parliament providing meeting logistics; decisions are taken by consensus. APPF maintains close working relations with APEC, ASEAN, and the Pacific Islands Forum but is an independent parliamentary body without legislative powers.
notes: Brunei Darussalam participated as an observer from the inaugural meeting in 1993 until granted full membership at the 29th Annual Meeting in Seoul in December 2021. APPF merged with the Asia-Pacific Parliamentary Leaders' Forum (APPLF) at the third Annual Meeting in Acapulco in 1995. A Meeting of Women Parliamentarians has been held on the occasion of each Annual Meeting since the Rules of Procedure were amended at the 26th Annual Meeting in Hanoi in 2018. Pacific Island and other national parliaments sometimes attend as observers and are not modeled as country includes.

recognition_status: Intergovernmental organization established by Saudi Arabia, Austria, and Spain under the 13 October 2011 Vienna establishment agreement; inaugurated on 27 November 2012 with endorsement from UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon
description: Intergovernmental organization founded by Saudi Arabia, Austria, and Spain to promote interreligious and intercultural dialogue, peacebuilding, and social cohesion worldwide. Established under a 13 October 2011 Vienna agreement and inaugurated on 27 November 2012; headquarters were in Vienna until relocation to Lisbon on 1 July 2022. Governed by a dual structure of a Council of Parties (member states) and a Board of Directors (representatives of major world religions); the Holy See participates as founding observer.
notes: Headquarters operated from Palais Sturany in Vienna from 2012 until relocation to Lisbon on 1 July 2022, following Austria's 2019 parliamentary motion to withdraw from the seat agreement. Portugal signed a new seat agreement in October 2021 and was invited to join the Council of Parties in November 2024. Programmes focus on Africa, the Arab region, Asia, and Europe, including the KAICIID Fellows Programme and partnerships with UNAOC, Religions for Peace, and the World Organization of the Scout Movement.

other_names.name: مركز الملك عبد الله بن عبد العزيز العالمي للحوار بين أتباع الأديان والثقافات
König-Abdullah-Zentrum für interreligiösen und interkulturellen Dialog

name: Dutch-speaking countries
recognition_status: Informal geographic and cultural concept (not a formal organization) describing territories where Dutch holds official status, commonly termed the Nederlands taalgebied (Dutch language area); anchored by the Dutch Language Union member states and the constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; distinct from the broader Afrikaans-speaking sphere in southern Africa
description: Cultural and linguistic region comprising sovereign states and Kingdom of the Netherlands constituent countries where Dutch is an official language. The core European states are the Netherlands and Belgium (where Dutch is co-official and dominant in Flanders); Suriname is the sole Dutch-official state in South America; Aruba, Caribbean Netherlands, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten complete the Caribbean component of the Kingdom. The concept aligns with the Nederlands taalgebied and the Dutch Language Union but excludes Afrikaans-official states such as South Africa and Namibia.
notes: This record reflects the seven Internacia country entities where Dutch is an official language (NL, BE, SR, AW, BQ, CW, SX). Belgium is included at country level because Dutch is nationwide co-official and the majority language in Flanders. South Africa and Namibia, where Afrikaans holds official status, are excluded because Afrikaans is treated as a separate language despite mutual intelligibility with Dutch. Broader definitions may add diaspora communities or Dutch-speaking minorities in France and Germany.

name: Community of Portuguese Language Countries
recognition_status: International organization and political association of Lusophone nations founded at the 1st CPLP Heads of State and Government Summit in Lisbon on 17 July 1996; nine member states and numerous associate observers participate in its multilateral cooperation forum

secretariat.head: Executive Secretary
secretariat.organization: Executive Secretariat of the Community of Portuguese Language Countries

description: Intergovernmental association of nine Lusophone member states across Africa, the Americas, Asia, and Europe. Founded at the 1st CPLP Heads of State and Government Summit in Lisbon on 17 July 1996, the CPLP promotes political and diplomatic cooperation, dissemination of the Portuguese language, and collaboration in education, health, science, culture, and other sectors. The Executive Secretariat is headquartered at Penafiel Palace in Lisbon.

other_names.name: Comunidad de Países de Lengua Portuguesa
communauté des pays de langue portugaise
Comunidade dos Países de Língua Portuguesa

notes: Governed by a biannual Conference of Heads of State and Government with an annual Council of Foreign Ministers and a Permanent Steering Committee. Timor-Leste joined in 2002 and Equatorial Guinea in 2014. The organization also maintains associate observer status for numerous countries and partner organizations.

name: Arab World
recognition_status: Informal geographic and cultural concept (not a formal organization) describing Arabic-speaking states mainly in West Asia and North Africa; the standard territorial definition comprises the 22 member states of the Arab League, though broader linguistic or diaspora-based definitions also exist in scholarship and policy discourse
description: Geographic and cultural region spanning West Asia and North Africa where Arabic is the lingua franca and shared Arab identity is a major political and cultural frame. At minimum the concept covers states where Arabs form a plurality; the standard territorial definition aligns with the 22 member states of the Arab League, stretching from the Atlantic to the Arabian Sea and divided conventionally into the Mashriq (east) and Maghreb (west).
notes: This record reflects the 22-state Arab League membership list (DZ, BH, KM, DJ, EG, IQ, JO, KW, LB, LY, MR, MA, OM, PS, QA, SA, SO, SD, SY, TN, AE, YE). Broader definitions may include Arabic-speaking minorities or diaspora communities; Chad, Eritrea, and Israel recognize Arabic officially but are not Arab League members and are excluded here. Malta, whose Maltese derives from Arabic, is likewise excluded.

name: Ibero-American Summits of Heads of State and Governments
recognition_status: Annual conference of heads of state and government from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries in Europe and the Americas, operating within the Organization of Ibero-American States (OEI); summit preparation and follow-up coordinated by the Ibero-American General Secretariat (SEGIB)
description: Annual intergovernmental conference of heads of state and government from 22 Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries in Europe and Latin America. Established at the first summit in Guadalajara, Mexico, in July 1991 within the Organization of Ibero-American States framework, it convenes yearly to coordinate political dialogue and adopt joint declarations on regional cooperation. Summit preparation and follow-up are supported by the Ibero-American General Secretariat (SEGIB) in Madrid.
notes: Andorra joined as a full member in 2004. Equatorial Guinea and the Philippines participate as associate members since 2009. Summits rotate among member countries; the 30th edition is scheduled for Spain in 2026.

other_names.name: 伊比利亚美洲首脑会议

name: Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
recognition_status: Specialized institution of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) concerned with education, science, culture, and communication; full OIC member states become ICESCO members upon signing the Charter and completing membership formalities

secretariat.head: Director-General
secretariat.organization: Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization

description: Specialized institution of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation headquartered in Rabat, Morocco, that strengthens cooperation among member states in education, science, culture, and communication across the Islamic world. Founded by the OIC in May 1979 and renamed the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO) in January 2020, it promotes dialogue among civilizations, preserves cultural identity, and supports the contribution of Islamic culture to world civilization through specialized centers, ministerial conferences, and programs spanning education, science and environment, social sciences, and culture and communication.

other_names.name: منظمة العالم الإسلامي للتربية والعلوم والثقافة
Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
Organisation du Monde Islamique pour l'Éducation, les Sciences et la Culture

notes: Renamed from Islamic Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ISESCO) to Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO) at the 40th Executive Council session in Abu Dhabi on 30 January 2020. Governed by a General Conference (every three years), an Executive Council, and a General Directorate headed by the Director-General. Operates specialized centers for translation and publishing, foresight and AI, civilizational dialogue, Arabic for non-Arabic speakers, chairs and prizes, and heritage in the Islamic world.

name: Dutch Language Union
recognition_status: Treaty-based intergovernmental institution governing Dutch language standardisation, established by the Netherlands and Belgium on 9 September 1980; Suriname joined as associate member in 2005; the treaty extends to Caribbean Netherlands since 2013; Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten cooperate under framework agreements; Indonesia and South Africa participate as special partners

secretariat.head: Secretary-General
secretariat.organization: Secretariat-General of the Dutch Language Union

description: Intergovernmental treaty organization for Dutch language policy, standardisation, and international education. Founded on 9 September 1980 by the Netherlands and Belgium (Flanders), it coordinates spelling reforms, publishes the Woordenlijst Nederlandse taal (Groene boekje), and supports Dutch teaching worldwide. Suriname became an associate member in 2005; the treaty extends to Caribbean Netherlands and framework agreements cover Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten.
notes: Governed by a Committee of Ministers (Dutch and Flemish education and culture ministers), an Interparliamentary Commission, a Council for Dutch Language and Literature, and a Secretariat-General with offices in The Hague and Brussels. Binational institutes include the Instituut voor de Nederlandse Taal in Leiden and the Royal Academy of Dutch Language and Literature in Belgium. Indonesia and South Africa participate as special partners. Administers the Prijs der Nederlandse Letteren and Toneelschrijfprijs.

name: Portuguese-speaking African countries
recognition_status: Informal cultural and linguistic grouping (with a formalized 1992 interstate cooperation framework among the five founding Portuguese-speaking African states) describing African countries where Portuguese is an official language; Equatorial Guinea was traditionally excluded from the PALOP acronym but is now commonly included in the expanded six-country Lusophone Africa definition after adopting Portuguese in 2011 and joining CPLP and FORPALOP in 2014
description: Cultural and linguistic grouping of six African countries where Portuguese is an official language — Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Equatorial Guinea (which adopted Portuguese in 2011). The five former Portuguese colonies formed the interstate PALOP cooperation framework in 1992; Equatorial Guinea, a former Spanish colony, joined the broader Lusophone African community through CPLP membership in 2014 and FORPALOP in 2014. PALOP countries cooperate on culture, education, and language preservation with Portugal, the European Union, and the United Nations.
notes: This record reflects six Internacia country entities where Portuguese is an official language in Africa (AO, CV, GW, MZ, ST, GQ). The five founding members (PALOP-5) established interstate cooperation in 1992; Equatorial Guinea adopted Portuguese as its third official language in October 2011 to facilitate CPLP accession (2014) and subsequently joined the FORPALOP political-diplomatic forum. Portuguese use in Equatorial Guinea remains limited. All six are members of CPLP alongside Portugal, Brazil, and Timor-Leste. Distinct from broader Lusophone definitions that include Portugal, Brazil, or Timor-Leste.

other_names.name: Países Africanos de Lengua Oficial Portuguesa
Países Africanos de Língua Oficial Portuguesa

name: Intergovernmental Foundation for Educational, Scientific and Cultural Cooperation
recognition_status: Intergovernmental non-profit organization established under the 25 May 2006 treaty signed at the CIS Council of Heads of Governments meeting in Dushanbe; operates in coordination with the Council for Humanitarian Cooperation of CIS Member States

secretariat.head: Executive Director
secretariat.organization: Intergovernmental Foundation for Educational, Scientific and Cultural Cooperation

description: Intergovernmental non-profit foundation of the Commonwealth of Independent States, headquartered in Moscow and established on 25 May 2006 in Dushanbe. Finances and supports joint humanitarian projects in education, science, culture, archives, information, sport, tourism, and youth affairs across CIS member states. Works with the CIS Council for Humanitarian Cooperation and has signed memoranda of understanding with CIS bodies, TURKSOY, and UNESCO.
notes: Seven states founded the fund in 2006; Azerbaijan joined in 2008 and Moldova in 2014. The Management Board is the highest governing body, chaired on a two-year rotating basis. Since 2007 the fund has supported more than one thousand multilateral projects, including the CIS Cultural Capital initiative. Activities are funded through member-state contributions and competitive project grants approved in annual plans.

other_names.name: Intergovernmental Foundation for Educational, Scientific and Cultural Cooperation
